(p-2) Surat al-Ma'idah is Medinan and has one hundred and twenty verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who have believed, fulfill the contracts.﴾ Al-wafa' (fulfillment) is carrying out the requirement of a contract, and likewise al-iifa'. Al-'aqd (contract) is a firm covenant, likened to the tying of a rope or the like. What is meant by "al-'uqud" (the contracts) is that which encompasses everything Allah the Exalted has obligated His servants to, and has bound upon them of religious duties and rulings, as well as what they bind among themselves of trusts, transactions and the like, which must be fulfilled, or which is good in religion, by interpreting the command in a sense that covers both obligation and recommendation. They were first commanded to this in general terms, and then began to detail the rulings that they were commanded to fulfill, starting with what relates to the necessities of their livelihood.

Then it is said: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle.﴾ Al-bahimah (beast) is every four-footed creature, and its being attributed to al-an'am (cattle) is for specification, like "a garment of silk," and its being singular is to intend the genus. That is: the eating of the beast of the cattle has been made lawful for you, and these are the eight pairs mentioned in Surat al-An'am. To them are added gazelles, wild cattle, and the like.

It is also said: the beast here is intended by the "beast" because the explanation of the lawfulness of cattle has preceded, and the attribution is due to the resemblance and similarity between them in chewing the cud and lacking fangs. Its benefit is to indicate the effective cause of the ruling, shared between the two attributed items, as if it were said: Lawful for you is the beast resembling cattle, whose lawfulness was explained earlier, equal to them in the basis of the ruling. The placing of the prepositional phrase before what stands in place of the subject is, as has been repeatedly mentioned, to show concern for what is placed first, since it brings forward delight and creates anticipation for what is delayed; when what should be first is delayed, the soul remains expectant of its arrival, and so it settles in with greater firmness.

﴿Except what is recited to you.﴾ This is an exception from "beast of cattle"; that is: except the forbidden [portion] of what is recited to you from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ and the like; or ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ is the verse of its prohibition.

﴿Not allowing hunting﴾; that is: hunting on land or eating its game. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "lakum" (for you). The meaning of their not making it lawful is affirming its prohibition in practice and belief, and this is common in the Book and the Sunnah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿while you are in a state of ihram﴾; that is: while you are in the state of ihram. It is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "muhilli" (allowing). The benefit of restricting the lawfulness of the beasts of cattle by what has been mentioned, namely that the game is not made lawful while in ihram, on the assumption that what is meant by them is gazelles and the like, is evident, since its lawfulness is not absolute. As if it were said: Lawful for you is game while you are abstaining from it at the time of your ihram. As for the first assumption, its benefit is completing the blessing and displaying favor by making them lawful, by reminding them of their need for it, since the prohibition of game during ihram is among the occasions of their need for the lawfulness of other things at that time. As if it were said: Lawful for you are cattle absolutely, while you are abstaining from obtaining what would suffice you from them at certain times, and in need of their lawfulness.

In attributing the non-allowance to them in the sense mentioned, although the purpose could be achieved by saying "not made lawful for you" or "game is forbidden to you while in ihram," there is added emphasis on favor and a confirmation of need by explaining its nearer cause: the prohibition of game for them necessitates their need for the lawfulness of what suffices them in its place, with respect to their prohibiting it for themselves in practice and belief, together with what this involves of describing them with what is befitting to them.

﴿Indeed, Allah decrees what He wills﴾ of rulings, according as His will requires, which is founded upon profound wisdoms; so there enter into it what has been mentioned of permission and prohibition, entering it primarily. The meaning of fulfilling both of them is conforming to their requirements in contract and in action, and abstaining from making unlawful what is lawful and from forbidding some of what is permitted, such as the bahirah and its like, whose explanation will come.

﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the sacred rites of Allah﴾. When He had stated the prohibition of violating the state of ihram (the sacred state entered for pilgrimage), which is one of the rites of Hajj, He followed it with a statement of the prohibition of violating all the other rites. He attributed them to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to honor them and to emphasize the gravity of violating them. The word is the plural of sha'irah (rite), which is a name for that which has been marked (ushʿira), i.e., made a sign and a token of the act of worship, such as the stations (mawaqit) of Hajj, the places where the pebbles are thrown (marami al-jimar), the Tawaf (circumambulation), the Sa'y (running between Safa and Marwah), and the acts that are the marks of the pilgrim by which he is recognized: the ihram, the Tawaf, the Sa'y, the shaving (halq) and the sacrifice (nahr). Violating them means treating their sanctity lightly, and preventing those who perform these rites from performing them, and causing, during the months of Hajj, something by which people are turned away from Hajj. It has been said that what is meant by them is the religion of Allah, based on His saying: ﴿And whoever honors the sacred rites of Allah﴾, meaning His religion. It has also been said that they are the sacred prohibitions of Allah, and it has been said that they are His obligations which He set for His servants. Violating them means failing to observe them. The first interpretation is more appropriate to the context.

﴿Nor the sacred month﴾, meaning: do not violate it by fighting in it. It has been said: by postponing it (al-nasi’). The first is the more fitting for the condition of the believers. What is meant by it is the month of Hajj. It has been said that it refers to the four sacred months, and the singular is used to denote the category.

﴿Nor the sacrificial animals (al-hadi)﴾, by being seized by force, or by being prevented from reaching their place of sacrifice. The hadi is what is sent as an offering to the Ka'bah of camels, cattle, or sheep. It is the plural of hadiyyah, like jadi and jadiyyah.

﴿Nor the garlands (al-qala’id)﴾. The qala'id is the plural of qiladah, which is what is hung around the neck of the hadi of sandals or tree bark, so that it may be known that it is a hadi and is not to be molested. What is meant is the prohibition of molesting the garlanded animals of the hadi, which are the camels (budn). Its being joined to the hadi, although it is included in it, is for the sake of extra emphasis on them, because of their distinction over the others, just as Gabriel and Michael are joined to the angels (peace be upon them), as if it were said: "and the garlanded ones among them in particular." Or the prohibition is against molesting the garlands themselves, as an intensification of the prohibition against molesting their owners, meaning: do not violate their garlands, let alone violate them, just as He forbade displaying adornment in His saying: ﴿And let them not display their adornment﴾, as an intensification of the prohibition against displaying its places.

﴿Nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾, meaning: do not violate a people intending to visit it by preventing them from that in any manner whatsoever. It has been said that there is an omitted genitive: meaning, the fighting against a people, or harming a people who are coming... etc. It was read: "wa la amme al-bayt al-haram" (nor those coming to the Sacred House) with the genitive construction.

His saying, ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and good pleasure﴾, is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in āmmīn, not an adjective of it, because the preferred view is that when the active participle is described, its government (ʿamal) is annulled. Meaning: intending to visit it while seeking that Allah reward them and be pleased with them. The indefiniteness of fadlan and ridwanan is for magnification. The phrase min rabbihim is related either to the verb itself, or to a deleted element that functions as an adjective of fadlan, replacing the description of what is conjoined to it: meaning, bounty existing from their Lord and good pleasure likewise. Mentioning the title of Lordship together with the pronoun referring to them is for honoring them and for hinting at the attainment of what they seek. It was read as "tabtaghūna" (you seek) in the second person, in which case the clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the addressees in "la tuhillū", with the purpose being to show the incompatibility of their state with the forbidden act, not to restrict the prohibition by it.

The attribution of the Lord to the pronoun of those coming is to hint at the restriction of honor to them, and the deprivation of the addressees from it and from attaining the sought-after; and in that there is, as is not hidden, a rationale for the prohibition and its emphasis, and an intensification of the reprehensibility of what is forbidden. From here it was said that what is meant by "those coming" are the Muslims only, and by this those who hold that the verse is muhkam (decisive, not abrogated) have held. It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Surat al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, so make lawful its lawful and make unlawful its unlawful." Al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "There is no abrogated (mansukh) ruling in it." And from Abu Maysarah: "In it are eighteen obligations, and there is no abrogated ruling in it." It has also been said: they are only the polytheists, because they are the ones who need the prohibition against the believers' violating them, not the believers, on the basis that the prohibition of violating them is established by way of the indication of the text (dalalat al-nass). And this is supported by the fact that the verse was revealed concerning al-Hutam ibn Dabi'ah al-Bakri, who had come to Madinah and left his horses outside it, then entered upon the Prophet ﷺ alone and promised him that he would bring his companions so that they might embrace Islam. Then he left from his presence, peace be upon him, and passed by the grazing herds of Madinah and drove them off. When the following year came, he set out from al-Yamamah as a pilgrim among the pilgrims of Bakr ibn Wa'il, with him great merchandise, and they had garlanded the hadi. The Muslims asked the Prophet ﷺ to leave them free to deal with him, but the Prophet ﷺ refused, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the sacred rites of Allah﴾, to the end of the verse.

The seeking of bounty was interpreted as seeking provision through trade, and the seeking of good pleasure as their supposing that they were upon rectitude in their religion, and that Hajj brings them closer to Allah, Exalted. So Allah described them by their supposition. And that corrupt supposition, although it is far from entailing His good pleasure, yet there is no remoteness in its being a means to the attainment of some of their worldly aims and their deliverance from immediate hardships, especially within the observance of the rights of Allah and the honoring of His rites. Qatadah said: "It means that He sets right their livelihoods in this world and does not hasten punishment for them in it." It has also been said: they are the Muslims and the polytheists, on the basis of what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father): that the Muslims and the polytheists used to perform Hajj together, so Allah forbade the Muslims from preventing anyone from visiting the House, by His saying: ﴿Do not violate﴾, to the end of the verse. Then after that there was revealed: ﴿The polytheists are indeed unclean, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque﴾, and His saying: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾.

Mujahid and al-Sha'bi said: "Do not violate" was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾. There is no doubt that the word "those coming" includes the polytheists definitively, either independently or jointly, based on His saying that will come: "And let not the hatred of a people...", to the end of the verse. So abrogation is required, in whole or in part.

In the last view, the interpretation of "bounty" and "good pleasure" must suit both groups. It was said: the seeking of bounty, i.e., provision, for believers and polytheists in general, and the seeking of good pleasure for believers in particular. It is permissible for "bounty" to be taken in its general sense, including the bounty of the Hereafter as well, and its seeking is then restricted to believers.

﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾. This is an explicit statement of what was indicated by His saying: ﴿while you are in ihram﴾, that the prohibition of hunting ends with the absence of its cause. The command is for permissibility after prohibition, as if it were said: "And when you have come out of ihram, then there is no blame upon you in hunting." It was read as "ahlaltum" (you have come out), which is a dialect of "halla". It was also read with a kasra on the fa', by transferring the vowel of the hamzat al-wasl onto it, and this is (very weak).

﴿And let not hatred of a people drive you﴾. This is a prohibition against violating a group of those coming, singled out for it, while being included in the prohibition against violating all of them generally, because of their independence in matters which may be thought to be justifications for their violation and motivations toward it. Jarama functions in meaning like kasaba (to earn), and in transitivity to one object and to two, it is said: jarama dhanban (he committed a sin), like kasabahu, and jarramtuhu dhanban (I made him commit a sin), like kassabtuhu iyyah. Except that jarama is used mostly for earning what has no good in it, and this is the reason for choosing it here over the second. The first may be transferred from each of them with the hamzah to the meaning of the second, so it is said: ajramtuhu dhanban and akhsabtuhu iyyah. Upon this is the reading of the one who read: "yujrimannakum" with a damma on the ya'.

﴿The hatred of a people﴾, with a fatha on the nun, and it was read with a sukun on it; both are verbal nouns (masdar) which are annexed to their object, not to their subject as it has been said, and it means the intensity of hatred and the utmost of abhorrence.

﴿That they barred you﴾ is related to "shana'an" (hatred) by the implied preposition of causation (lam al-‘illah), meaning: because they barred you in the year of Hudaybiyyah.

﴿From the Sacred Mosque﴾: from visiting it and circumambulating it for 'Umrah. This is a clear verse concerning the definite inclusion of polytheists under "those coming". It was read "an sadduukum" (that they barred you) as a conditional clause interposed, whose answer is dispensed with by "la yajrimannakum", having brought forth the actual barring which had occurred in the matter of the presumed, for the sake of rebuke and alerting that its occurrence should only be on the basis of supposition and assumption.

﴿That you transgress﴾, meaning: against them. It was omitted because it is understood from the context, and as a hint that the primary aim of the prohibition is to prevent the transgression from proceeding from the addressees, in order to protect the honoring of the rites, not to prevent it from falling on the people out of consideration for them. It is the second object of "yajrimannakum", meaning: let not the intensity of your hatred for them earn you transgression against them, and the taking of vengeance upon them for the sake of satisfaction because of their barring you from the Sacred Mosque. And although this is, by apparent meaning, a prohibition of hatred from earning transgression for the addressees, in reality it is a prohibition to them from transgression in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, for the prohibition of the causes of a thing and its precursors which lead to it is a prohibition against it by way of demonstrative argument, and a nullification of its causal relation. The prohibition may be directed at the effect while what is meant is the prohibition of the cause, as in his saying: "I should not see you here," meaning by it: forbidding his interlocutor from being present before him. Perhaps the delay of this prohibition after His saying: "And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt", despite the clear connection to what precedes, is to announce that the sanctity of transgression does not end with leaving the state of ihram, as the sanctity of hunting ends with it, but rather it remains as long as their connection with the rites has not been cut off completely; and by this it is known that the sanctity of molesting the rest of those coming remains by a fortiori reasoning.

﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾. Since transgression is generally by way of mutual support and cooperation, they were commanded, after what they had been forbidden, to cooperate in everything that falls under righteousness and piety, and in following command and avoiding desire. So included in it is what we are concerned with, namely cooperation in pardon and overlooking what has occurred from them, as a primary inclusion. Then they were forbidden from cooperating in everything that belongs to the category of wrongdoing and sins, by His saying: ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾. So included in it is the prohibition of cooperating in transgression and retaliation by way of demonstrative argument. The original form of "la ta'awanu" is "la tata'awanu", so one of the two tas was deleted for lightness. The prohibition was placed after the command despite the precedence of the negative (takhliyah, clearing away) over the positive (tahliyah, adorning), in haste to make obligatory what is the intended aim in itself, for the intended purpose of obligating the abandonment of cooperation in sin and aggression is only the achieving of cooperation in righteousness and piety.

Then they were commanded by His saying: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, by being mindful of Him in all matters, of which among them is violating the commands and prohibitions mentioned, so the obligation of being mindful in them is established by way of demonstrative argument.

Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾, meaning: for whoever does not fear Him, so He will certainly punish you if you do not fear Him. The manifestation of the glorious Name, for what has passed many times, is for bringing awe, cultivating reverence, and strengthening the independence of the clause.(p-6)

**Forbidden to you is carrion** (﴿حُرِّمَتْ عَلَيْكُمُ المَيْتَةُ﴾). This begins the explanation of the prohibited things that were alluded to in His words: "﴿except what is recited to you﴾". *Carrion* (al-maytah) is that from which the soul has departed without slaughter (dhabh).

**And blood** (﴿والدَّمُ﴾); that is, flowing blood (al-masfuh), in accordance with His words: "﴿or blood poured forth﴾". The people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era) used to pour it into the intestines and roast them, and they would say: "What is let (blood) from a person (fuzid) is not forbidden"; that is, from one who was bled (fusid lahu).

**And the flesh of swine, and that over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked** (﴿وَلَحْمُ الخِنْزِيرِ وما أُهِلَّ لِغَيْرِ اللَّهِ بِهِ﴾); that is, the voice was raised for other than Allah at the time of its slaughter, as when they say: "In the name of al-Lat and al-'Uzza."

**And the strangled** (﴿والمُنْخَنِقَةُ﴾); that is, that which died by strangling.

**And the beaten to death** (﴿والمَوْقُوذَةُ﴾); that is, that which was killed by being struck with wood or the like, from *waqadtuhu*, meaning when you strike him.

**And the fallen** (﴿والمُتَرَدِّيَةُ﴾); that is, that which fell from a height, or into a well, and died.

**And the gored** (﴿والنَّطِيحَةُ﴾); that is, that which another animal gored and it died from the goring. The *ta'* (in the word) is for transference (al-naql, i.e., it marks the noun as transferred from adjective to noun). It has also been read as *al-manṭūḥah*.

**And what the beast of prey has eaten** (﴿وَما أكَلَ السَّبُعُ﴾); that is, what the beast of prey ate of, so that it died. It has been read with a sukun on the *bā'* (*al-sab'*), and read as *wa-akīl al-sab'*. In this there is evidence that if hunting animals (jawāri al-ṣayd) eat from what they have caught, it is not lawful.

**Except what you have slaughtered** (﴿إلا ما ذَكَّيْتُمْ﴾); except what you reached in time to slaughter (dhakāh), and in it there remains a residue of life, so that it convulses like a slaughtered animal. It has been said: the exception is specific to what the beast of prey has eaten. In the Shari'ah, *dhakāh* is by cutting the windpipe (ḥulqūm) and the gullet (marī') with a sharp instrument.

**And what is sacrificed on the stones (nuṣub)** (﴿وَما ذُبِحَ عَلى النُّصُبِ﴾). It has been said: *nuṣub* is singular. It has been said: it is the plural of *niṣāb*. It has been read with a sukun on the ṣād. Whatever the case, it is the singular of *al-anṣāb*, and these are stones that were set up around the House (the Ka'bah), upon which they would slaughter, and they considered that an act of worship (qurbah). It has been said: they are the idols.

**And that you seek decision by the arrows** (﴿وَأنْ تَسْتَقْسِمُوا بِالأزْلامِ﴾). *Azlām* is the plural of *zalam*, which is the arrow-shaft; that is, seeking decision by arrow-shafts is forbidden to you. This is because when they intended to do something, they would strike three arrow-shafts, one of which was inscribed: "My Lord commands me," and the second: "My Lord forbids me," and the third was blank. If the one commanding came out, they proceeded with that; if the one forbidding came out, they refrained from it; and if the blank came out, they cast them again a second time. So the meaning of *istiqsām* is seeking knowledge of what has been apportioned to them by the arrows. It has been said: it is the apportioning of a slaughtered camel by the arrow-shafts upon the known portions.

**That** (﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾) is a reference to seeking decision by the arrows, and the sense of distance in it serves to indicate the remoteness of its rank in evil.

**Is grave sin** (﴿فِسْقٌ﴾): rebellion and going beyond the limit, and entering into knowledge of the Unseen, and misguidance by the belief that it is a path to it, and slander against Allah, glorified is He, if by their words "my Lord" what is meant is Allah; and polytheism (shirk) and ignorance, if what is meant is the idol. It has been said: "That" refers to the partaking of the forbidden things enumerated, because the meaning of their prohibition is the prohibition of partaking of them.

**Today** (﴿اليَوْمَ﴾): the *al-* here is for a known reference (al-'ahd), and what is meant by it is the present time and what is connected to it of past and future times. It has been said: it is the day of its revelation. It was revealed after the 'Asr prayer on the day of Jumu'ah, on the Day of 'Arafah, in the Farewell Pilgrimage, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was standing at 'Arafat upon al-'Ḍaba' (his she-camel), and the camel's shoulder nearly broke from its weight, so it knelt down. Whatever the case, it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), governing His words: "﴿Those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾"; that is, of its abolition and your returning from it by permitting these abominations or others, or of their overcoming you in it, because they witnessed that Allah, mighty and majestic, fulfilled His promise when He made it prevail over all religions. This is most suitable with His words: "﴿So do not fear them﴾"; that is, lest they prevail over you.

**And fear Me** (﴿واخْشَوْنِ﴾); that is, devote your fear sincerely to Me.

**Today I have perfected for you your religion** (﴿اليَوْمَ أكْمَلْتُ لَكم دِينَكُمْ﴾): by victory and by making it prevail over all religions, or by the explicit statement of the foundations of the beliefs and the affirmation of the principles of the laws and the rules of independent reasoning (ijtihad). The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa-al-majrūr) is to announce from the outset that the perfecting is for their benefit and welfare, as in His words: "﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾"

"**For you**" (*'alaykum*) in His words: "﴿and I have completed My favor upon you﴾" is connected to *atmamtu* (I have completed), not to *ni'mati* (My favor), because the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) cannot have its complement (*ma'mūl*) preceding it. Its fronting over the explicit object (*maf'ūl ṣarīḥ*) is for what has passed many times; that is: I have completed it by the conquest of Makkah and their entering it safe and triumphant, and the demolition of the landmarks of the Jahiliyyah and its rites, and the prohibition of the polytheist's pilgrimage and the naked circumambulation of the House. Or it means by the completion of the religion and the laws, or by guidance and success. It has been said: the meaning of "﴿and I have completed My favor upon you﴾" is: I have fulfilled for you My promise by My saying: "﴿and that I may complete My favor upon you﴾."

**And I have approved for you Islam as a religion** (﴿وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ الإسْلامَ دِينًا﴾); that is, I have chosen it for you from among the religions, and it is the religion with Allah, and no other. From 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man from the Jews said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, there is a verse in your Book that you recite; if it had been revealed to us, the Jewish community, we would have taken that day as a festival." He said: "Which verse?" He said: "﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you﴾, the verse." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We know that day and the place where it was revealed upon the Prophet (ﷺ), when he was standing at 'Arafah on the day of Jumu'ah." He, may Allah be pleased with him, indicated that this day is a festival for us.

It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, wept. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What makes you weep, O 'Umar?" He said: "It made me weep that we were in an increase of our religion, but now it has been completed, and nothing that is completed fails to decline." He, peace be upon him, said: "You have spoken truly." So this verse was the announcement of the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he did not remain after that except eighty-one days.

**Whoever is compelled** (﴿فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ﴾) is connected to the mention of the forbidden things, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tirāḍ) with what necessitates that it be avoided, namely that partaking of them is grave sin, and their prohibition is part of the religion, and the complete blessing, and the approved Islam. That is: whoever is compelled to partake of any of these forbidden things.

**In a state of severe hunger** (﴿فِي مَخْمَصَةٍ﴾); that is, in famine, in which he fears death or its onset.

**Not inclining toward sin** (﴿غَيْرَ مُتَجانِفٍ لإثْمٍ﴾). It has been said: not leaning or deviating toward it, by eating it for pleasure, or exceeding the limit of the concession, or snatching it from another compelled person, as in His words: "﴿neither desiring nor transgressing﴾."

**Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful** (﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾): He does not call him to account for that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 4:

﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them.﴾ This begins the detailing of the lawful things, some of which were mentioned in summary form right after the explanation of the prohibited things, as if they had asked about them when their opposites were being explained. Because the question contains the sense of saying, the phrase is treated as the object of the verb: "ma" is the subject (mubtada'), and "uhilla lahum" (it has been made lawful for them) is its predicate. The third-person pronoun refers back to them because "yas'alūna" is in the third-person form; just as the reported speech of the one quoted is taken into account (as in saying "Zayd swore, 'I will certainly do it'"), so too the speaker's own situation is taken into account (as in saying "Zayd swore that he would certainly do it"). The thing asked about is the foods that have been made lawful for them.

﴿Say: What is good has been made lawful for you;﴾ that is, whatever sound natures do not find repugnant or recoil from, as in His saying, ﴿and He makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the foul things﴾.

﴿And what you have taught from the hunting beasts and birds﴾ is a conjunction with "al-tayyibāt" (the good things), with the omission of a modifier (that is, "the game of"), where "ma" is a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun is omitted; that is: "and the game of what you have taught them." Or it is a subject (mubtada') where "ma" is a conditional particle, and the answer of the condition is "then eat." It has also been permitted that it be a subject with "ma" as a relative pronoun, with the predicate being "eat," and the fa' entered because the relative pronoun is being likened to the conditional noun. "Min al-jawāriḥ" (from the hunting animals) is a circumstantial phrase either from the relative pronoun or its omitted pronoun. "Al-jawāriḥ" means the predatory animals among beasts and birds. It has been said that they were named so because they usually wound (jarh) the game.

﴿Trained as hunters (mukallibīn)﴾ means teaching them to hunt. The "mukallib" is the one who disciplines the hunting animals and trains them to hunt; the word is derived from "kalb" (dog), because discipline often takes place with it, or because every predator is called a "kalb." This is due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ concerning 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab when he wished to travel to Syria: "O God, set upon him one of Your dogs," and then a lion devoured him. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial phrase from the subject of "'allamtum" (you taught), and its purpose is to emphasize the teaching, since the term "mukallab" applies only to one who is trained in its knowledge. It has been read "mukhlibīn" with lightening, and the meaning is the same.

﴿You teach them﴾ is a second circumstantial phrase from it, or a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in "mukallibīn," or a resumptive statement.

﴿From what God has taught you﴾ of the stratagems and methods of teaching and training, for knowledge of it is an inspiration from God Most High, or it is acquired through reason, which is a gift from Him; or [it means] from what He has made you aware you should teach them: following the game by sending forth its owner, returning when he calls it back, desisting when he calls it off, holding the game for him, and not eating from it.

﴿So eat of what they hold for you﴾ It has been mentioned earlier that this sentence, if "ma" is a conditional particle, is the answer of the condition; and if "ma" is a relative pronoun in the nominative as subject, it is its predicate. As for if it is a conjunction with "al-tayyibāt," it is a clause branching off from the explanation of the lawfulness of the game of trained hunting animals, clarifying the omitted modifier which is the conjoined term, and through which the permission actually applies; and it points to the result and effect of teaching, falling under the command. So the "fa'" in it is like in the saying:

"I commanded you to do good, so do what you were commanded."

"Min" (of) is partitive, since some parts are not something that eating applies to, such as hides, bones, feathers and other things. "Mimmā" is a relative pronoun, or a qualifying noun whose returning pronoun is omitted, and "'alā" is connected to "amsakna" (they held); that is: eat some of what they held for you, which is what they did not eat from. As for what they ate from, it is what they held for themselves, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to 'Adi ibn Hatim: "If it eats from it, do not eat, for it held only for itself." Most jurists followed this view. Some said that non-eating is not a condition for birds of prey, since training them to this degree is impossible. Others said that this is not a condition at all; it has been narrated from Salman, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with them all, that if the dog ate two-thirds of it and one-third remained, and you have mentioned God's name over it, then eat.

﴿And mention the name of God over it﴾ The pronoun refers to "what you have taught"; that is, invoke God's name over it when you send it forth, or to "what they have held"; that is, invoke God's name over it when you reach its slaughter.

﴿And fear God﴾ regarding His prohibitions.

﴿Indeed God is swift in reckoning﴾ that is, swift in bringing His reckoning, or swift in completing it: once He begins, it is completed in the shortest possible time. The meaning under both interpretations is that He will swiftly call you to account for everything, great and small. The placing of the noble Name in place of the pronoun serves to cultivate awe and to give the reason for the ruling.

(p-9) ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾. It is said that by "the days" (ayyam, in ﴿al-ayyam al-thalatha﴾, "the three days") is meant one single time; the phrase was repeated for emphasis, and because of the differing events that occurred in it, its repetition is fine. The meaning of "the good things" (al-tayyibat) is as already mentioned.

﴿And the food of those who were given the Book﴾; that is, the Jews and the Christians. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) made an exception for the Christians of Banu Taghlib, saying: "They are not upon Christianity; they took from it nothing but drinking wine." Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) also held this view. By "their food" is meant whatever includes their slaughtered animals and other things.

﴿is lawful for you﴾; that is, permissible. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that he was asked about the slaughtered animals of the Arab Christians, and he said: "There is no harm in it." This is also the view of the majority of the Followers (tabi'un), and Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) and his companions adopted it. According to him, the ruling on the Sabians is the ruling on the People of the Book. His two companions said: they are two categories: one category reads the Psalms (Zabur) and worships the angels (upon them be peace), and another category does not read any book and worships the stars; these are not among the People of the Book. As for the Magians (majus), the Prophet (ﷺ) set for them the sunnah of the People of the Book in regard to taking the jizya from them, but not in eating their slaughtered animals or marrying their women, due to his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book, except that you may not marry their women nor eat their slaughtered animals."

﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾; so there is no fault upon you in feeding them and selling it to them. Had it been forbidden to them, that would not be permissible. ﴿And the chaste women from among the believers﴾ is in the nominative case, as a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) has been omitted, because of what preceded it, meaning: they are lawful for you too. By "them" is meant free, chaste women. Their being singled out for mention is for encouragement toward what is better, not to negate what lies beyond them; for the marriage of believing slave-women is valid by consensus, and likewise the marriage of unchaste women among them. As for the Kitabi slave-women, they are like the Muslim women according to Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him), contrary to al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him).

﴿And the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾; that is, they too are lawful for you, even if they are from the people at war (harbi). Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: the women of the warring people are not lawful.

﴿When you have given them their wages﴾; that is, their dowries (muhur). Restricting the permissibility to giving them is to emphasize its obligation and to urge what is better. It is also said: by giving them is meant committing to them. "Idha" (when) is adverbial, its operator being the omitted verb "halla" (became lawful). It is also said: it is conditional, its answer omitted; that is: when you give them their wages, they become lawful for you.

﴿Chaste, not fornicating﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of the subject of ﴿ātaytumūhunna﴾; that is, while you are chaste through marriage. Likewise His statement ﴿not fornicating﴾. It is also said that it is a ḥāl of the pronoun in "muḥṣinīn"; it is also said that it is an attribute of "muḥṣinīn"; that is, not openly committing adultery.

﴿Nor taking secret lovers﴾; that is, nor keeping them secretly. The khidn (secret companion) is a friend, applied to both male and female. It is either in the genitive case, conjoined to "musafiḥīn", with "lā" added to emphasize the negation implied by "ghayr"; or it is in the accusative, conjoined to "ghayra musafiḥīn", considering its three aspects.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith﴾; that is, whoever denies the laws of Islam, of which what is set out here regarding the rulings on what is lawful and unlawful is a part, and refuses to accept them.

﴿His deeds are null﴾: the righteous deeds he did before that.

﴿And in the Hereafter he will be among the losers﴾. Here "huwa" is a mubtada' and "min al-khasirin" is its khabar; the prepositional phrase "fi" is connected to whatever the predicate connects to, namely the general sense of existence. It is also said it is connected to an omitted element indicated by what is mentioned, that is: "losing in the Hereafter." It is also said it is connected to "al-khasirin", with "al" being definite rather than relative, because what follows the relative particle cannot govern what precedes it. It is also said that adverbs admit what other words do not, as in the verse:

I raised him until he became a grown man (tamaʿdada),
so my reward became that I be beaten with a stick.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 6:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ This begins the explanation of the laws concerning their religion, after the explanation of what concerns their worldly affairs.

﴿When you rise to prayer﴾; that is, when you intend to rise to it, as in His saying, ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾. He expressed the intention of the act by the act that results from it, metaphorically, for brevity and to draw attention to the fact that whoever intends prayer should hasten to it, such that he is never separated from the intention to perform it. Or it means: when you intend prayer, using the name of one of its two necessary concomitants for the other necessary concomitant. The apparent meaning of the noble verse requires ablution for everyone who rises to prayer, even if he is not in a state of ritual impurity, since the imperative denotes obligation definitively, and the consensus is against that. It has been narrated that "the Prophet ﷺ prayed the five prayers on the day of the Conquest with one ablution, and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: 'You have done something you did not used to do.' He ﷺ said: 'I did it deliberately, O 'Umar,'" meaning: as an explanation of permissibility. Taking the imperative, with respect to one who is not in a state of impurity, to mean recommendation has no justification. The correct view is that the address is specific to those in a state of impurity, by the indication of the circumstance, and by the condition of impurity in tayammum, which is its substitute. As for what is reported of the Prophet ﷺ and the caliphs, that they used to perform ablution for every prayer, there is no proof in it that they did so as an obligation at all. How could it be otherwise, when what is reported from him, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "Whoever performs ablution while already in a state of purity, Allah writes for him ten good deeds," is explicit that this was done by them as a recommendation? As for what is said, that this was at the beginning of the matter and then abrogated, his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, refutes it: "Surat al-Ma'ida is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, so make lawful its lawful and make unlawful its unlawful."

﴿so wash your faces﴾; that is, pass water over them. There is no need for rubbing, contrary to Malik.

﴿and your hands up to the elbows﴾. The majority hold that the two elbows are included in what is washed, and for this reason it has been said that "ila" (up to) here means "ma'a" (with), as in His saying, ﴿and He will add strength to your strength﴾. It has also been said that "ila" only conveys the sense of a limit in general, and as for whether what follows it is included in the ruling or excluded from it, it has no indication of this in itself; rather it is a matter that depends on external evidence, as in: "I memorized the Qur'an from its beginning to its end," and His saying, ﴿then [grant him] postponement until a time of ease﴾; for inclusion in the first and exclusion in the second is certain on the basis of the existence of evidence. Since that is not established in the verse, and the hands do cover the elbows, it is ruled that they are included, as a precaution. It has also been said that "ila," in terms of conveying a limit, requires its exclusion; but since the limit is not distinguished here from that which is limited, it is obligatory to include it, as a precaution.

﴿and wipe your heads﴾. The "ba'" is extra (ziyada), though it has been said that it is for partiality (tab'id), since it is what distinguishes between your saying "I wiped the handkerchief" and "I wiped with the handkerchief." Its realization is that it indicates the verb is imbued with the meaning of adhesion, as if it were said: "and make the wiping adhere to your heads." That does not require covering the whole, as would be required if it were said: "and wipe your heads," for it is like His saying, ﴿so wash your faces﴾.

The scholars differed concerning the required amount. Al-Shafi'i required the least that the term applies to, taking the certain. Abu Hanifa, by the explanation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in that he wiped over his forelock and estimated it at a quarter of the head. Malik wiped the whole, taking the precautionary course.

﴿and your feet up to the ankles﴾ in the accusative, conjoined to "your faces." This is supported by the widespread Sunna, the practice of the Companions, and the statement of most of the imams, and by the limitation, since wiping has not been known to be limited. It has also been read in the genitive by attraction (jiwar), and its parallel in the Qur'an is abundant, as in His saying, ﴿the punishment of a painful day﴾, and its like. The grammarians have a separate chapter on this. Its benefit is to draw attention to the fact that one should be moderate in pouring water over them, and wash them with a washing close to wiping; and in separating it from its fellows there is a hint of the preferability of the order. It has also been read in the nominative; that is, "and your feet are washed."

﴿And if you are in a state of major impurity, then purify yourselves﴾; that is, wash your whole body. It has also been read: (fa-ṭhharu), that is, purify your bodies. In tying the command of the major purification to the major impurity there is an indication of the condition of the command of minor purification upon the minor impurity.

﴿And if you are ill﴾: an illness by which destruction is feared, or its increase by the use of water.

﴿or on a journey﴾; that is, settled upon it.

﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself, or you have touched women, and you do not find water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it﴾. "Min" here denotes the starting point of the limit; it has also been said to be partitive, and it is connected to "wipe." It has been read: (fa-ummū ṣaʿīdan). The interpretation of this noble verse has already been discussed at length in Surat al-Nisa', so let it be referred to there; and perhaps the repetition is so that the discussion of the kinds of purification may be continuous.

﴿Allah does not intend﴾; that is, He does not intend by the command to purify for prayer, or by the command to perform tayammum.

﴿to put upon you any difficulty﴾ of constraint in complying with it.

﴿but He intends﴾, by that, ﴿to purify you﴾; that is, to cleanse you, or to purify you of sins, since ablution expiates them; or to purify you with dust when water is unavailable to you for purification. The object of "intends" in both places is omitted; the "lam" denotes cause, and it has been said it is extra. The meaning: Allah does not intend to place upon you any hardship in the matter of purification, to the extent that He would not grant you the concession of tayammum; rather He intends to purify you with dust when water for purification is lacking to you.

﴿and to complete﴾ by His legislation that which is a purifier for your bodies and an expiation for your sins.

﴿His favor upon you﴾ in the religion; or, to complete by His concessions His bounty upon you through His firm commands.

﴿that you may be grateful﴾ for His favor. Among the subtleties of this noble verse is that it contains seven pairs: two purifications, the original and the substitute; the original is of two kinds, comprehensive and non-comprehensive; by the nature of the act, washing and wiping; by the place, limited and unlimited; their instruments are liquid and solid; what makes them obligatory is the minor and major impurity; what permits resort to the substitute is illness and journey; and what is promised upon both is the purification of sins and the completion of blessing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 7:

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾ by (the gift of) Islam, so that it reminds you of the Benefactor and encourages you to thank Him.

﴿And His covenant with which He bound you﴾; that is, His firm covenant which He took from you.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when you said, "We hear and we obey"﴾ is a temporal clause (zarf) attached to "bound you with it", or to an implied element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the genitive "with it" (bihi), or from "His covenant" (mithaqihi); that is: existing at the time of your saying, "We hear and we obey". The purpose of restricting it to this time is to emphasise the obligation to observe it, by recalling their acceptance of it and their commitment to preserving it. This is the covenant which He took from the Muslims when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pledged them to hear and obey in hardship and ease, in what they like and what they dislike. It has also been said that it is the covenant made on the night of 'Aqaba and in the Pledge of Ridwan. Its attribution to Him, exalted is He, although it proceeded from the Prophet (peace be upon him), is because the return of the pledge is to Him, as expressed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah﴾. Mujahid said: it is the covenant which Allah, exalted is He, took from His servants when He brought them forth from the loins of Adam (peace be upon him).

﴿And fear Allah﴾; that is, regarding forgetting His favour and breaking His covenant, or regarding everything you do and everything you leave undone, so that what has been mentioned enters into it as a primary inclusion.

﴿Indeed Allah is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾; that is, of its hidden matters, which are attached to them with a complete attachment that justifies the application of the term "companion" (sahib) to them, so He will reward you for them. How then about the manifest deeds? The sentence is a concluding parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh tadhyili) and the reason for the command to be mindful of Allah. Placing the noble Name in the position of a pronoun serves to cultivate awe, to give the reason for the ruling, and to strengthen the independence of the sentence.

﴿O you who have believed﴾ This begins the explanation of the rulings concerning what takes place between them and others, following the explanation of what pertains to themselves.

﴿Be persistent in standing firm for Allah﴾, upholding His commands, complying with them, glorifying them, and observing their rights.

﴿Witnesses in justice﴾; that is, with justice.

﴿And do not let hatred of a people﴾; that is, let not... ﴿hatred of a people﴾ move you ... ; that is, the intensity of your enmity toward them.

﴿Prevent you from being just﴾, so that you do not bear witness concerning their rights with justice, or so that you do not transgress against them by committing what is not permitted, such as mutilation, slander, killing women and children, breaking covenants out of a desire for revenge, and other such things.

﴿Be just; that is nearer to righteousness﴾; that is, justice (is nearer to righteousness) — the one you have been commanded to observe. He explicitly stated to them the command to act justly, and clarified that it is in a position of nearness to righteousness, after having forbidden them from injustice, and clarified that it is what desire demands. If the obligation of justice toward the disbelievers is at this standing, then what do you think of its obligation toward the Muslims?

﴿And fear Allah﴾: He commanded taking heed of God after explaining that justice is nearer to it, out of concern for its matter and as an alert that it is the foundation of the affair.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾: of deeds, so He will recompense you accordingly. The repetition of this ruling is either due to a difference in the cause, as it has been said: the first was revealed concerning the polytheists, and this one concerning the Jews; or for the sake of greater emphasis on justice and exaggerating in extinguishing the flame of anger. The sentence serves as a reason for what precedes it, and the manifestation of the Majestic Name (Allah) rather than a pronoun is for what has passed several times. Since its content signals promise and threat, he followed with the promise for those who preserve obedience to Him, the Exalted, and with the threat for those who neglect it.

It is said: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, among which are justice and piety.

﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. The second object of "promised" (waʿada) has been omitted, since this sentence dispenses with it. It is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf, a new sentence that follows on from what precedes it) that explains that omitted object. It is also said that the clause occupies the position of the object, since promising is a kind of speech, so it is as if it were said: "He promised them this statement."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 10:

﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs﴾, which among their whole body are the explicit texts recited that speak of command, justice and piety.

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described with what was mentioned of disbelief and denial of the signs.

﴿They are the companions of the Hellfire﴾, those who are inseparably bound to it with everlasting connection. From the noble Qur'anic practice (sunnah saniyyah) is the pairing of promise with threat, and the combining of encouragement (tarhib... targhib) with warning (tarhib): fulfilling the due of the claim through good tidings and admonition.(p-13)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 11:

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾ — a reminder of the blessing of deliverance from harms, following the reminder of the blessing of bringing good, which is the blessing of Islam and what follows from it of the covenant. "Upon you" (ʿalaykum) is connected either to "favor of Allah," or to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) describing it.

And His saying, Most High: ﴿when a people determined﴾ — according to the first view it is an adverbial phrase (ẓarf) of the favor itself; according to the second view, it is an adverbial phrase of what is connected to "upon you." It cannot be an adverbial phrase of "remember," because their two times are incompatible; i.e., remember His Most High's bounty upon you, or remember His favor existing upon you at the time of their determination.

﴿to extend their hands toward you﴾ — i.e., by striking you with killing and destruction. It is said: "basata ilayhi yadahu" (he extended his hand to him) when he assaulted him, and "basata ilayhi lisanahu" (he extended his tongue to him) when he insulted him. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the explicit object is to hasten the explanation that the harm and danger of the extension return to them, carrying them from the outset to regard the favor of its repulsion as a blessing; just as the fronting of "lakum" in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth﴾ is for the purpose of hastening the explanation that the created thing is among their benefits, expediting the joy.

﴿But He withheld their hands from you﴾ — conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "hum" (them), and it is the favor whose reminder is intended, and a mention of it to them; to signal its occurrence at the time of greatest need for it. The fa' (then) indicates sequence, implying the completeness and perfection of the favor. The explicit mention of "their hands" in place of a pronoun is for added emphasis; i.e., He restrained their hands from being extended toward you immediately after their determination to do so, not that He withheld it from you after they had extended it toward you. In this there is an indication of the perfection of the favor in that it was not tainted by the harm of fear and the agitation, which the withholding after the extension rarely lacks, a matter whose place is not hidden. This is what is narrated: that the polytheists saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions at ʿUsfan during the expedition of Dhi Amarr, which is the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa', and it was the seventh of his campaigns (peace be upon him). They stood up together for the noon prayer. When they had prayed, the polytheists regretted that they had not fallen upon them, and said: "Indeed, they have a prayer after it which is dearer to them than their fathers and their sons," meaning the afternoon prayer, and they intended to attack them when they stood for it. So Allah, Most High, turned back their scheme by sending down the prayer of fear.

It is also said: it is what is narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) came to the Banu Qurayza, with him the two Shaykhs and ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them, seeking a loan from them for the blood-money of two Muslims whom ʿAmr ibn Umayya al-Damri had killed by mistake, thinking them to be polytheists. They said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim, sit until we feed you and give you what you asked.' So they seated him in a veranda and determined to assassinate him. ʿAmr ibn Jihash resolved to take a great millstone to drop upon him, but Allah, Most High, withheld his hand, and Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and informed him, so he (ﷺ) went out from them."

It is also said: it is what is narrated that "he (ﷺ) stopped at a place and his companions dispersed among the acacia trees seeking shade under them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hung his sword on a tree. A bedouin came, took it, and unsheathed it, and said: 'Who will protect you from me?' He (ﷺ) said: 'Allah, Most High.' Jibril (peace be upon him) made it fall from his hand, and the Messenger (ﷺ) took it and said: 'Who will protect you from me?' He said: 'No one. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.'"

﴿And fear Allah﴾ — conjoined to "remember"; i.e., fear Him by observing the rights of His favor and do not neglect its thanks; or, in all that you do and abstain from, whereby what has been mentioned is included as a primary entry.

﴿And upon Allah﴾ — i.e., upon Him, Most High, exclusively and not other than Him, whether independently or in association.

﴿So let the believers put their trust﴾ — for He suffices them in bringing every good and repelling every evil. The sentence is a concluding affirmation confirming what precedes it. The choice of the imperative form of the third person, and attributing it to the believers, is to make trust in God obligatory upon the addressed in a demonstrative manner, and to indicate that what they were described with at the address, namely the attribute of faith, is a motive toward what they were commanded with of trust and piety, and a restraint against neglecting both. The explicit mention of the Glorious Name in place of a pronoun is to give the reason for the ruling and to strengthen the independence of the concluding sentence.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 5, verse 12:**

﴿And God had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾. This is a resumed statement (*kalam mustaʾnaf*) that includes mention of some of the betrayal and breaking of the covenant that came from the Children of Israel, and of the consequences that followed from it. It is directed at establishing the believers in remembering God's blessing, in observing the right of the covenant with which He bound them, and in warning them against breaking it. Or it is meant to establish what was mentioned about the intention to lay hands on them (*al-hamm bil-batsh*), and to confirm it on the assumption that this came from the Banu Qurayza, as has passed in the narration, showing that treachery and betrayal were an ancient habit among them, which they inherited from their forefathers. The mention of the Exalted Name (*al-ism al-jalil*) serves to cultivate awe, to magnify the covenant, and to emphasise the gravity of breaking it, along with preserving the right of the resumed statement that this requires, in order to mark a break from what precedes it.

The shift (*iltifat*) in God's words ﴿and We raised up from among them twelve chieftains﴾ is for the sake of following the customary manner of majesty (*sunan al-kibriya*), or because the raising up was through Musa, peace be upon him, as will come. The placing of the prepositional phrase (*al-jarr wal-majrur*) before the direct object is, as has passed many times, for the sake of giving importance to what is placed first and creating anticipation for what comes later. The word *naqib* (chieftain, representative) is on the pattern *fa'il* with the meaning of *fa'il* (active participle), derived from *al-naqb*, which means searching. From it comes God's words ﴿so they searched through the lands﴾. He was so named because he searches into the conditions and secrets of his people. Al-Zajjaj said: its root is from *al-naqb*, which is the wide hole.

It is narrated that when the Children of Israel settled in Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh, God, Mighty and Majestic, commanded them to set out for Arihā, the land of Syria, which was inhabited by the tyrannical Canaanites (*al-Kan'aniyyun*). He said to them: "Indeed I have written it for you as a home and a dwelling place, so go out to it and fight those who are in it, and I am your helper." Musa, peace be upon him, was commanded to take from each tribe a trustworthy chieftain who would be a guarantor over his people for fulfilling what they had been commanded, as a bond upon them. He chose the chieftains and took the covenant from the Children of Israel, and he entrusted the chieftains with them and set out with them. When he drew near the land of Canaan, he sent the chieftains to spy, and they saw enormous bodies, strength and might. They were frightened and returned and told their people what they had seen. Musa had forbidden them from this, so they broke the covenant, except Kalib ibn Yuqunna, chieftain of the tribe of Yahudha, and Yusha' ibn Nun, chieftain of the tribe of Ifrayim ibn Yusuf al-Siddiq, peace be upon him.

It was said: when the chieftains headed to their land for spying, they encountered Uj ibn Unuq. His height was three thousand, three hundred and thirty-three cubits, and he lived for three thousand years. There was a bundle of firewood on his head. He seized them and placed them in the bundle, and set off with them to his wife and said: "Look at these people who claim they want to fight us." He threw them before her and said: "Shall I not crush them with my foot?" She said: "No, but release them until they inform their people of what they have seen." So he did, and they began to inspect their circumstances. A single cluster of their grapes was carried by five men or four. When the chieftains went out, some of them said to others: "If you inform the Children of Israel of the news of the people, they will turn back from the Prophet of God. But conceal it, (p-15) except from Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, so that the two of them will see their opinion." So some of them took an oath from others, then they returned to Musa, peace be upon him, and they had with them a single grape from their cluster. One man fled, and they broke their pledge. Each of them began to forbid his tribe from fighting them and to inform them of what he had seen, except Kalib and Yusha'. The camp of Musa was one farsakh by one farsakh. Uj came until he looked at them, then he returned to the mountain and hewed from it a great rock the size of the camp, then carried it on his head to drop it upon them. God, Exalted, sent the hoopoe, which pierced the rock at its middle, opposite his head, so it became a hole, and it fell around Uj's neck and encircled him and felled him. Musa, peace be upon him, approached, and his height was ten cubits, as was the length of his staff. It leapt into the sky ten cubits, and it did not strike anything but his ankle while he was fallen, and it killed him. They said: then a group came with daggers until they cut off his head.

﴿And God said﴾: that is, to the Children of Israel alone, since they are the ones in need of what has been mentioned of encouragement and warning, as the shift indicates, along with what it contains of cultivating awe, and of emphasising what the statement includes of promise.

﴿Indeed I am with you﴾: that is, with knowledge, power and support, not with support alone. For alerting them to His knowledge of everything they do and everything they omit, and to their being under His power and dominion, is something that moves them to earnestness in complying with what they were commanded and in refraining from what they were forbidden. It is as if it were said: "Indeed I am with you: I hear your speech, I see your deeds, and I know your inner thoughts, so I will recompense you accordingly."

That said, it has been said: the covenant here means the covenant of faith and monotheism, and the chieftains are the kings of the Children of Israel who search into their conditions and manage their affairs through commanding good, forbidding evil and establishing justice. This is the more suitable reading in light of God's words ﴿If you establish prayer, give zakat, and believe in My messengers﴾; that is, in all of them. The *lam* is a preparatory particle for the omitted oath. The placing of faith after the establishing of prayer and giving of zakat, although these two are branches that follow from it, is because they were acknowledging their obligation while they were committing the denial of some of the messengers, peace be upon them, and for the sake of observing the parallel between it and God's words ﴿and support them﴾; that is, you help them and strengthen them. Its root meaning is defending. It has been said: it means honouring, revering and praising with good. It is read *wa-ʿazartumūhum* with the lightened form (*al-takhfif*).

﴿and lend to God﴾: by spending in the way of good, and by giving the recommended charities.

God's words ﴿a goodly loan﴾ are either an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar muʾakkid*) that comes in a form other than the verbal noun's usual pattern, as in God's words ﴿So her Lord accepted her with goodly acceptance and made her grow with a goodly growth﴾, or a second object of *aqraḍtum* (you lent), on the basis that it is a noun for the wealth lent.

God's words ﴿I will surely remove from you your misdeeds﴾ are the answer to the oath indicated by the *lam*, standing in place of the answer to the condition.

﴿and surely admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ is a conjunction with what precedes it, included with it in the ruling of the answer, and later than it in its occurrence as well, since clearing (*al-takhliya*) necessarily precedes adorning (*al-tahliya*).

﴿Whoever disbelieves﴾: that is, in My messengers, or in something of what has been enumerated within the scope of the condition. The *fa'* is for ordering the statement of the ruling on whoever disbelieves after the statement of the ruling on whoever believes, in order to strengthen the encouragement with the warning.

﴿after that﴾: the emphasised condition to which the great promise is tied, which necessitates faith with certainty.

﴿among you﴾ is connected to an implied element that stands as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of *kafara* (disbelieved). The reason the construction was changed, in that it does not say "and if you disbelieve," as a conjunction with the preceding conditional sentence, is to remove the disbelief of all of them from the realm of possibility, and to drop "whoever disbelieves" from the level of direct address. The intention is not to produce disbelief after faith, but to include also persistence in it. It is as if it were said: "whoever attains the attribute of disbelief after that." Except that by using a form that indicates occurrence, the purpose is to explain their progression through the degrees of disbelief. For attaining a quality after the arrival of what requires abandoning it, even if it is persistence in it, is in terms of its designation a new act and a fresh deed.

﴿then he has indeed strayed from the right way﴾: that is, from the middle of the clear path, with manifest error, and he has missed it with gross mistake, with no excuse whatsoever, unlike one who disbelieved before that, since perhaps he may have a doubt and a pretext may be imagined for him. (p-16)

**﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾** The *bāʾ* is causal (*bāʾ al-sababiyya*, the "bāʾ of cause"), and *mā* is redundant (*zāʾida*, an extra particle) for emphasis and to fix the statement firmly in the mind. The meaning is: because of their breaking of their binding covenant, and not because of anything else, either alone or combined with it.

**﴿We cursed them﴾** We drove them away and banished them from Our mercy. Or: We transformed them into apes and swine. Or: We humiliated them by imposing the poll-tax (*jizya*) upon them. The explanation given here is restricted to what has been mentioned, although the proper order would be to first establish the occurrence of the curse and the breaking itself, by saying, for example: "So they broke their covenant, and We cursed them." This is because the simple form of a thing must precede its compound form. The explanation has been placed here to indicate that the occurrence of both is clear and needs no explanation. What requires explanation is the causal link between them (*al-sababiyya wa'l-musabbabiyya*, the relation of cause and effect).

**﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾** So that they are not affected by the signs or by reflection. It has also been said: We granted them respite and did not hasten punishment upon them until their hearts became hard. Or: We forsook them and withheld from them the divine favours (*alṭāf*, subtle graces) until they became like this. It has been recited as *qasiyyatan* (قَسِيَّةً). This is either an intensive form of *qāsiyatan* (قَاسِيَةً), or it means "bad," from the saying "a *qasiyy* dirham," that is, a bad one, when it is adulterated and has dryness and roughness. It has also been recited with a kasra on the qāf (قِسِيَّةً), in imitation of the sīn (*itbāʿan lahā bi'l-sīn*, by assimilation to the following sīn).

**﴿They distort words from their places﴾** This is a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*, a new sentence) explaining the degree of the hardness of their hearts, for there is no greater degree than that which permits daring to alter the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and to slander Him. The form of the present tense (*muḍāriʿ*) indicates renewal and continuity. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the object of *la'annāhum*.

**﴿And they forgot a portion﴾** That is, they abandoned a substantial share.

**﴿of what they were reminded of﴾** From the Torah, or from following Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said: they distorted the Torah, and some of its matters slipped from their memory. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "A person may forget some knowledge because of sin," and he recited this verse: **﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾**. That is, *khā'ina* (خَائِنَة) is treated as a verbal noun (*khiyāna*, treachery), like *lāghiya* and *kādhiba*; or it is an action that is treacherous (*fa'la khā'ina*), meaning "possessing treachery"; or a treacherous group (*ṭā'ifa khā'ina*); or a treacherous person (*shakhṣ khā'ina*), with the *tāʾ* being for intensification (*lil-mubālagha*); or a treacherous soul (*nafs khā'ina*). The phrase **﴿from them﴾** is attached to an implied element that serves as a qualifier of the noun. On the first two possibilities, *min* is for origin (*ibtidā'iyya*): meaning "treachery" or "a treacherous action proceeding from them." On the remaining possibilities, *min* is partitive (*tab'īḍiyya*). The meaning is that betrayal and treachery are a constant habit among them and their forefathers, such that they hardly abandon or conceal them, so you will not cease to observe this from them.

**﴿except a few of them﴾** This is an exception from the pronoun in **"from them"** under all the interpretations. It has also been said that the exception is from **"treachery"** under the last three possibilities, and the intended "few" are those among them who believed, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his like. It has also been said that the exception is from **"treachery"** under the second possibility, so the intended "few" refers to a few actions, and *min* is for origin, as explained above. The meaning is: except a few actions proceeding from them.

**﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾** That is, if they repent and believe, or if they make a covenant and commit to paying the poll-tax. It has also been said that this is an unrestricted command (*muṭlaq*) that was abrogated (*nusikha*, see *naskh*, abrogation) by the verse of the sword.

**﴿Indeed, Allah loves the good-doers﴾** This is a reason (*taʿlīl*) for the command, an exhortation to comply with it, and an indication that pardon in absolute terms is a matter of excellence (*iḥsān*).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 14:**

﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ قالُوا إنّا نَصارى أخَذْنا مِيثاقَهُمْ﴾ ("And from those who said, 'We are Christians,' We took their covenant") is an explanation of the abominations and crimes of the Christians, following the explanation of the abominations and betrayals of the Jews. The phrase *min* ("from") is connected to *akhadhna* ("We took"), since the sense is: "And We took from those who said, 'We are Christians,' their covenant." The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for emphasis, and because mentioning the condition of one of the two groups prompts the listener to wonder what the condition of the other is. So it is as if it were said: "And from the other group too, We took their covenant." It has also been said that *min* is connected to an omitted element that functions as the predicate of an omitted subject, whose descriptive phrase or relative clause takes its place. The meaning would be: "And among them are a people from whom We took their covenant," or "those from whom We took their covenant." The pronoun in *mithaqahum* ("their covenant") refers to the implied described noun in this case, and in the first case to the relative pronoun. It has also been said that it refers to the Children of Israel, meaning: "We took from these people the covenant of those [others]," that is, a covenant like their covenant of faith in God and His messengers, and what follows from that of good deeds. The Qur'an attributes the naming "Christians" to themselves rather than saying "from the Christians," to indicate that in their saying "We are the helpers of God," they are far from truthfulness, for it is pure fabrication on their part, and they have no share in God's help at all. Alternatively, it serves to show the full extent of their evil conduct by demonstrating the contradiction between their words and their deeds, for their claim to help God requires their steadfastness in His obedience and their observance of His covenant.

﴿فَنَسُوا﴾ ("Then they forgot") immediately after taking the covenant, without hesitation. ﴿حَظًّا﴾ ("a portion") means a generous share.

﴿مِمّا ذُكِّرُوا بِهِ﴾ ("of what they had been reminded of") refers to what was included within the covenant, such as faith in God Most High and other matters, as has passed just above. It has also been said that it is what was written for them in the Gospel, namely that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ). They abandoned it, cast it behind their backs, followed their desires, and so they disagreed and split apart into the Nestorians, the Jacobites, and the Melkites, as helpers of Satan.

﴿فَأغْرَيْنا﴾ ("So We stirred up") means: We made [them] cling and adhere. The verb *gharra bi al-shay'* means to cling to a thing and stick to it when one is attached to it, while *aghrahu* means that someone else caused this. From this comes *al-ghira'* (glue).

The words of God Most High ﴿بَيْنَهُمُ﴾ ("among them") are either an adverb of place for *aghrayna*, or connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state of its object, meaning: "We stirred up" [enmity] "among them."

﴿العَداوَةَ والبَغْضاءَ﴾ ("enmity and hatred") are present among them. There is no way to make it an adverb of place for both, because a verbal noun (*masdar*) cannot govern what precedes it.

The words of God Most High ﴿إلى يَوْمِ القِيامَةِ﴾ ("until the Day of Resurrection") are either a limit for the stirring up, or a limit for the enmity and hatred. The meaning is that they will be hostile and hateful toward one another until the Day of Resurrection, in accordance with what their divergent desires and deviant opinions require, which lead to splitting into the three sects. Thus the pronoun in "among them" refers to them specifically. It has also been said that it refers to them and to the Jews as well, meaning: "We stirred up enmity and hatred among the Jews and the Christians."

﴿وَسَوْفَ يُنَبِّئُهُمُ اللَّهُ بِما كانُوا يَصْنَعُونَ﴾ ("And God will soon inform them of what they used to do") is a severe threat of requital and punishment, like a man saying to one he threatens: "I will tell you what you did." The meaning is that He will recompense them for what they did in persisting in breaking the covenant and forgetting their generous share of what they had been reminded of. The particle *sawfa* ("soon") serves to emphasize the threat, and the shift to mentioning the majestic Name serves to instill awe and dread, intensifying the threat. The expression of the act as "making" (*sun'*) indicates that they are firmly established in it, and the expression of the recompense as "informing" (*tanbi'a*) serves to alert that they do not truly know the evil deeds they do and what they entail of punishment, so that the ordering of the punishment upon them is, in conveying knowledge of their true state, equivalent to informing them of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 15:

﴿O People of the Book﴾ This is a turn (iltifat) to addressing both groups, on the basis that "the Book" is a comprehensive genus including the Torah and the Gospel. It comes right after the description of their states of treachery and other kinds of vile conduct, and it is a call to them to believe in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. Addressing them with the title of being People of the Book gathers into the opening address what pertains to the Book, and it also serves to intensify the reproach, for being People of the Book is among the things that require honoring it, acting by its implications, and making clear the rulings it contains. Yet they committed concealment and distortion, while knowing what they were doing.

﴿Our Messenger has come to you﴾ The attribution (idafa) is for honor and to announce the obligation of following him.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿making clear to you﴾, it is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "Our Messenger." The choice of a verbal sentence over other forms indicates the renewal of clarification; that is: Our Messenger has come to you while making clear to you, gradually, as the public interest requires.

﴿much of what you used to conceal of the Book﴾; that is, of the Torah and the Gospel, such as the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), the verse of stoning in the Torah, and the good news of Jesus concerning Ahmad (peace be upon them both) in the Gospel. The placement of "much" (kathiran) after the prepositional phrase is for the reason repeated many times: to show concern for what is fronted, since bringing forward the pleasant news hastens joy and arouses anticipation for what comes later, and what should be fronted, when delayed, leaves the soul awaiting its arrival, so that it settles more firmly when it arrives. Also, the delayed element contains a kind of detail which fronting might disrupt the interlocking of the noble structure. The phrase "mimma" (of what) is connected to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of "kathiran," and "ma" is a relative noun whose following words are its relative clause, the returning pronoun to it being omitted. "Min al-Kitab" is connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause from the omitted returning pronoun.
