The combination of the past and present verb forms indicates their continued concealment and hiding; that is: He makes clear to you much of what you hide, continuously, while it is from the Book of which you are its people and those who hold fast to it.

﴿and pardons much﴾; that is: He does not disclose much of what you hide, when no religious motive calls for it, to protect you from further exposure, as the expression of not disclosing by "pardoning" makes clear. In it is an encouragement for them not to conceal, by way of both enticement and warning. The clause is conjoined to the circumstantial clause and falls under its judgment. It has been said: "He pardons much of you and does not take you to account for it."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There has come to you from Allah a light﴾, it is a resumptive clause brought to explain that the benefit of the Messenger's coming is not confined to what was mentioned of making clear what they used to hide, but he has countless benefits. "From Allah" is connected to "came," and "min" denotes the starting point of the act metaphorically, or it is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause of "light." Whichever it is, it is an explicit statement of what the attribution of the Messenger implies regarding his coming from the presence of Him, Mighty and Majestic. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the subject is to hasten the explanation that the coming is from His exalted direction, and to arouse anticipation for the one who comes, and because it includes a kind of lengthening which fronting might disrupt the harmony of the noble structure, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And there has come to you in this the truth, and an admonition and a reminder for the believers﴾.

The nunation of "light" (nur) is for magnification. What is meant by it, and by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and a clear Book﴾, is the Qur'an, because of what it contains of uncovering the darkness of polytheism and doubt, and clarifying what was hidden from people of the truth, and its manifest inimitability. The conjunction serves to treat the difference in designation as if it were a difference in essence. It has been said: what is meant by the first is the Messenger (ﷺ), and by the second, the Qur'an.

﴿Yahdi bihi Allahu﴾ (by it Allah guides): the unification of the pronoun in the prepositional phrase is because the referent is one in essence, or because the two are treated as one thing, or it is intended to mean: "by what has been mentioned." Fronting the prepositional phrase (taqdim al-jarr wa'l-majrur) serves to give it emphasis, and the explicit mention of the Divine Name (izhar al-jalala) serves to show the full concern with the matter of guidance. The clause (jumla) is in the nominative position as a second qualifier (sifa thaniya) of kitab (a Book), or in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from it, since it has become specific through its qualifier.

﴿man ittaba'a ridwanahu﴾ (whoever follows His pleasure): that is, His good pleasure, by believing in Him. Man is either a relative pronoun (mawsula) or a qualifying noun (mawsufa). (p-19)

﴿subula al-salam﴾ (the paths of peace): that is, the ways of safety from punishment and deliverance from retribution, or the paths of God Most High, which are His law (shari'a) that He has prescribed for people. It has been said that it is the second object of yahdi (guides). The correct view is that its accusative case is by the removal of the preposition (naza' al-khafid), following the manner of His statement, Most High: ﴿wa-ikhtara Musa qawmahu﴾ (And Musa chose his people from among his folk). It is transitive to the second object with ila (to), or with al-lam (for), as in His statement, Most High: ﴿inna hadha al-Qur'an yahdi lillati hiya aqwam﴾ (Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright).

﴿wa-yukhrijuhum﴾ (and brings them out): the pronoun refers to man, and the plural is in view of the meaning, just as the singular in ittaba'a is in view of the wording.

﴿min al-zulumat﴾ (from the darknesses): that is, the darknesses of the various kinds of disbelief and misguidance; ﴿ila al-nur﴾ (into the light): into faith; ﴿bi-idhnihi﴾ (by His permission): by His facilitating it, or by His will.

﴿wa-yahdihim ila sirat mustaqim﴾ (and guides them to a straight path): this is the nearest of paths to God Most High, and one that inevitably leads to Him. This guidance is the very same as the guidance to the paths of peace, and it is conjoined to it as a treatment of the descriptive difference (al-taghayur al-wasfi) as if it were an essential difference (al-taghayur al-dhati), as in His statement, Most High: ﴿wa-lamma ja'a amrina najjayna Hudan wa'lladhina amanu ma'ahu bi-rahmatin minna wa-najjaynahum min 'adhabin ghalizin﴾ (And when Our command came, We delivered Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We delivered them from a severe punishment).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 17:

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾ That is, "Allah is none other than" (la ghayruhu), as one says, "Generosity is nothing but piety" (al-karam huwa al-taqwa). They are the Ya'qubiyya (Jacobites), who hold that He, exalted is He, may indwell the body of a particular human being, or his soul. It was said: none of them explicitly stated this, but since they believed that He is characterized by the особый attributes of Allah, and they acknowledged that Allah, exalted is He, exists, it followed for them to say that He is the Messiah and no other. It was also said: because they claimed that there is divinity (lahut) in him, and said, "There is no god but One," it followed for them that he must be the Messiah; so the necessary implication of their saying was attributed to them, to clarify their ignorance and expose their belief.

﴿Say﴾: that is, to rebuke them, to show the falsehood of their corrupt saying, and to silence them.

The fa' in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then who could prevent Allah from anything﴾ is fasiha (introducing a conditional clause), and "min" is interrogative for denial and reproach. Al-mulk is complete control and firm possession. "Min" is connected to it with an elided genitive (mudaf); that is: if the matter is as you claim, then who would prevent anything from His power and His will? Its real meaning is: who is able to hold back anything from them?

﴿If He willed to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and everyone on earth, all together﴾. It is incumbent on whoever is a god that nothing be related to him, nor to any of his affairs, but rather that the power of another over any existent thing in any way is excluded, let alone that he be unable to repel any of them when they are tied to his destruction. Since his inability is clear without doubt, it became evident that he is far removed from what they have fabricated concerning him.

By destruction is meant causing death and annihilation in general, not by way of wrath and anger. The explicit mention of the Messiah in the form in which they attributed divinity to him, in the place of the pronoun, is for emphasis, and to specify that he falls under His dominion and sovereignty by that very same aspect. The negation of the ownership mentioned, by the interrogative of denial, applies to everyone, while the obligation and rebuke are established by negating it from the Messiah alone, by saying: "Then does he possess anything from Allah if He wills ... etc.," to establish the truth by negating divinity from everything other than Him, glorified is He, and to establish the sought-after matter within it by way of demonstrative proof. For when the negation of ownership, which necessitates the impossibility of divinity, is manifested with respect to all, it is manifested with respect to the Messiah in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, so the impossibility of divinity becomes certain. The generalization of the will of destruction to all, while the aforementioned verification is achieved by restricting it to him, is in order to magnify the matter and show complete powerlessness, by demonstrating that all are under His dominion and sovereignty, so no one can repel what is willed against him, let alone what is willed against others. It also serves to announce that the Messiah is a model for the rest of creatures in being subject to destruction, just as he is a model for them in the aforementioned powerlessness and lack of deserving divinity.

The specific mention of his mother, although she is included among those on earth, is to further emphasize the Messiah's powerlessness. Perhaps placing her in the category of those whose destruction was supposed, although her destruction had already occurred before that, is for the emphasis of rebuke and the greater establishment of the content of the statement, making her condition a model for the condition of the rest of those whose destruction was supposed, as if it were said: "Say: who could prevent Allah from anything if He willed to destroy the Messiah, his mother, and everyone on earth? He has already destroyed his mother, so did anyone prevent Him? Likewise is the case with the rest of those existing other than her."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾: that is, what is between the two extremities of the physical world, not merely between the surface of the earth and the concave of the moon's sphere alone, so it includes what is in the heavens of the angels, peace be upon them, and what is in the depths of the earth and the seas of creatures. It is an explicit statement that all is under His dominion and sovereignty, following the allusion to the fact that some (i.e., those on earth) are so; that is, to Him alone belongs the dominion of all existents, and the absolute disposal over them, by bringing into being and annihilating, giving life and causing death, to no one other than Him, either independently or by partnership. Thus it is a verification of the exclusivity of divinity to Him, exalted is He, following the explanation of its negation from everything other than Him.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ is a resumed sentence brought in to explain some rulings of dominion and divinity in a manner that removes the doubt that afflicted them regarding the Messiah's birth without a father, the creation of the bird, the raising of the dead, and the healing of the blind and the leper. That is: He creates what He wills of the kinds of creation and bringing into being. "Ma" here is an indefinite qualified noun, in the accusative in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), not as an object; as if it were said: He creates whatever creation He wills. Sometimes He creates without any origin, like the creation of the heavens and the earth; and at other times from an origin, like the creation of what is between them. He brings into being from an origin not of its own kind, like the creation of Adam and many animals; and from an origin of its own kind, either from a male alone, like the creation of Eve, or a female alone, like the creation of Jesus, peace be upon him, or from both, like the creation of all other people. He creates without the intermediation of any created thing, like the creation of most creatures; and sometimes He creates through the intermediation of another created thing, like the creation of the bird by the hand of Jesus, peace be upon him, as a miracle for him, and the raising of the dead, and the healing of the blind and the leper, and other than that. So all of it must be attributed to Him, exalted is He, not to the one through whose hand it was carried out.

﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾: an appended concluding clause, confirming the content of what precedes it. The explicit mention of the glorious Name serves as a reason and to strengthen the independence of the sentence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 18:

﴿And the Jews and the Christians said: "We are the sons of God and His beloved."﴾ This is a report of the false claim issued by both groups, and an explanation of its falsehood after mentioning what one of the two groups said and showing its falsehood. That is: the Jews said, "We are the followers of His son 'Uzair," and the Christians said, "We are the followers of His son, the Messiah," just as it was said to the followers of Abu Khubayb, who was 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, "the Khubaybiyyun," and just as the close relatives of kings say when boasting, "We are the kings." Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "The Prophet ﷺ invited a group of Jews to the religion of Islam and warned them of the punishment of God Most High. They said: 'How do you frighten us with it when we are the sons of God and His beloved?'" It was also said: the Christians recite in the Gospel that the Messiah said to them, "I am going to my Father and your Father." It was also said: they meant that God Most High is like a father to us in tenderness and compassion, and we are like sons to Him in nearness and rank. In sum, they claimed that they had a superiority and distinction with God Most High over the rest of creation, and He refuted them in this. It was also said: it was addressed to the Messenger of God ﷺ.

﴿Say﴾ to rebuke them and to silence them.

﴿Why then does He punish you for your sins?﴾ That is: if what you claim is true, then for what reason does He punish you in this world with killing, captivity and transformation? You know that He will punish you in the Hereafter with the Fire for days equal in number to the days of your worship of the calf. Had the matter been as you claim, these things would not have happened to you, nor would what befell you have befallen you.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Rather, you are mortals﴾ is a conjunction with an implied clause that the speech carries; that is: you are not so; ﴿rather, you are mortals﴾.

﴿of those He has created﴾; that is: of the same kind as those whom God Most High created, without any superiority for you over them.

﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾ of those creatures, namely those who believed in Him, Exalted is He, and in His messengers.

﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾ of them, namely those who disbelieved in Him and in His messengers, like you.

﴿And to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ of existing things; none of them belongs to Him, Glorified is He, except through sovereignty, servitude, and subjugation under His dominion. He disposes of them as He wills, in bringing into existence and annihilating, in giving life and causing death, in rewarding and punishing. So how could they claim what they claimed?

﴿And to Him is the final return﴾ in the Hereafter specifically, not to any other, whether independently or jointly; so He will recompense each of the doer of good and the doer of evil according to what his deed requires, without any turning-away that averts Him or any inclination that diverts Him.

O People of the Book, this is a repetition of the address by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), and a gentleness in the call.

﴿Indeed there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "rasulana" (Our Messenger). The choice of the present-tense verb yubayyinu (making clear) over the participle mubayyinan (one making clear) is due to what has passed earlier; that is: he makes clear to you the laws and the religious rulings coupled with promise and threat, and among them is what he has made clear in the preceding verses of the refutation of your abominable assertions, and what will come of the reports of the earlier nations. The object has been omitted, relying on the manifest fact that the coming of the Messenger is for the purpose of making these clear; or the meaning is: he provides you with clarification and bestows it upon you in everything about which you need clarification in matters of religion. As for supplying something similar to what preceded in His words, ﴿much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture﴾, as has been said, then, apart from its being a repetition without benefit, it is refuted by His words, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿after a lull in the messengers﴾. For the cessation of sending and the cutting off of revelation only necessitates the clarification of the laws and rulings, not the clarification of what they concealed. "After a lull" (ala fatratin) is connected to "has come to you" as an adverbial of time, as in His words, ﴿and they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon﴾; that is: he has come to you at a time of lull in sending and cessation of revelation, and of greater need for clarification of the religious laws and rulings. Or it is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in "yubayyinu," or of the pronoun in "lakum"; that is: he makes clear to you what has been mentioned while he is after a lull of messengers, or while you are upon it, most in need of clarification. "From the messengers" (min al-rusul) is connected to an omitted element that stands as an attribute of "fatra"; that is: a lull existing from the messengers, initiated from their side.

His words, ﴿lest you should say﴾, are a causal clause for the coming of the Messenger with clarification, with an omitted noun; that is: lest you should say, making excuses for your negligence in observing the rulings of the religion.

﴿There has not come to us any bearer of good tidings or any warner﴾: the traces of the earlier laws had been obliterated and their reports cut off. The addition of "min" to the subject is for emphasis in negating the coming, and the indefiniteness of "bashir" and "nadhir" is for diminution. This, as you see, requires that what is presumed, or intended, in what preceded is the laws and rulings, not in whatever form they were, but accompanied by what has been mentioned of promise and threat.

His words, ﴿So there has indeed come to you a bearer of good tidings and a warner﴾, are connected to an omitted element indicated by the eloquent "fa" (fa'l-fasiha), and it shows that it is causally linked to it. The tanwin of "bashir" and "nadhir" is for magnification; that is: do not offer excuses with that, for there has indeed come to you a bearer of good tidings, what a bearer of good tidings, and a warner, what a warner.

﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾: so He is able to send messengers in succession, as He did between Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, where there were one thousand seven hundred years and a thousand prophets between them; and to send after a lull, as He did between Jesus and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them both, where there were six hundred years between them, or five hundred and sixty-nine years, or five hundred and forty-six years, and four prophets according to what al-Kalbi narrated: three from the Children of Israel, and one from the Arabs, Khalid ibn Sinan al-Absi.

It has been said: after Jesus, peace be upon him, there was none but the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this is most fitting with the magnification conveyed by the tanwin of "fatra," which befits the context of favour bestowed upon them, in that the Messenger was sent to them when their need for him was complete, because a long age had passed since the cessation of revelation, so that they would rejoice in him and count him the greatest blessing from Allah, the Exalted, and an opening of a door to mercy; and the proof is established against them, so that they cannot plead tomorrow that no one was sent to them from among themselves, out of their heedlessness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 20:

﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah), brought in to explain what the Children of Israel did after the covenant was taken from them, and to detail the manner of their breaking it, and its connection to what came before it, in that what is mentioned therein includes matters for which the Prophet ﷺ was described as making them clear, and in that it includes the absence of a period of messengers among them. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative, being the object of a verb understood, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, by way of shifting the address (talwin al-khitab) and turning it away from the People of the Book, so as to enumerate against them the crimes committed by some of them. That is: and mention to them the time when Moses said to his people, advising them and winning them over by attributing them to himself.

﴿O my people, remember the favor of God upon you﴾ The directing of the command to remember toward the time, rather than toward the events that occurred in it, although the events are the primary object, is for the sake of emphasizing the obligation to remember them, because obligating the remembrance of the time is an obligation to remember what occurred in it by way of demonstration (al-tariq al-burhani), and because the time comprises what occurred in it in detail; so when it is brought to mind, what occurred in it is present with all its details, as though it were witnessed with the eye. "ʿAlaykum" (upon you) is connected to the favor itself when it is taken as a verbal noun (masdar), and to a omitted element that stands as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it when it is taken as a noun (ism); that is: remember His bestowal upon you, or remember His favor existing upon you. Likewise "idh" in His words, exalted is He: ﴿when He made among you prophets﴾; that is: remember the bestowal of God, exalted is He, upon you at the time of His making, or remember the favor of God, exalted is He, existing upon you at the time of His making among you, from your kinsmen, prophets, of great number and of great station, since no nation among the nations was sent such prophets as were sent to the Children of Israel.

﴿and made you kings﴾ This is coordinated with "made among you," and falls under its ruling; that is: He made among you, or from among you, many kings, for kings multiplied among them just as prophets did. The adverbial phrase was omitted because the matter was evident, or because the whole is placed in the position of bestowing favor upon them by making them kings, since the relatives of kings say at times of boasting: "We are the kings." That course was not taken in the preceding clause because the station of prophethood is of great weight, of high desirability, and of difficult attainment, and it is not fitting that one be attributed to it, even metaphorically, who is not among those whom God, exalted is He, has chosen for it.

It has been said: they were enslaved in the hands of the Copts, and God delivered them, and He called their deliverance "kingship." It has been said: a king is one who has a spacious dwelling in which there is flowing water. It has been said: one who has a house and servants. It has been said: one who has wealth with which he does not need to strain at labors or bear hardships.

﴿and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds﴾ Such as the parting of the sea, the drowning of the enemy, the shading of the cloud, the sending down of manna and quail, and other great matters that God, exalted is He, bestowed upon them. By "the worlds" is meant the nations that passed before their time; it has been said: among the worlds of their own time.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 21:

﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land﴾. He repeated the address with the honorific attribution (al-idafah al-tashrifiyyah), out of concern for the matter and as an intensification in urging them to comply with it. "The land" (al-ard) is the land of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was so named because it was the abode of the prophets and the dwelling of the believers. It has been said that it is Mount Tur and what surrounds it; it has also been said that it is Damascus, Palestine and part of Jordan; and it has been said that it is al-Sham (Greater Syria).

﴿Which Allah has prescribed for you﴾; that is, He wrote in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) that it would be a dwelling for you if you believed and obeyed, according to His words to them after they disobeyed: ﴿Therefore it is forbidden to them﴾.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿and do not turn back on your heels, for you will become losers﴾. The arrangement of ruin and loss upon turning back indicates, definitively, that the prescription is conditional upon the striving that follows from faith and obedience; that is: do not return retreating out of fear of the tyrants. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa-al-majrur) is linked to an omitted element, being a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "turn back" (tartaddu). It is also permissible for it to be linked to the verb itself. It has been said: when they heard of their condition from the chieftains (al-nuqaba'), they wept and said: "Would that we had died in Egypt! Come, let us appoint a leader who will turn us back toward Egypt." Or: "Do not turn back from your religion through disobedience and lack of trust in Allah, exalted is He." His words "so you will turn about" (fa-tanqalibu) are either in the jussive mood, conjoined to "turn back" (tartaddu), or in the subjunctive mood, as an answer to the prohibition. The loss is the loss of religion and of the world, especially the loss of entering what was prescribed for them.

﴿Qalu﴾ (They said) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf mabni), arising from the course of the discourse, as if it were said: "What did they say in response to his command, peace be upon him, and his prohibition?" So it was said: "They said, not complying with that."

﴿O Musa, indeed there are in it a people of tyrants (jabbarin)﴾ — dominant ones, against whom it is not possible to contend, nor is it feasible to confront them. The jabbar (tyrant) is the arrogant one who compels people, coercing them to do whatever he wills, whoever he may be and whatever it may be; it is an intensive form (fa''al) from jabarahu 'ala al-amr, i.e., he compelled him to it.

﴿And indeed we will never enter it until they leave it﴾ — without any action on our part, for we have no ability to expel them from it.

﴿So if they leave it﴾ — by some cause among the causes with which we have no connection.

﴿Then indeed we will be entering﴾ — at that time. They employed this conditional sentence even though its content was already understood from what preceded, namely the restriction of non-entry to their leaving it; this was to state the intended meaning explicitly and to make clear that their refusal to enter it was due only to the presence of those people in it. In the apodosis they used a nominal sentence introduced by the particle of emphasis (harf al-tahqiq), indicating the establishment and firmness of the entry when the condition is certainly fulfilled, and to show their complete eagerness for it and for complying with the command.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 23:

﴿Said two men﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as previously mentioned, as if it were said: Did they agree upon that, or did some of them oppose them? So it was said: "Said two men."

﴿Of those who fear﴾; that is, they fear God Most High rather than the enemy, and they guard against Him by disobeying His command and prohibition. Ibn Mas'ud recited it this way (with the verb "yakhafun," they fear). Within this there is an implication that whoever other than these two do not fear God Most High, but rather fear the enemy. It was also said: "Of those who fear the enemy," meaning: they are of them in lineage, not in fear. These two were Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, of the chieftains (nuqaba'). It was also said: they were two men of the giants (jababira) who embraced Islam and went to Moses, peace be upon him. In that case, the waw (in "yakhafun") refers to the Children of Israel, and the relative clause (al-mawsul) refers to the giants, and the omitted returning pronoun (al-'a'id al-mahdhuf) refers to them; that is: "of those whom the Children of Israel fear." This is supported by the reading of the one who read "yukhafun" in the passive form; that is, "those who are feared." According to the first (interpretation), this is from causing fear; that is: "of those who are made to fear God Most High through admonition, or whom the threat frightens."

﴿God has bestowed His favor upon them both﴾; that is, with steadfastness, the strengthening of hearts, reliance upon His affairs, and trust in His promise, or with faith. This is a second attribute of "two men," or a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh). It was also said: it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yakhafun," or from "two men," since it is specified by the attribute; that is: they spoke to them, addressing them and encouraging them.

﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾; that is, the gate of their city. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before it is for emphasis on it, because the intent is only entering the gate while they are in their city; that is: surprise them, press upon them in the narrow passage, and prevent them from coming out into the open, so that they will find no room for war.

﴿When you have entered it﴾; that is, their city while they are in it.

﴿Then you will surely be victorious﴾ without any need for fighting, for we have seen them and witnessed that their hearts are weak, even though their bodies are large. So do not fear them, and attack them in the narrow passages, for they cannot advance or retreat there. It was also said: they judged victory only because they knew it from Moses, peace be upon him, and from the words of God Most High: ﴿God has prescribed for you﴾; or because they knew of His Majesty's custom (sunnah) in supporting His messengers, and what they knew of His action toward Moses, peace be upon him, in subduing his enemies. The first is more fitting with linking the victory to entering.

﴿And upon God﴾ alone ﴿put your trust﴾ after arranging the means, and do not rely upon them, for they are far from having any real effect; the effect is only from God, the Mighty, the Powerful.

﴿If you are believers﴾; that is, believers in Him, Most High, affirming His promise, for that necessarily requires trust in Him without exception.

They said: this is a resumptive sentence (istinaf), as before. That is, they said, paying no heed to the two of them or to their words, addressing Moses, peace be upon him, to show their persistence in the first statement and to declare openly their opposition to him, peace be upon him.

﴿O Moses, indeed we will never enter it﴾: that is, the land of the tyrants, let alone entering its gate while they are in their own land.

﴿Ever﴾: that is, for a long time. ﴿As long as they are in it﴾: that is, in their land. This is a substitution (badal) for "ever," a partial substitution (badal al-ba'd), or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan).

﴿So go﴾: the fa' is explanatory (fasihah). That is, if the matter is so, then go.

﴿You and your Lord, and fight﴾: that is, fight them. They only said this out of contempt and mockery toward Him, glorified is He, and toward His messenger, and out of disregard for the two of them. They actually intended their departure, as the extreme of their ignorance and the hardness of their hearts indicates. It has been said that they meant: their intention and purpose, as when you say, "I spoke to him and he went to answer me," as if they said: "So intend to fight them and aim at them." It has also been said that the implied meaning is: "So go, you and your Lord, and may He help you and assist him." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and fight﴾ without mentioning Harun or the two men, indicates that they did not commit to their going, or that they did not care about fighting alongside them.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, we are sitting right here﴾ supports the first interpretation, and by it they meant not advancing, not not lagging behind.

﴿He said﴾ (peace be upon him), when he saw from them what he saw of obstinacy, in the manner of distress and grief and complaint to God Exalted, together with a tenderness of heart by the like of which mercy is drawn down and help is sent down.

﴿My Lord, I own none but myself and my brother﴾: this is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with "myself." It is also said to be a conjunction with the pronoun in "I own," meaning: I own nothing but myself, and my brother owns nothing but himself. It is also said to be a conjunction with the pronoun in "I do not own," with the pronoun used for separation (faṣl).

﴿So part between us﴾: he means himself and his brother. The fa' (so) indicates the ordering of the separation, or a supplication for it following what precedes it.

﴿and between the defiant people﴾, those who have gone out of Your obedience and persist in disobeying You, by Your judging for us what we deserve and against them what they deserve. It is also said that it means distancing between us and them, and freeing us from their companionship.

﴿He said, "Then indeed it"﴾: that is, the Holy Land. The *fa'* (فَاءُ, the particle of consequence) indicates that what follows is the result of what precedes it, namely the supplication.

﴿is forbidden to them﴾, a prohibition of prevention (*tahrim man'*) and not a prohibition of worship (*tahrim ta'abbud*). They shall neither enter it nor possess it, because their being granted it was conditional upon faith and jihad. When they turned back on their heels, they were deprived of it and became the losers.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿forty years﴾: if it is construed as an adverbial complement (*zarf*) of *muharramah* (forbidden), then the prohibition is time-limited and not perpetual, and so it does not contradict the apparent meaning of His saying, ﴿God has prescribed for you﴾. The meaning of its prohibition for them is that none of them shall enter it during this period. But this does not mean that all of them will enter it after it, rather some of those who remained did so. This accords with what is narrated: that Musa, peace be upon him, led those of the Children of Israel who remained to Jericho (*Ariha*), with Yusha' ibn Nun at the head of his vanguard. He conquered it and remained there for as long as God willed, after which he (Yusha') passed away, peace be upon him. It was also said: none of those who said, "We will never enter it" entered it, and only the young ones (*al-nawashi*) from their descendants entered it with Musa, peace be upon him. Thus the period of forty years is, in reality, the prohibition of it upon their descendants, and the prohibition was attributed to them because of the complete connection between them, which borders on identity.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿they will wander in the land﴾, that is: they will be bewildered in the desert. It is either a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) explaining the manner of their deprivation, or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *'alayhim* (upon them). It was also said that it is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) related to *yatihun* (they will wander), in which case the wandering is time-limited and the prohibition is absolute. It was said: they were six hundred thousand fighting men, the length of the desert was ninety farsakhs, and they wandered within six farsakhs, or nine farsakhs within thirty farsakhs; and it was said: within six farsakhs out of twelve farsakhs. It is narrated that each day they would travel earnestly, and when evening came they found themselves at the place from which they had set out. The cloud would shade them from the heat of the sun, a column of light would appear for them at night to illuminate them, manna and quail would descend upon them, their hair would not grow long, and when a child was born to them, he would have a garment like a fingernail which grew with his growth. These favours upon them were given despite their being punished, because their punishment was by way of rubbing down and discipline. It was said: Musa and Harun were with them, but that was for them a spirit and safety, like the fire for Ibrahim and the angels of punishment, peace be upon them. It is also narrated that Harun died in the wandering, and Musa died a year after him in it, and Yusha' entered Ariha three months after his death. The apparent wording of the noble verse does not support this, for after He accepted his supplication against the Children of Israel and punished them with the wandering, it is far-fetched that He would save some of those against whom he prayed or their offspring, and decree the death of the two of them within the place of punishment in an apparent manner, even if that was for them a station of comfort and ease. It has also been said that the two of them were not with them in the wandering, and this is most appropriate to the interpretation of the *farq* (separation) as distancing. As for the one who says that the two of them were with them in it, he interprets the *farq* as the judgment mentioned, by what each group deserves.

﴿So do not grieve﴾: do not sorrow, ﴿over the defiant people﴾. It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, regretted his supplication against them, so it was said to him: do not regret and do not grieve, for they are deserving of that because of their defiance.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 27:**

﴿And recite to them﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with an implied clause, to which the words of the Exalted ﴿when Moses said﴾ ... etc. are connected. Its connection to that clause is in that it is a preface (tamhid) for the later transgressions of the Children of Israel, after what was prescribed for them had been prescribed and the Messengers had come to them with the clear proofs (bayyinat) they brought.

﴿the story of the two sons of Adam﴾: they are Qabil and Habil. It is transmitted from al-Hasan and al-Dahhak that they were two men from the Children of Israel, on the evidence of the end of the story. This is not so. God, Mighty and Majestic, inspired Adam to marry each of them to the twin (tawama) of the other. Qabil's twin was the more beautiful, and her name was Uffalima. So he envied his brother for her and was incensed, and he claimed that this was not from God the Exalted but from Adam, peace be upon him. So he (peace be upon him) said to them both: "Offer an offering (qurban), and whichever of you is accepted shall marry her." They did so, and a fire descended upon the offering of Habil and consumed it, and it did not touch the offering of Qabil. So Qabil's envy and anger increased, and he did what he did.

﴿with the truth﴾ is connected to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier (sifa) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: a recitation accompanied by truth and correctness. Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿recite﴾, or from its object, meaning: while you are accompanied by truth. Or the meaning is: inform them of it with truth and sincerity, as it is established in the books of the earlier peoples.

﴿when they offered an offering﴾: it is in the accusative, governed by ﴿the story﴾ as an adverb of time (zarf) for it. That is: recite their story and inform them of it at that time. It was said that it is an apposition (badal) from it, with an omitted modifier (mudaf), meaning: recite to them the story of the story of that time, and this was refuted on the ground that ﴿idh﴾ (when) is not prefixed by anything other than a time-noun, such as ﴿waqti'idhin﴾ (at that time) and ﴿hina'idhin﴾ (at that time). The qurban (offering) is a name for what one draws near to God by, of a rite (nusuk) or a charity, like the hulwan, a name for what is given as a gift (yuhla), that is, given. Its singular form is used because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar). It was said that its implied form is: when each of them offered an offering.

﴿so it was accepted from one of them﴾: this is Habil. It was said: he was the owner of livestock and offered a fat camel, so a fire descended and consumed it.

﴿and it was not accepted from the other﴾: this is Qabil. It was said: he was the owner of crops and offered the worst of the wheat he had, so the fire did not touch it at all.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf), built upon a question arising from the flow of the discourse, as if it were said: "What did the one whose offering was not accepted say?" So it is said: he said to his brother, because his anger and envy were intensified when his excellence before God, Mighty and Majestic, became manifest to him.

﴿I will surely kill you﴾: that is, by God, I will surely kill you, with the doubled nun, and it has been read with the single nun.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence as before. That is: the one whose offering was accepted said, when he saw that his brother's envy was due to the acceptance of his offering and the non-acceptance of his own.

﴿Indeed God accepts only﴾: that is, the offering.

﴿from the righteous﴾, not from others. He accepted my offering and rejected yours because of the piety (taqwa) that is in us and its absence in you. That is: you were brought about by yourself, not by me, so why would you kill me? Except that he did not state this explicitly, but took the course of allusion (taʿrid), out of fear of arousing his anger, and to lead him toward piety and to desisting from what he intended. For this reason the verb was attributed to the majestic Name, to cultivate awe.

(p-27)

Then he declared his piety in a manner that would calm his anger, had he possessed a restraining intellect, for he said by way of emphasis: ﴿If you stretch out your hand against me to kill me, I shall not stretch out my hand against you to kill you.﴾ Here he opened the conditional sentence with the lam of preparation for an oath (al-lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam), and he placed the prepositional phrase before the direct object, signalling from the outset that the harm and consequence of the stretching out would return upon him. The response of the oath, which takes the place of the response of the condition, was not made a verbal sentence matching what is in the condition; rather it was a nominal sentence introduced by the Hijazi "ma" (ma al-hijaziyyah), which serves to emphasise the negation, with the ba' in its predicate, for the sake of intensifying the declaration of his innocence from stretching out the hand, by showing its continuity in negating the stretching out. This is like the Exalted's saying: ﴿And they are not believers﴾, and His saying: ﴿And they are not going to come out of it﴾. For just as the affirmative nominal sentence indicates, by the aid of context, the permanence of the established state, so the negative one indicates by the aid of context the permanence of the negation, not the negation of permanence. This is by considering permanence and continuity after considering the negation, not before it, so that the negation would not fall upon something restricted by permanence and thereby lift its restriction. That is: "By God, even if you undertake to kill me, as you have threatened, and that is realised from you, I shall not be one who does the like of it to you at any time."

Then he gave the reason for that by his saying: ﴿Indeed I fear God, Lord of the worlds.﴾ In this is a guidance to Qabil towards the fear of God, the Exalted, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, which is not hidden. It is as if he said: "I fear Him, the Exalted, that if I stretch out my hand against you to kill you, He would punish me; and even if that is from me to repel your enmity towards me, then what do you think of your own state, while you are the aggressor and transgressor?" In describing Him, the Exalted, with the lordship of the worlds, there is emphasis on the fear.

It has been said: Habil was stronger than him, but he refrained from killing him and submitted out of fear of God, the Exalted, because killing for defence was not permissible at that time. It has also been said: he did so seeking what is better, as he (peace be upon him) said: "Be the servant of God who is killed, and do not be the servant of God who kills." But the justification by his fear of God, the Exalted, rejects this, unless it is claimed that leaving the better course, in his view, was equal to disobedience in its entailing harm, as an intensification of purity.

Here is a further explanation of His saying, ﴿Indeed, I intend that you should bear my sin and your sin﴾. It is another justification (ta'lil) for his refraining from opposing him, presented as a purpose that comes later than that refraining, just as the first motive (ba'ith) comes before it. The sentence is not joined to the preceding one by a conjunction, to draw attention to the fact that each of the two is sufficient as a cause. The meaning is: "By my submitting to you and my refraining from attacking you, I intend that you should return bearing my sin, that is, the like of my sin had I stretched out my hand to you, and bearing your sin for stretching out your hand to me." This is like his words, upon him be peace: "The two who revile each other, the sin falls on the one who begins, so long as the wronged one does not transgress." That is, the sin of his abuse falls upon the one who begins, and the like of the abuse of his companion, by virtue of his being the cause of it.

It has been said that the meaning of "my sin" is the sin of killing me, and the meaning of "your sin" is that on account of which your offering was not accepted. Both are in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal, a word or phrase describing the condition of the subject at the time of the action); that is, "you return being burdened with the two sins, carrying them both." Perhaps his primary intention is simply that he himself not be burdened with sin, not that his brother be burdened with it.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of "sin" is its punishment. There is no doubt that it is permissible to desire the punishment of a disobedient person when it is known that he will not desist from disobedience at all, though the context rejects this reading.

As for His saying, ﴿so you will be among the companions of the Fire﴾: his being among them follows only from his returning bearing the two sins, not from his being afflicted with the punishment for them.

Taking the punishment to be another kind of punishment that follows from it, namely the punishment of the Fire, is refuted by His saying, ﴿and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾, for it is explicit that being among the companions of the Fire is the complete and full punishment. The sentence is a concluding clause (tadhyil) confirming the content of what precedes it. He pursued every avenue of admonition and reminder to turn him away from the evil he intended, encouraging him at one time and warning him at another, yet this only produced in him persistence in error and immersion in corruption.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 30:

﴿So his soul made the killing of his brother seem good to him﴾; that is: it widened for him and made it easy, from "ta'a lahu al-marta'" (the pasture became spacious for him), i.e., when it expanded. The sequence of the "making seem good" is according to what is related of the statements of Habil, together with his (Qabil's) certainty of it beforehand as well, as his saying "I will surely kill you" makes clear. This is because the continuation of an act after the establishment of what removes it of strong motives, although it is a continuation outwardly, is in reality a new occurrence and a fresh act, as in your saying: "I admonished him, but he did not heed." Or because this degree of making seem good had not been present before that, on the basis of his hesitation about his ability to kill, since Habil was stronger than him; it came about only after he perceived Habil's submission and his not resisting him. The explicit mention of his being his brother serves to highlight the abhorrence of what his soul had embellished for him. It has been read as ﴿fa-tawa'at﴾ (fa-ṭāwaʿat), either as a form of "fā'ala" with the meaning of "fa'ala," or on the basis that "qatla akhihi" (the killing of his brother) is as if he urged his soul to undertake it, and it complied with him and did not refuse; and "lahu" is for added connection, as in your saying: "I guarded for Zayd what was his."

﴿Then he killed him﴾. It is said: Qabil did not know how to kill Habil, so Iblis appeared in the form of a man, took a bird, placed its head upon a stone and crushed it with another stone, and he learned from this; so he crushed Habil's head between two stones, while Habil was submissive and did not resist him. It is also said: he assassinated him while he was asleep. Habil was twenty years old on the day he was killed. The place of his killing is disputed: it is said at the ascent of Hira', it is said in Basra at the site of the Great Mosque, and it is said on a mountain called Bud. When he had killed him, he left him in the open, not knowing what to do with him, and he feared that wild beasts would get to him, so he carried him on his back in a sack for forty days; it is said a year, until he decomposed, while birds and beasts gathered around him, watching when he would throw him down so that they could eat him.

﴿So he became one of the losers﴾, in religion and in worldly life.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 31:

﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the earth, to show him how to conceal the naked body of his brother.﴾ It is related that Allah, exalted is He, sent two crows, and they fought, and one of them killed the other. Then it dug a hole for it with its beak and its feet, and cast it into it. The pronoun in "yuriyahu" (to show him) refers either to Allah, exalted is He, or to the crow. The lam on the first reading is attached to "ba'atha" (sent) definitively, and on the second reading to "yabhathu" (scratching). It is also permissible for it to be attached to "ba'atha" as well. "Kayfa" (how) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yuwari" (conceal), and the clause is the second object of "yuriya" (to show). What is meant by "sawata akhihi" (the naked body of his brother) is his dead body.

﴿Said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the flow of the discourse, as if it were said: "What did he say upon witnessing the state of the crow?"

So it was said: he said, "Woe is me!" (ya waylata) is an expression of distress and lamentation, and the alif is a substitute for the ya' of the first person (the speaker). The meaning: "O my woe, come forth, for this is your time." Al-waylu and al-waylah mean destruction.

﴿Am I incapable of being﴾; that is: "Am I incapable of being?" (ʿan an akuna, i.e., "from being").

﴿like this crow, and conceal the naked body of my brother?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at his failure to be guided to what the crow was guided to. His saying, exalted is He, "﴿fa-uwariya﴾" with the accusative is coordinated (ʿatf) upon "an akuna". It was also read in the nominative, meaning: "so I conceal."

﴿So he became among the regretful﴾; that is, regretful over his killing, because of what he endured of bewilderment about his affair and carrying the body on his neck for a long period. It is related that when he killed him, his body turned black, though it had been white. Adam asked him about his brother, and he said: "Am I my brother's keeper?" He said: "Rather you killed him, and that is why your body has turned black." Adam remained after him for one hundred years without laughing. It is also said: when Qabil killed Habil, he fled to Aden in the land of Yemen. Iblis came to him and said: "Only the fire consumed the offering of Habil, because he used to serve it and worship it. If you also worship it, you will attain your aim." So he built a fire temple and worshipped it, and he was the first to worship fire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 32:

﴿Because of that﴾ is the beginning of what is the purpose of reciting the account: the explanation of another of the transgressions and sins of the Children of Israel. That is an indication of the great gravity of killing and the extreme ugliness of it. Both meanings are understood from what is mentioned within the story: Abel's regarding it as grave, his complete avoidance of committing it, even though that was by way of defending himself and submitting to being killed out of fear of its punishment; the explanation that it entails the killer bearing the sin of the one killed; and that Cain, by committing it, was among those who lost both their religion and their worldly life; and his remorse over his deed, together with the arrogance, intense obstinacy and hardness of heart in him. The word ajal (cause, reason) is originally a verbal noun: ajala sharran means he committed an evil. It is used to give the reason for crimes, as in their saying: "min jarraka fa'altuhu," meaning: "because of your dragging and committing it." Then its use was extended, and it came to be used for every kind of causal explanation. It has been read as ﴿min ijli﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, which is a dialectal form of it. It has also been read as ﴿min ajli﴾ with the hamza dropped and its vowel placed on the nun.

And "min" (from) denotes the starting point, and it is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾. Placing it before the verb is for restriction: that is, the beginning of the prescribing is from that and arises from it and from nothing else; that is, We decreed upon them and made clear.

﴿that whoever kills a soul﴾, one soul out of souls, ﴿without a soul﴾, that is, without killing a soul that requires retaliation.

﴿or corruption in the land﴾, that is, corruption that requires the forfeiture of its blood. This is a conjunction with what "ghayr" was added to, not with the meaning of negating both matters together, as in your saying: "Whoever prays without ablution or tayammum, his prayer is invalid," not negating one of them, as in your saying: "Whoever prays without ablution or clothing, his prayer is invalid." The basis of the two usages is considering whether the negation applies to what is understood from the word "aw" (or), namely the alternation between the two matters, which indicates choice and permissibility; and considering the reverse. The criterion for the two considerations is the difference in the state of what "ghayr" is added to among the two matters, according to whether the negation of the ruling is conditioned on the realization of one of them, or conditioned on the realization of both together. In the first case, the negation applies to the alternation between the two matters before it is applied, so it yields the negation of both together. In the second case, the alternation applies to the negation, so it yields the negation of one of them necessarily, since before the negation is applied there is no alternation for its reverse to be conceived. The clarification of this is that every ruling conditioned on the realization of one of two things, for example, has its negation conditioned on the absence of both together; and every ruling conditioned on the realization of both together has its negation conditioned on the absence of one of them, since the negation of everything is conditioned on the negation of its condition. There is no doubt that the negation of the particular affirmative, as in the first ruling, is the universal negative, and the negation of the universal affirmative, as in the second ruling, is its removal, which entails the particular negative. Thus it is established that the negation of the first is conditioned on the absence of both together, and the negation of the second is conditioned on the absence of one of them. Since the ruling in your saying, "Whoever prays with ablution or tayammum, his prayer is valid," is conditioned on the realization of one of them indefinitely, its negation in your saying, "Whoever prays without ablution or tayammum, his prayer is invalid," (p-30) is conditioned absolutely on the opposite of the stated condition, which is the absence of both together. Thus the alternation between ablution and tayammum, with the word "aw," is necessarily the object of the negation that is derived from "ghayr," and so the realization of both together is negated, by necessity of the general scope of the negation applied to the indefinite.

On this rests what they said: when it is said, "Sit with the scholars or the ascetics," and then the prohibitive "la" is placed before it, the doing of all of them is forbidden, as in: ﴿and do not obey from among them any sinner or ungrateful one﴾, since the meaning is: do not do either of them; so whichever of them one does, it is one of them. As for your saying, "Whoever prays with ablution or clothing, his prayer is valid," since the ruling there is conditioned on the realization of both matters, its negation in your saying, "Whoever prays without ablution or clothing, his prayer is invalid," is conditioned on the opposite of the stated condition, which is the absence of one of them. Thus the alternation applies to the negation, and so it yields the negation of one of them. There is no concealing that the permissibility of killing is conditioned on one of the mentioned matters, killing or corruption, and it necessarily follows that its prohibition is conditioned on the absence of both together. Thus the alternation applies to the negation without doubt, as if it were said: whoever kills a soul without one of them.

﴿it is as if he had killed all mankind﴾. Whoever says in its interpretation "or without corruption" has moved away from giving the noble composition its right. The "ma" in "ka'annama" is a *kaffa* particle, preparing the verb to come after it. "Jami'an" is a circumstantial accusative from "al-nas" or an emphatic. The basis of the comparison is that both acts share in violating the sanctity of blood, in defiance of God Almighty, in emboldening people to kill, and in entailing retribution and provoking the anger of God Almighty and His great punishment.

﴿And whoever gives it life﴾, that is, he causes the survival of one soul described as free of the killing and corruption in the land mentioned, either by forbidding its killer from killing it, or by rescuing it from all the causes of destruction in some way.

﴿it is as if he had given life to all mankind﴾. The basis of the comparison is evident. The intent is to magnify the matter of killing and to exalt the importance of giving life, by depicting each of them in a form fitting to it in producing awe and desire. For this reason the noble composition begins with the pronoun of the matter, which indicates the completeness of its fame and prominence, and its immediate occurrence to minds upon mention. The pronoun, which produces an increase in fixing what follows in the mind, is not understood from it at first except as an indefinite matter of great importance, so the mind remains awaiting what follows it, and when it arrives it becomes firmly established more than before. It is as if it were said: "The matter, this great one, is..."

﴿And We had certainly sent to them Our messengers with clear proofs﴾. This is a standalone sentence, not conjoined to "We prescribed," reinforced with the oath of emphasis, and the particle of confirmation (la-qad) for complete concern with the realization of its content. The reason they did not say "And We certainly sent to them..." etc. is to make explicit that the message reached them, since that is more indicative of their extreme obstinacy and arrogance; that is: by God, Our messengers did certainly come to them, as We sent them, with the clear verses that state what We prescribed upon them, as confirmation of the obligation to observe it and as affirmation of the inescapability of preserving it.

﴿Then indeed many of them, after that﴾, that is, after what has been mentioned of the prescription, and the reinforcement of the matter by the sending of messengers successively, and the renewal of the covenant time after time. The placing of the demonstrative noun in the position of the pronoun indicates its complete distinction, and its inclusion for that reason among the evident matters, and what it carries of the sense of distance, to indicate the height of its rank and the remoteness of its station in great importance. "Thumma" (then) denotes delay in rank and remoteness.

﴿on the earth﴾ is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿are indeed transgressors﴾, and likewise the preceding adverbial phrase. The intervening lam does not harm this, since it is the lam of the beginning, whose proper place is to enter upon the subject, but its entry upon the predicate is because of "inna," so it is in its original place in terms of rule. Excess (israf) in any matter is going beyond the limit of moderation together with not caring about it; that is: they are transgressors in killing, not caring about it. Since their excess in the matter of killing entails their neglect of the matter of giving life, both in existence and in mention, and since it is the worse and more monstrous of the two, it suffices to mention it in the context of condemnation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 33:

﴿Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) brought to explain the ruling for one kind of killing and what is connected to it of corruption (fasad) by seizing property and its like, and to specify its immediate and deferred consequence. This follows the explanation of the great gravity of killing without right, and within it is included the explanation of what was alluded to in summary of the corruption that makes killing permissible. It was said: that is, they wage war against His Messenger. The mention of Allah the Exalted is for the sake of preparing for and alerting to the elevated status of the Messenger (ﷺ) with Him, Mighty and Majestic. Waging war against the people of His law and those who follow His path among the Muslims is waging war against him (ﷺ). Thus the ruling covers whoever wages war against them, even after ages, by way of the literal wording (ʿibarah) and not by implication (dalalah) or analogy (qiyas), because the revelation of the text is not by way of direct address (khitab al-mushafahah) such that its ruling would be restricted to those obligated at the time of revelation, so that extending it to others would need another proof.

It was also said: he made waging war against the Muslims into waging war against Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, as an honouring of them, and the meaning is: they wage war against their allies (awliya'uhuma). The root of harb (war) is seizure (salb), and what is meant here is: highway robbery (qat' al-tariq). It was said: it is open defiance by way of brigandage, even if it occurs within a city (misr).

﴿And they strive in the land﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) upon "they wage war," and the prepositional phrase is connected to it.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿corruption (fasadan)﴾, it is either a verbal noun (masdar) occupying the position of a circumstantial state (hal) from the subject of "yas'awna," meaning "causing corruption"; or an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning "for the sake of corruption"; or a verbal noun emphasizing "yas'awna," since it carries the sense of "mufsidun," with it being a masdar of aftsada with the augmentations removed; or an ism al-masdar (verbal noun of the form not of the masdar type).

It was said: the verse was revealed concerning the people of Hilal ibn ʿUwaymir al-Aslami, with whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had made a truce (wada'ahu) on condition that he would not help anyone against him and no one would help against him, and whoever among the Muslims came to him would be safe and not molested, and whoever passed by Hilal on the way to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would be safe and not molested. Then a group from Banu Kinanah, wishing to embrace Islam, passed by people of Hilal's tribe, and Hilal was not present that day; so they cut off the way against them, killed them and took their property. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the 'Uraniyyun, and their story is well known. It was also said: concerning a people of the People of the Book who had a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then they broke the covenant, cut off the road and spread corruption in the land.

Since war and corruption come in differing degrees and various forms — killing without seizing property, killing together with seizing it, seizing it without killing, and frightening (al-ikhafah) without killing or seizing — a specific penalty was prescribed for each of these degrees by way of distribution. Thus it was said: ﴿that they be killed (an yuqattalu)﴾; that is, as a prescribed penalty (hadd) without crucifixion, if they only committed killing. Even if the guardians of the victims pardon, this is not regarded, because it is the right of the Law (haqq al-shar'); and there is no difference whether the killing is by a cutting instrument or not.

﴿Or be crucified (aw yusallabu)﴾; that is, together with killing, if they combined killing with seizing of property: they are crucified alive and their bellies are pierced with a spear until they die. According to the apparent narration (zahir al-riwayah), the ruler (imam) has discretion: if he wishes, he may suffice with that; and if he wishes, he may cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides (min khilaf), and kill them and crucify them. The form of the verb with doubled middle letter (tafil) in both verbs indicates intensification. It has also been read with the lightened form in both.

﴿Or their hands and feet be cut off on opposite sides (min khilaf)﴾; that is, their right hands and left feet, if they confined themselves to seizing property from a Muslim or a dhimmi, and the amount was such that if divided among them each would receive ten dirhams, or an amount equal in value to it. As for cutting off their hands, it is for seizing property; and as for cutting off their feet, it is for frightening the road by destroying its security.

﴿Or they be banished from the land (aw yunfaw min al-ardi)﴾ if they did nothing but frightening and striving for corruption. The meaning of banishment (nafy) according to us is imprisonment (al-habs), for it is banishment from the face of the earth to repel their evil from its inhabitants; and they are also disciplined (yuʿazzarun) for engaging in the abhorrent act of terrorizing and removing security. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, banishment is from one city to another, where he is continually pursued while being a fugitive in fear. It was also said: it is banishment from his city only; and they used to banish them to Dahlak, which is a town at the farthest end of Tihamah, and Nasu'a, which is a town in the lands of Abyssinia.

﴿That﴾; that is, what has been detailed of rulings and penalties. It was said: it is the subject (mubtada').

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for them is disgrace (lahum khizy)﴾ is a clause of a predicate placed before the subject.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿in this world (fi al-dunya)﴾ is connected to an omitted element that occupies the position of a qualifier of "khizy," or connected to "khizy" as an adverb of place/time, and the clause is in the nominative position as the predicate of "that." It was said: "khizy" is the predicate of "that," and "lahum" is connected to an omitted element occupying the position of a circumstantial state (hal) from "khizy," because originally it was a qualifier of it, and when it was placed first it took the accusative of a state. "In this world" is either a qualifier of "khizy" or connected to it, as already stated. Al-khizy: humiliation and disgrace.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter﴾ other than this, ﴿is a great punishment (adhab 'azim)﴾ whose extent cannot be measured, because of the extreme magnitude of their crime. So His saying, the Exalted: "﴿lahum﴾" is the predicate placed first, "adhab" is the deferred subject, and "in the Hereafter" is connected to an omitted element occupying the position of a circumstantial state from "adhab," because originally it was a qualifier of it, and when it was placed first it took the accusative of a state; meaning: existing in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 34:

﴿Except for those who repent before you have power over them﴾ is an exception specific to what concerns the rights of God, Mighty and Majestic, as indicated by His words, ﴿So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. As for what concerns the rights of the guardians (awliya'), such as retaliation (qisas) and the like, that is up to them: if they wish, they may pardon, and if they prefer, they may exact it. The obligation to exact it falls away through repentance, but not its permissibility.

It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that al-Harith ibn Badr came to him repentant after he had been committing highway robbery, and he accepted his repentance and waived the punishment from him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 35:

﴿O you who believe, fear God﴾. When the gravity of killing and corruption (fasad) was mentioned and their rulings were explained, and when, within that, a hint was given of God's forgiveness for whoever repents of his crime, the believers were commanded to fear Him in everything they do and everything they leave undone. This is done by abstaining from the sins that must be guarded against, among which is what was mentioned of killing and corruption, and by performing acts of obedience, among which is striving to preserve lives, repelling corruption, and hastening to repentance and seeking forgiveness.

﴿And seek﴾; that is, seek for yourselves, ﴿to Him﴾; that is, to His reward and nearness to Him.

﴿the means (al-wasilah)﴾: it is on the pattern fa‘īlah (فَعَيْلَةٌ) in the sense of that by which one seeks a means of approach and draws near to God Almighty through performing acts of obedience and abandoning sins, from "wasala ila kadhā," meaning he drew near to it by means of something. "To Him" (ilayhi) is connected to it, and it has been placed before it for emphasis on it. It is not a verbal noun (maṣdar) so that it could govern what comes before it. Perhaps what is meant by it is the commanded taqwa (God-consciousness), for it is the foundation of the whole matter, as was indicated, and a means to attaining every good and a deliverance from every harm. In that case the sentence runs, relative to what precedes it, in the manner of elucidation and emphasis. Or it may mean the means in general, and this (taqwa) enters it as its first and most immediate instance. It has been said: the first clause is a command to abstain from sins, and the second is a command to perform acts of obedience.

Since in both abstaining from sins that the soul desires and performing acts of obedience that the soul dislikes there is burden and hardship, the command concerning them is followed by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And strive in His way﴾, by fighting His enemies, both the open and the hidden, ﴿so that you may prosper﴾ by attaining His good pleasure and succeeding in obtaining His honors.(p-33)

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 5, Verse 36:**

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ is an independent sentence (*kalam mubtada'*, an independent statement) brought to emphasize the obligation of complying with the earlier commands, and to encourage the believers to hasten to obtain the means of reaching Him, Mighty and Majestic, before its time passes. It does so by showing that the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection cannot possibly reach salvation from the punishment, let alone attain reward, through the strongest of means.

﴿Even if they had﴾: that is, each one of them, as in His saying, ﴿And even if every soul that did wrong had﴾ etc. (Q. 10:54). It does not mean all of them together, since that would not give the same degree of terrifying the matter and making the condition appear monstrous.

﴿whatever is on the earth﴾: that is, of its kinds of wealth, its treasures, and all of its benefits in their entirety. It is the subject (*ism*) of *inna*, and "for them" (*lahum*) is its predicate (*khabar*). Its place in the case is nominative (*raf'*) without dispute, except that according to Sibawayh it is nominative as a subject (*mubtada'*), and no predicate is needed for it, since its relative clause (*silah*) contains a predicate and its subject. It is distinguished from all other nouns-in-meaning (*ma yu'awwalu bil-ism*) by occurring after *law* ("if"). If it is said that the predicate is omitted, then it has been said that it is to be supposed as preceding: that is, "if the existence of what is on the earth for them is established." It has also been said that it is to be supposed as following: that is, "if the existence of what is on the earth for them is established." According to al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj, and the Kufans, it is nominative as the agent (*fa'iliyyah*), and the verb is supposed after *law*: that is, "if it were established that what is on the earth belongs to them."

His saying, ﴿all together﴾, is either an emphasis of the reference (*tawkid lil-wusul*) or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from it. ﴿And the like of it﴾ with the accusative case is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon it.

His saying, ﴿with it﴾, is an adverbial phrase of place/time (*zarf*) which occurs as a circumstantial clause from the conjoined noun, and the pronoun refers to the relative pronoun. Its benefit is to state explicitly the supposition of their being together with them by way of accompaniment, not by way of succession, to affirm the full horror of the matter, along with a kind of indication that the two are one thing, and as a preparation for the singular pronoun referring back to them.

The *lam* in His saying, ﴿so that they may ransom themselves with it﴾, is connected to what the predicate of *inna* is connected to, namely the stability (*al-istiqrar*) supposed in "for them," and to the predicate supposed according to the view of those who see the predicate as supposed preceding or following, and to the verb supposed after *law* according to the opinion of al-Mubarrad and those who follow his approach. There is no doubt that the basis of ransoming with what has been mentioned is its being theirs, not the establishment of its being theirs, although the latter entails the former. The *ba'* in "with it" is connected to "ransom," and the pronoun refers to the relative pronoun and "the like of it" together. Its singular form is either for what has been indicated, or because it is treated in the manner of a demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*), as if it were said "with that," as in the verse:

*"As if upon the skin were the spotting of leukoderma."*

That is, "as if that were..."

It has also been said that it refers to the relative pronoun, and that the pronoun referring to the conjoined noun, namely "the like of it," is omitted, as the predicate was omitted from *Qayyar* in the verse:

*"Indeed I and Qayyar here are strangers."*

That is, "and Qayyar too is a stranger."

It has also been permitted that the accusative of "and the like of it" be as an object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ahu*), its governing element being the verb supposed after *law*, following the view of al-Mubarrad and those who share his opinion. You know that this would lead to the agent of the nominative not being the governing element of the object of accompaniment, because the meaning, on the basis of accompaniment between what is on the earth and its like in being theirs, is not on the basis of the establishment and realization of that being. There is no justification for making its governing element the stability supposed in "for them," because Sibawayh has explicitly stated that the demonstrative noun and the prepositional phrase implying stability do not govern an object of accompaniment, and that the saying "this is for you and your father" is ugly, even though some grammarians permitted it with adverbials and prepositional phrases.

His saying, ﴿from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection﴾, is also connected to ransoming: that is, "if what is on the earth and its like were established as theirs, so that they might make it a ransom for themselves from the punishment befalling them on that day."

﴿It will not be accepted from them﴾: that is, that, and it is the answer (*jawab*) of *law*. Its arrangement upon the supposition that it belongs to them so that they might ransom themselves with it, without mentioning the ransoming itself, such as saying "and they ransomed themselves with it," even though rejection and acceptance are only consequent upon the ransoming and not upon its beginnings, is to indicate that it is a matter whose occurrence is certain and needs no mention. What needs supposing is only their ability to do what has been mentioned. Or it is for the sake of emphasis on the certainty of the rejection, and to imagine that it occurred before the ransoming, along the lines of His saying, ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you.﴾ Then, when he saw it placed beside him (Q. 27:40), where He did not say "so he brought it, and he saw it, and when..." etc. And like His saying, ﴿And she said, "Come out before them." So when they saw him, they were amazed at him﴾ (Q. 12:31), without mention of his going out before them, peace be upon him, and their seeing him. The counterfactual clause (*al-jumlah al-imtina'iyyah*) with its own status is the predicate of "indeed those who disbelieve."

The intended meaning: an illustration of the certainty of the punishment for them, and the impossibility of their being saved from it by any of the established or supposed ways.

From the Prophet ﷺ it is related that it will be said to the disbeliever: "Tell me, if you had the fullness of the earth in gold, would you ransom yourself with it?" He will say, "Yes." It will be said to him, "You were asked for something easier than that, and that is the word of testimony (*kalimat al-shahadah*)."

His saying, ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, is an explicit statement of what was indicated, that their ransom will not be accepted, for the sake of further affirming it and explaining its terror and severity. It has been said: its place in the case is accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). It has been said: nominative, as a conjunction upon the predicate of *inna*. It has been said: it is a conjunction upon "indeed those who," and so it has no place in the case, like the thing it is conjoined to.

(p-34)

﴿They desire to come out of the Fire﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istiʼnaf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), used to describe their condition while they endure the punishment. It answers a question that arises from what precedes it, as if it were said: "How will their condition be?" or "What will they do?" So it is said: "They desire..." and so on. Within this clause it is made clear that their punishment is the punishment of the Fire. It has been said that they intend this and seek a way out, but the flame of the Fire strikes them and lifts them upward, and there they desire to come out, ﴿but it is no longer the time for escape﴾.
