It has also been said that they nearly come out of it because of the Fire's intensity and its increasing lifting of them. And it has been said that they wish for it and desire it in their hearts.

As for the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And they will not be coming out of it﴾, this is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the subject of *yurīdūn* ("they desire"), or a parenthetical clause (*iʼtirāḍ*). Whichever it is, the choice of a nominal sentence over a verbal one, introduced by *mā* in the Hijazi construction (*mā al-ḥijāziyya*, the negation particle used according to the dialect of the Hijaz, which makes the predicate take the *bāʼ*), indicates the emphasis of the negation. This serves to show the complete wretchedness of their condition by the continuation of their not coming out of it. For a affirmative nominal sentence, as it conveys, with the help of context, the continuity of the affirmation, a negative nominal sentence likewise conveys, with the help of context, the continuity of the negation, not the negation of continuity, as was explained in the words of the Exalted: ﴿I shall not stretch out my hand to you﴾ (5:28), and so on.

It is also read as *an yukhrajū* (with the verb in the passive form, from *ikhrāj*, "to cause to come out").

﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾ is an explicit statement of what was alluded to just before, namely that its duration does not end, after the explanation of its severity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 38:

﴿And as for the thief, male and female﴾ is the beginning of an explanation of the ruling on minor theft (al-sariqah al-sughra) after the explanation of the rulings on major theft (al-sariqah al-kubra). You have already learned that the context calls for the inclusion of what lies between them of discourse. Since theft was customary among women as among men, He explicitly mentioned the female thief as well, although the established practice in the Book and the Sunnah is to include women within rulings revealed concerning men by way of implication (dalalah), for greater emphasis on clarification and for intensifying the deterrence. The phrase is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate according to Sibawayh is omitted; its estimate is: "And among what is recited to you, or among what has been enjoined upon you, is the thief, male and female," that is, their ruling. According to al-Mubarrad, [the predicate is as follows].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so cut off their hands﴾. The fa' (so) is present because the subject contains the meaning of a condition (shart), since the meaning is: "The one who steals and the one who steals (feminine)." It has been read in the accusative, and Sibawayh preferred it over the reading in the nominative, because an imperative (insha') does not occur as a predicate except with an interpretation (ta'wil) and an implied element (idmar). Theft (al-sariqah) is the taking of another's property secretly, and it necessitates amputation only when the taking is from a secure place (hirz), and the item taken is worth ten dirhams or more, together with conditions that are detailed in their proper place.

By ﴿their hands﴾ is meant their right hands, as is made clear by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "And the male thieves and the female thieves, cut off their right hands." For this reason it was permissible to place the plural in the position of the dual, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then your hearts have certainly inclined﴾, by suffice of the dual of the genitive (al-mudaf ilayhi). The "yad" (hand) is a term for the complete limb, and for this reason the Kharijites held that the place of amputation is the shoulder, while the majority hold that it is the wrist, because peace and blessings be upon him was brought a thief and he ordered that his right hand be cut off at the wrist.

﴿As a recompense﴾ is in the accusative, being either an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: "So cut off for the recompense," or an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid) for its verb which is indicated by "so cut off," meaning: "So recompense them as a recompense."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for what they have earned﴾ is, according to the first view, connected to "recompense," and according to the second, to "cut off." The ma' is verbal-masdarial (masdariyyah), meaning: "because of the earning of the two," or relative (mawsulah), meaning: "what they have earned from the theft which is carried out by the hands."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as an exemplary punishment﴾ is also an object of purpose, by way of substitution (badaliyyah) from "recompense," because they are of one kind. It has been said: the amputation is caused by the exemplary punishment. It has also been said: it is in the accusative governed by "recompense," according to the method of interlocking circumstances, for it is a cause of the recompense, and the recompense is a cause of the amputation, as when you say: "I struck him as discipline for him, as a kindness to him," for the striking is caused by the discipline, and the discipline is caused by the kindness. They have permitted, in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down, out of envy that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants﴾, that "out of envy" be an object of purpose governed by "that they disbelieve," then they said: His saying, exalted is He, "that Allah should send down," is an object of purpose governed by "out of envy," on the basis that the sending down is a cause of the envy, and the envy is a cause of the disbelief.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to an omitted element that occurs as an attribute of "exemplary punishment," meaning: "an exemplary punishment proceeding from Him, exalted is He."

﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾: Overpowering in His command, executing it as He wills, without any rival contending with Him or any opponent preventing Him.

﴿Wise﴾: In His laws, He does not decree except what wisdom and benefit require, and for this reason He legislated these laws, which encompass various kinds of wisdom and benefits.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 39:

﴿Then whoever repents﴾; i.e., from among the thieves, turns back to Allah the Exalted.

﴿after his wrongdoing﴾, which is his theft. The explicit mention of it, although repentance cannot be conceived before it, serves to show the greatness of Allah the Exalted's favor by reminding one of the greatness of his crime.

﴿and makes amends﴾; i.e., he sets his affair right by making good the consequences of what he did and by resolving not to return to it.

﴿then indeed Allah will accept his repentance﴾; i.e., He accepts his repentance, so He does not punish him in the Hereafter. As for the cutting of the hand, repentance does not remove it according to us (the Hanafis), because it involves the right of the one from whom the property was stolen; and it does remove it according to al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions.

﴿Indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾: emphatic in forgiveness and mercy, and for this reason He accepts his repentance. This is a justification for what precedes it, and the mention of the Majestic Name serves to signal the cause of the ruling and to affirm the independence of the sentence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 40:

And likewise in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾

﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ The title of divinity (ʿunwan al-ulūhiyyah) is the pivot of the rulings of their sovereignty (malakūt). The prepositional phrase "lahu" is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and "mulku as-samawati wal-ard" (the dominion of the heavens and the earth) is the subject (mubtada'); the whole clause is the predicate of "inna" (indeed). According to the majority (al-jumhur), this clause together with what is within its scope serves as the two objects of "taʿlam" (do you know). What is contained in it of repetition of the predication is for strengthening the ruling. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by way of talwin (shifting of address). It was said: it is addressed to everyone who is fit for address. The interrogative is one of denial, for affirming knowledge, and its purpose is to cite this as evidence of His, may He be exalted, power over what will follow of punishment and forgiveness, in the most eloquent and complete manner; that is: Do you not know that to Allah belongs the overpowering sovereignty and the dazzling dominion, which necessitate complete power over disposing of the whole of them both, and of what is in them, by bringing into existence and annihilating, giving life and causing death, and beyond that, as His will requires.

﴿He punishes whom He wills﴾ to punish him.

﴿and forgives whom He wills﴾ to forgive him, without any equal who shares with Him nor any opposite who contends with Him. The mention of punishment before forgiveness is to observe the order between their causes (sababayhima). The clause is either a confirmation that the sovereignty (malakut) of the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, glory be to Him, or a predicate of "inna."

﴿and Allah is over all things competent﴾ so He is able to do what has been mentioned of punishment and forgiveness. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is as has passed many times. The clause is a concluding remark (tadhyil) that confirms what precedes it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 41:**

﴿O Messenger, let not those who race to disbelief grieve you﴾. He is addressed, peace be upon him, by the title of Messengership, for honour and to indicate what makes grief unnecessary. *Al-musara'a* (hastening) in a thing means falling into it quickly and eagerly. The use of *fi* ("in") rather than *ila* ("to"), which appears in His words ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden﴾, is to indicate that they are settled in disbelief and do not leave it. They only move, through hastening, from some of its branches and rulings to others, such as showing loyalty to the polytheists and displaying acts of plotting against Islam, and the like. This is as in His words ﴿Those hasten in good deeds﴾, for they are constantly upon good and hasten in its kinds and instances. Referring to them by the relative pronoun serves to point to the basis of the grief through what is contained in its clause. Although this is apparently a prohibition to the disbelievers against causing him, peace be upon him, grief by their hastening in disbelief, it is in reality a prohibition to him, peace be upon him, against being affected by that and against caring about them, in the most emphatic and forceful manner. For prohibiting the causes and beginnings of a thing that lead to it is a prohibition against it by way of demonstration, and a uprooting of it from its origin. The prohibition may also be directed at the effect while what is meant is the prohibition of the cause, as in the saying "I should not see you here," meaning: a prohibition of the one addressed from being present before him.

It is also read: ﴿لا يُحْزِنْكَ﴾ (*yuhzinka*) from *ahzanahu*, transitive form of *hazina* with the *ra'* vowelled with kasra. And it is read: ﴿يُسْرِعُونَ﴾ (*yusri'una*), from "*asra'a fihi al-shayb*," meaning: grey hair fell upon it quickly. That is: do not grieve, and do not care about their rushing headlong into disbelief quickly.

His words ﴿from those who say, "We believe" with their mouths﴾ are an explanation of those who hasten into disbelief. It has been said that it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of "they hasten." It has also been said that it is from the relative pronoun, meaning: "being among those who..." etc. The *ba'* (with) is connected to "they say," not to "we believe."

His words ﴿and their hearts have not believed﴾ are a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*) from the pronoun in "they say." It has been said that it is coordinated with "they say."

His words ﴿and from those who are Jews﴾ are coordinated with "from those who say" etc., and by this the explanation of those who hasten into disbelief is completed, by dividing them into two groups: the hypocrites and the Jews.

His words ﴿listeners to falsehood﴾ are the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*) referring to both groups, or to those who hasten. As for its referring to those who are Jews, this undermines the generality of the threat that follows and its beginnings for all, as you will see. Similarly, making "and among those who..." etc. a predicate, on the basis that "listeners" is a qualifier of an omitted subject, meaning: "and among them are a people who are listeners," etc., leads to restricting the listed vices and the worldly and otherworldly calamities that result from them to them alone. So the correct view is the one mentioned first, namely: they are listeners. The *lam* is either to strengthen the operation, or to include the meaning of acceptance in "listening," or it is the *lam* of purpose with the object omitted. The meaning is: they are excessive in listening to falsehood, or in accepting what their rabbis fabricate of lies against God, glorified is He, and the distortion of His Book; or they are listeners to your reports and your talk in order to lie about you by distorting them through addition, subtraction, substitution and alteration; or they are listeners to the reports and sayings of people circulating among themselves, in order to lie in them by spreading rumours of the killing of believers, the defeat of their expeditions, and similar things that harm them.

In any case, the clause is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustanifa*) functioning as a justification for the prohibition. Their being listeners to falsehood in the aforementioned ways, and their affairs being built on what has no basis of fabrications and rumours, requires not caring about them and not regarding what they do or leave undone, because the falsity of their lies is certain to become evident, and the corrupt actions they built upon them will collapse, leading to disgrace and punishment, as will come. It is also read: ﴿سَمّاعِينَ لِلْكَذِبِ﴾ in the accusative, as a censure.

His words ﴿listeners for another people﴾ are a second predicate of the omitted subject, confirming the first and clarifying what is meant by "falsehood" in the first two interpretations. The *lam* is like that in "God hears those who praise Him" (*sami'a Allahu liman hamidah*), in returning to the meaning of *min* ("from"): that is, He accepted from him his praise. The meaning is: they are excessive in accepting the speech of another people. As for it being the *lam* of causation, meaning "listening from him, peace be upon him, for the sake of another people who sent them as spies to convey to them what they heard from him, peace be upon him," or it being connected to "falsehood" on the basis that the second "listeners" is a repetition for emphasis, meaning "listening in order to lie for another people," this hardly accords with the noble structure of the text at all.

His words ﴿who have not come to you﴾ are another qualifier of the people, meaning: they did not attend your assembly, and they kept away from you out of arrogance and extreme hatred. It has been said: they are the Jews of Khaybar, and the listeners are the Banu Qurayza.

His words ﴿they distort the words from their places﴾ are another qualifier of the people, described first by their difference from the listeners, to draw attention to their independence and originality in opinion and planning; then by their not attending the assembly of the Messenger, peace be upon him, as a notice of the completeness of their transgression in error; then by their persistence in distortion, as a clarification of their excess in obstinacy and insolence, and their audacity in fabricating against God, exalted is He, and as a specification of the lie that the listeners heard. That is: they incline it and remove it from its places after God had placed it there, either verbally by neglecting it or changing its arrangement, or in meaning by applying it to what is not intended and using it in a place where it does not belong. It has been said: the clause is a resumed clause with no place in the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*), denouncing their shameful acts. It has also been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject referring to the people.

His words ﴿they say﴾ are like the preceding clause in the aforementioned respects, and it is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "they distort." As for permitting it to be a qualifier of "listeners," or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in it, this has no pathway at all. How could it be so, since the content of the speech shows that its speaker is among those who do not attend the assembly of the Messenger, peace be upon him, while the one addressed is among those who attend it? How could the listeners, who frequent him, peace be upon him, say it to the one who certainly does not come near him? To claim that the listeners said it to their followers who mix with the Muslims is an evident strain, disrupting the eloquence of the noble structure. The truth from which there is no escape is that the distorters and speakers are the other people; that is, they say to their followers, the listeners to them, when they convey to them their false sayings, pointing to their false speech:

﴿If you are given this﴾ from the Messenger, peace be upon him,

﴿then take it﴾ and act upon its requirement, for it is the truth.

﴿But if you are not given it﴾ rather you are given something else,

﴿then beware﴾; that is: beware of accepting it, and keep away from it. In placing the command to beware upon the mere non-giving of the distorted ruling, there is an exaggeration in warning that is not hidden. It is narrated: "A nobleman from Khaybar committed adultery with a noblewoman, and both were married, and the punishment for them in the Torah is stoning. They disliked stoning them because of their nobility, so they sent a group of them to the Banu Qurayza to ask the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, about that, and they said: 'If he orders you to flog and blacken them, accept it, and if he orders you to stone them, do not accept it.' They sent the two adulterers with them, and he ordered them to be stoned, but they refused to act on it. Gabriel, peace be upon him, said: 'Put between you and them Ibn Suriya,' and described him to him. He, peace be upon him, said: 'Do you know a fair-skinned, one-eyed young man who lives in Fadak, called Ibn Suriya?' They said: 'Yes, and he is the most learned Jew on the face of the earth in what God revealed to Musa son of 'Imran in the Torah.' He said: 'Then send for him.' They did so, and he came. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said to him: 'Are you Ibn Suriya?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'And are you the most learned of the Jews?' He said: 'So they claim.' He said to them: 'Do you accept him as a judge?' They said: 'Yes.' The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said to him: 'I ask you by God, besides whom there is no god, who split the sea and saved you and drowned the family of Pharaoh, who shaded you with the clouds and sent down upon you manna and quails, who raised the mount above you and sent down upon you the Torah in which is its lawful and its unlawful, do you find in your Book the stoning of one who is married?' He said: 'Yes, and by the one through whom you reminded me, were it not that I feared that the Torah would burn me if I lied, or changed what I have acknowledged to you, but how is it in your Book, O Muhammad?' The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'When four reliable men testify that he entered her as the kohl stick enters the kohl pot, stoning becomes obligatory for him.' Ibn Suriya said: 'By the one who sent down the Torah to Musa, thus God sent down in the Torah to Musa.' Then the base among the Jews fell upon him, and he said: 'I feared that if I lied to him, God would send down punishment upon us.' Then he asked the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, about things he used to know from his signs, and said: 'I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that you are the Messenger of God, the unlettered Arab Prophet whom the messengers foretold.' The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, ordered the two adulterers, and they were stoned at the gate of the mosque."

﴿And whoever God wills to test﴾; that is: whoever God wills to lead astray, or to expose, whoever he may be. The aforementioned are included in this by primary inclusion. The absence of an explicit statement that they are such is to indicate that it is completely evident and needs no mention.

﴿then you will not avail for him﴾; that is: you will not be able for him

﴿against God in anything﴾ to avert it. The clause is a resumed clause confirming what precedes it, and clarifying that they will never be free from the aforementioned vices.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the aforementioned hypocrites and Jews, and what is in the demonstrative of distance indicates the distance of their rank in corruption. It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is His words: ﴿those whose hearts God did not will to purify﴾; that is: from the filth of disbelief and the foulness of error, because of their immersion in both, their persistence in them, and their turning away from directing their choice toward attaining guidance entirely, as is indicated by their description of hastening into disbelief at the outset and the enumeration of the branches of their errors at the end. The clause is a resumed clause clarifying that God's will for their testing is conditioned on their bad choice and the evil of their conduct, which necessitates it, not that it is initiated by Him, exalted is He.

﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾. As for the hypocrites, their disgrace is their exposure and the tearing away of their veil through the manifestation of their hypocrisy among the Muslims. As for the disgrace of the Jews, it is humiliation and the poll tax, and being exposed through the evidence of their lying in concealing the text of the Torah. The indefiniteness of "disgrace" is for magnification. It is the subject, and "for them" is its predicate, and "in this world" is connected to what the predicate is connected to, namely the being established. The same applies to His words ﴿and for them in the Hereafter﴾; that is: in addition to the worldly disgrace.

﴿is a great punishment﴾, which is abiding in the Fire. The pronoun in "for them" in both clauses refers to the hypocrites and the Jews together, not to the Jews alone as has been said. The repetition of "for them" despite the unity of reference is for additional confirmation and emphasis. The two clauses are a resumed clause built upon a question arising from the detailing of their actions and conditions that necessitate punishment, as if it were said: "What then is their punishment?" So it is said: "For them in this world," etc.

[p-37] [p-38] [p-39]

﴿They are listeners to falsehood﴾ is another predicate (khabar) for an implied subject (mubtada'), repeated to emphasize what came before it and to prepare for what follows it, namely Allah's words ﴿devourers of the illicit gain﴾. It is also another predicate for the implied subject, coming in the mode of censure. Alternatively, the meaning of "falsehood" (al-kadhib) is what the bribe-takers invent before those who devour the illicit gain.

"Al-suht" (السُّحْتُ), with a ḍammah on the sīn and a sukūn on the ḥā', originally means anything whose earnings are not lawful. It is said to mean any forbidden thing in general, from "saḥatahu," meaning he uprooted it. It is so called because its blessing is annihilated (mashūt al-barakah). Here it may mean the bribes that the distorters took in return for their distortion and their other deviant rulings, which is the well-known view. Or it may mean the wealth that their poor took from their rich in order to keep them in Judaism, as has been said. Or it may mean forbidden things in general, which encompasses what has been mentioned in an initial sense. It is also recited as ﴿lil-suhuti﴾ (لِلسُّحُتِ) with a ḍammah on the sīn and the ḥā', with a fatḥah on both, with a fatḥah on the sīn and a sukūn on the ḥā', and with a kasrah on the sīn and a sukūn on the ḥā'. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every flesh that illicit gain has made grow, the Fire is more deserving of it."

﴿If they come to you﴾. When he (ﷺ) had explained the details of their worthless matters and their various conditions, which made it necessary not to care about them or their actions, as he had been commanded, he (ﷺ) was addressed with some of the rulings that are built upon this, by way of derivation (tafrī'). The fa' is eloquent (faṣīḥah), meaning: and when their condition is as described, then if they come to you seeking judgment (mutaḥākimīn) concerning the disputes that arose among them, ﴿then judge between them or turn away from them﴾, without being concerned about them and without fearing them at all.

As you see, this is an option (takhyīr) given to him (ﷺ) between the two matters. It has been said that this concerns a specific matter, namely what was mentioned about the fornication of a married person. It has also been said: "Concerning a slain man who was killed from among the Jews, from the Banu Qurayza and the Banu al-Nadir. They took their dispute to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Banu Qurayza said: 'Our brothers, the Banu al-Nadir, have one father, one religion, and one prophet. When they kill one of us, they do not accept retaliation (qawad) but give us seventy wasq of dates. When we kill one of them, they kill the killer and take from us double: one hundred and forty wasq of dates. If the slain is a woman, they kill a man of ours for her, and for a man of theirs they kill two men of ours, and for a slave of theirs they kill a free man of ours. So judge between us.' So the Prophet (ﷺ) made the blood-money equal." It has also been said that it is general concerning all judgments. Then they differed. Some say it is established (thābit), which is the view narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Shaʿbī, Qatādah, Abū Bakr al-Aṣamm, and Abū Muslim. Others say it is abrogated (mansūkh) by naskh, which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and ʿIkrimah. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "Only two verses have been abrogated from al-Mā'idah: His words ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah﴾, which was abrogated by His words ﴿kill the polytheists﴾, and His words ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾, which was abrogated by His words ﴿and judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾." Our shaykhs held this view.

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ explains the state of the two matters following His giving him (ﷺ) the option between them. The mention of the state of turning away first is to hasten to clarify that there is no harm in it, since it was the place where harm was expected. This is because they would not take their disputes to him (ﷺ) except to seek what was easier and lighter for them. So if he turned away from them and refused to rule between them, that would be hard for them, and their enmity and their harming of him (ﷺ) would intensify. So Allah, mighty and majestic, assured him with His words ﴿they will not harm you at all﴾, meaning with any harm, for Allah is the One who protects you from people.

﴿And if you judge, then judge between them with justice﴾, with the justice you were commanded to, just as you judged by stoning.

﴿Indeed Allah loves the just﴾. It is part of His necessity that He protects them from every disliked and feared thing. (p-40)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 43:

﴿How is it that they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of God?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their seeking judgment from one in whom they do not believe, nor in his Book, while the ruling is explicitly stated in their own scripture, which they claim to believe in. It also indicates that by seeking judgment they did not intend to know the truth or to establish the Sharia; rather they sought what was easier for them, even though that was not God's judgment according to their own claim. Here, ﴿while they have the Torah﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of "they make you judge," and ﴿in which is the judgment of God﴾ is a circumstantial clause referring to "the Torah," if "in which" is taken as a predicate complement of the Torah; if the Torah is taken as the subject (mubtadaʾ), then it is a circumstantial clause referring to the pronoun within the predicate. It has also been said that it is a resumptive (isti'nāf) sentence, brought to clarify that they have with them that which suffices them from seeking judgment. The feminine form of the verb (ʾ-n-th) for it is because "Torah" is like a feminine noun in their speech, as in "mawmāh" and "dawdāh."

﴿Then they turn away﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "they make you judge," falling within the scope of the expression of wonder, and "then" (thumma) here indicates delay in rank (tarākhī fī al-rutba).

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿after that﴾, meaning: after they had made you judge, this is an explicit statement of what is known with certainty, for the sake of emphasizing the sense of remoteness and wonder; that is: then they turn away from your judgment, which agrees with their Book, after they had consented to your judgment.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And those are not believers﴾, it is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) confirming the implication of what precedes it. The demonstrative pronoun (ism al-ishāra) is used in place of the pronoun "they," aiming to bring their vices to mind by the qualities they were described with, as an indication of the cause of the ruling, and that they have distinguished themselves from others with the fullest distinction, so that they are counted among the evident matters. The sense of distance in it is to announce the remoteness of their rank in obstinacy and stubbornness. That is: and those described with what has been mentioned are not believers, that is, in their Book, because they turned away from it first, and from your judgment, which agrees with it, second, or both. It has also been said: and those are not perfect in faith, mocking them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 5, verse 44:**

﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah﴾ is a new, independent statement (*kalam mustanaf*), brought to show the exalted status of the Torah (*al-Tawrat*), the obligation to observe its rulings, and that it has always been observed among the prophets and those who follow them, generation after generation. It was accepted by every judge and every litigant, and it was protected from alteration and substitution. This confirms what was said about the distorters, that they did not believe in it, and it establishes their disbelief and wrongdoing.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wherein is guidance and light﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the Torah. The rulings and laws in it are guidance, insofar as they direct people to the truth from which there is no deviation. And insofar as they clarify and reveal what is obscure among the rulings and the matters connected with them that are hidden in the darkness of ignorance, they are light.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾: that is, the prophets of the Children of Israel. It was also said: Moses and the prophets after him. This is a new independent clause (*jumla mustanafa*) explaining the elevated rank of the Torah and the lofty stature of its class. It has also been permitted that this be a circumstantial clause referring to the Torah, in which case it is a future circumstantial clause (*hal muqaddara*): that is, they judged by its rulings and compelled the people to follow them. Those who held that the law of those before us is a law for us, so long as it has not been abrogated, relied on this. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the subject (*al-jarr wa'l-majrur*) is for the reason mentioned many times: the attention given to the matter placed first, and the building of anticipation for what comes later. Also, what comes later together with its complement has a kind of length which, if placed earlier, might disrupt the harmony of the parts of the noble composition. (p-41)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿who submitted﴾ is an attribute applied to the prophets in the manner of praise, not of specification or clarification. Yet the intention is not truly to praise them with it, since prophethood is certainly greater than submission (*Islam*). Describing them with it after describing them with prophethood is a descent from the higher to the lower. Rather, it is to draw attention to the importance of the attribute, for displaying an attribute in the context of praising the great indicates the greatness of the attribute without doubt, as in the description of the prophets with righteousness and the description of the angels with faith, upon them be peace. For this reason it has been said: "The attributes of the noble are the noblest of attributes." In it there is also an elevation of the status of the Muslims and an allusion against the Jews, that they are far removed from submission and from following the religion of the prophets, peace be upon them, especially when one considers what they were described with in His saying: ﴿for those who were Jews﴾, which is connected to "judge." The lam here may be to indicate that the ruling is specific to them, whether it is for them or against them in general, as if it were said: "for the sake of those who were Jews." Or it is to signal that it benefits the one judged against as well, by removing responsibility from him. Or it is to indicate that they fully accepted it and submitted to it, as if it were a matter beneficial to both parties, so there is an allusion against the distorters. It was also said: the sense is "for those who were Jews and against them," and what was omitted is omitted because what was mentioned indicates it. It was also said: it is connected to "We revealed." It was also said: it is connected to "guidance and light," and in that case there is a separation between the verbal noun and its complement. It was also said: it is connected to an omitted element that functions as an attribute of both: that is, guidance and light existing for those who were Jews.

﴿And the rabbis and the scholars﴾: that is, the ascetics and scholars from the descendants of Aaron, who adhered to the way of the prophets and kept away from the religion of the Jews. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The *Rabbaniyyun* are those who govern people by knowledge and nurture them with its minor matters before its major matters. The *Ahbar* are the jurists (*fuqaha'*); their singular is *habr*, with fatha and kasra, and the second is more eloquent, and it is the opinion of al-Farra', derived from *tahbir* and *tahsin* (embellishment and beautification), for they embellish knowledge, adorn it, and make it clear." It is conjoined to "the prophets": that is, they also judge by its rulings. Placing the ones judged between the two conjoined items is to signal that the origin of judging by it, and of compelling people to what is in it, belongs to the prophets, while the rabbis and the scholars are their successors and deputies in that.

As His saying indicates: ﴿by what they were entrusted with﴾: that is, by that which they were entrusted with from the side of the prophets, namely the Torah, for they were asked to preserve it from alteration and substitution in every respect. There is no doubt that this, from them, peace be upon them, is a delegation to them in carrying out its rulings without omitting anything from it, and in its (initial) general statement.

Then its specification comes second, in His saying: ﴿of the Book of Allah﴾, which magnifies and glorifies it in essence and in attribution, and emphasizes the obligation to preserve it and act upon what is in it, which is evident. Its presentation under the title "Book" alludes to the obligation to preserve it against alteration in terms of writing. The preposition *ba'* attached to the relative pronoun is connected to "judge," but not as a complement to it, as in His saying ﴿by it﴾, so as to avoid two prepositions of identical meaning being attached to one verb. Rather, it is causal: that is, the rabbis and scholars also judge by reason of what they preserved of the Book of Allah, as their prophets enjoined on them and asked them to preserve it. What is meant by its causality for their judging is not causality in terms of its essence, but in terms of its being entrusted, for attaching their judging to the relative clause indicates that the causality of preservation, which necessarily follows from what is in the relative clause's scope of being entrusted with it, is what is meant. It was also said: the *ba'* is a complement of an omitted verb conjoined to His saying: ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾, conjoining one clause to another. The sense: and the rabbis and scholars judge by the ruling of the Book of Allah, which their prophets asked them to preserve from alteration.

﴿And they were witnesses over it﴾: that is, guardians who protect it so that alteration and substitution cannot approach it in any way. The change of style is for the excellences mentioned. It was also said: "by what they were entrusted with" is a substitute for His saying "by it," with the governing element repeated, but this is far-fetched. Likewise, permitting that the pronoun in "were entrusted" refers to the prophets, the rabbis and the scholars all together, with the entrusting coming from the side of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: that is, Allah obligated them to preserve it and to be witnesses over it.

His saying, Exalted and Sanctified is He: ﴿So do not fear people﴾ is addressed to the chiefs and scholars of the Jews by way of *iltifat* (a shift in address). As for the rulers of the Muslims, the prohibition encompasses them by way of implication (*dalala*) rather than explicit expression (*ibara*). The *fa'* (so) is for ordering the prohibition upon what was detailed about the state of the Torah, its being a matter of importance among the prophets, peace be upon them, and those who follow them of the rabbis and scholars who came before, in practice and preservation. This is because that necessitates avoiding any neglect of the duties of observing it and safeguarding it in any manner, let alone distortion and alteration. Since the root of their audacity in this was fear of a powerful ruler, or desire for worldly advantages, they were forbidden from each of these explicitly. That is: if its state is as mentioned, then do not fear people, whoever they may be, and follow, in observing and preserving its rulings, those among the prophets before you and their adherents.

﴿And fear Me﴾: in neglecting the rights of observing it. How much more so, then, should one fear touching it with harm.

﴿And do not exchange My signs﴾: *al-ishtira'* is exchanging merchandise for a price, that is, taking it in place of the price, not paying the price in order to obtain it, as has been said. Then it was used figuratively for taking something in place of what one had, whether concrete or abstract, taking that is tied to desire for what is taken and turning away from what was given and cast aside, as detailed in the explanation of His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who bought error in exchange for guidance﴾. The meaning is: do not substitute for My signs, which contain guidance, by removing them from it, or by leaving off acting upon them and taking for yourselves something in their place.

﴿A small price﴾: of bribery, status, and all other worldly advantages. For these, however great, are small and despicable in themselves, especially compared with what is lost to them by abandoning acting upon the signs. The phrase expresses the *mushtara* (what is bought), which is the principal element in contracts of exchange and the essential aim, by the *thaman* (price), whose nature is to be a means to obtaining it. The signs, which by right ought to be what competitors compete for, are presented in the manner of tools and intermediaries, since they are joined to the *ba'* that accompanies means. This signals the extent of their reversing things, by making the ultimate aim a means and the lesser means an aim.

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down﴾: whoever he may be, beyond the addressees specifically, since they are included in it in a primary way. That is: whoever does not judge by that, treating it with contempt and denying it, as their deeds of distorting the signs of Allah, Exalted is He, clearly require.

﴿Then those﴾: a reference to "whoever," and the plural is in view of its meaning, just as the singular earlier is in view of its wording.

﴿They are the disbelievers﴾: because of their contempt for it. The *hum* may be the separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*), or a subject with what follows it as its predicate. The clause is the predicate of "those." Its detailed treatment has already been given at the opening of Surah al-Baqarah. The clause is a concluding remark (*tadhyil*) that confirms what precedes it in the most emphatic way and warns against neglecting it with the strongest warning, since the ruling of disbelief is attached in it merely to abandoning judgment by what Allah, Exalted is He, has sent down. How much more so when judging by its opposite is added to it, especially with the direct commission of what they were forbidden: distorting it, placing something else in its place, and claiming that it is from Allah, in order that they might exchange it for a small price.

(p-43)

﴿And We prescribed﴾ is coordinated with "We sent down the Torah."

﴿upon them﴾; that is, upon those who were Jews. It is also read: "And God sent down upon the Children of Israel."

﴿therein﴾; that is, in the Torah.

﴿that the life is for the life﴾: that he is to be subjected to retaliation (qisas) with it if he kills him unjustly.

﴿and the eye﴾ is to be gouged out ﴿for the eye﴾ if it was gouged out unjustly.

﴿and the nose﴾ is to be slit ﴿for the nose﴾ that was cut off unjustly.

﴿and the ear﴾ is to be cut off ﴿for the ear﴾ that was cut off wrongfully.

﴿and the tooth﴾ is to be pulled out ﴿for the tooth﴾ that was pulled out unjustly.

﴿and for wounds, retaliation﴾; that is, wounds are subject to retaliation when it is possible to establish equality. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they used not to kill a man for a woman, and so this was revealed. It is also read: "And that the wounds are subject to retaliation." It is also read: "and the eye" through to the end in the nominative case, coordinated with the position (mahall) of "that the life": because the meaning is, "the life for the life was prescribed upon them," either by treating "We prescribed" as equivalent to "We said," or because the meaning of the sentence, which is your saying "the life for the life," is something that can be the object of writing just as it can be the object of recitation. You say, "I wrote 'al-hamdu lillah'," and "I recited 'a surah which We sent down'" (Qur'an 24:1).

﴿Then whoever forgoes it﴾; that is, of those entitled to it.

﴿with it﴾; that is, with the retaliation; that is, whoever pardons him. Expressing it as "forgoes" (tasaddaqa) is for emphasis in encouraging it.

﴿it is﴾; that is, the forgoing.

﴿an expiation for him﴾; that is, for the one who forgoes: Allah the Exalted expiates his sins by it. It has also been said: for the offender, when the rightful claimant overlooks him, what was binding on him falls away. It is also read: "then it is his expiation for him"; that is, the one who forgoes has his expiation, which he deserves by forgoing, and nothing of it is diminished. This is an exaltation of what he did, like the Exalted's saying: ﴿So his reward is with Allah﴾ (Qur'an 4:100).

﴿And whoever does not judge﴾, whoever he may be, so it clearly includes those Jews who do not regard killing a man for a woman as lawful.

﴿by what Allah has sent down﴾ of rulings and laws, whatever they may be, so the rulings related here enter it first and foremost.

﴿then those — they are the wrongdoers﴾: those who go to extremes in wrongdoing, who transgress Allah the Exalted's limits, who place a thing in other than its place. The sentence is a concluding statement affirming the obligation to act by the rulings mentioned.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 46:**

﴿And We followed in their footsteps﴾: this begins the explanation of the rulings of the Injil (Gospel) after the explanation of the rulings of the Tawrat (Torah). It is a conjunction (ʿatf) on "We sent down the Tawrat," meaning: in the footsteps of the aforementioned clarifications. One says قَفَّيْتُهُ بِفُلانٍ (qaffaytuhu bi-fulan) when you make him follow someone, so the object is omitted because the prepositional phrase indicates it. The meaning is: We made them follow.

﴿with Isa, son of Maryam﴾: that is, We sent him after them.

﴿confirming what was before him of the Tawrat﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from Isa, peace be upon him.

﴿And We gave him the Injil﴾ is a conjunction on "We followed," and it has been read with a fatha on the hamza (وَآتَيْناهُ الإنْجِيلَ, with the hamza vowelled differently in one reading).

﴿in it is guidance and light﴾, as in the Tawrat. It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from "the Injil," meaning: existing with that in it, as if it were said: containing guidance and light. The tanwin on "guidance and light" is for emphasis (tafkhim), and within this are the proofs of his prophethood, peace be upon him.

﴿and confirming what was before him of the Tawrat﴾ is a conjunction on "him," falling under the same circumstantial status, and the repetition of "what was before him of the Tawrat" is for additional affirmation.

﴿and guidance and admonition for the God-fearing﴾ is a conjunction on "confirming," joined with it in the same circumstantial status. All of it is described as guidance after it was described as containing guidance, where it says "guidance." The specification of it being "guidance and admonition" for the God-fearing is because they are the ones guided by its guidance and who benefit from its bounty.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 47:

﴿Let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein﴾ is a fresh command (amr mubtada') for them to judge and to act by what is in it, among the matters of which are the proofs of his messengership, peace be upon him, the evidences of his prophethood, and what the noble Shari'ah (the sacred law) has established of his rulings. As for his abrogated rulings, judging by them is not judging by what Allah has revealed therein; rather, it is nullification and suspension of it, since it bears witness to their abrogation (naskh) and to the expiry of the time for acting by them. Its testimony to the validity of what abrogates them from the Shari'ah is a testimony to their abrogation, and [its testimony] that its rulings are what that Shari'ah established, whose validity it testified to, as will come in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Book, you are not upon anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel﴾, the verse.

It was also said: it is a narration of the command directed at them, with a verb supplied and conjoined to "We gave him" (ātaynāhu); that is, "And We said: Let the People of the Gospel judge..." etc. It was recited as "wa-an li-yaḥkum" (وأنْ لِيَحْكم), on the basis that "an" is a relative-linking particle connected to the command, as in your saying: "I commanded him that qum" (أمَرْتُهُ بِأنْ قُمْ), as if it were said: "And We gave him the Gospel and commanded that the People of the Gospel judge..." etc. It was also recited in the present-tense form with the lam of purpose (wa-li-yaḥkum), on the basis that it is connected to a supplied element, as if it were said: "And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein; We gave him it." It has also been conjoined to "guidance and admonition" (hudan wa-mawʿiẓah), on the basis that both are objects of purpose, as if it were said: "And for guidance and admonition We gave him it, and for judging by what Allah has revealed therein."

﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed﴾ denying it and scorning it.

﴿Then those are the defiant ones (al-fāsiqūn)﴾, the rebellious ones who have left faith. The sentence is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) that confirms the meaning of the preceding sentence and emphasizes the obligation of complying with the command. It indicates that the Gospel contains rulings, and that ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, was independent in the law, commanded to act by what is in it of rulings, whether few or many, and not only by what is in the Torah. To interpret it as meaning "and let them judge by what Allah has revealed therein, namely the obligation to act by the rulings of the Torah" is contrary to the apparent meaning.

And We have sent down to you the Book: that is, the perfect, true singular (of the Book), such that it deserves to be called "the Book" absolutely, because it possesses all the perfect attributes of the genus of heavenly Books and surpasses the rest of its individual members. This is the Noble Qur'an. The definite article (al-) is for previous reference (lil-'ahd), and the clause is coordinated (ʿatf) with "We sent down" and what is coordinated with it.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿with the truth﴾ is connected to an omitted element and occupies the position of a emphasizing circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the Book": that is, accompanied by truth and sincerity. It has been said that it relates to the subject of "We sent down," and it has been said that it relates to the *kaf* in "to you."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the Book": that is, being a confirmer of what preceded it, either in respect of its being sent down in the manner in which the previous Books described it, or in respect of its agreeing with them in narratives, promises, the call to the truth and justice among people, and the prohibition of sins and abominations. As for what appears to be its contradiction with them in some particular rulings that change according to the changing of the ages, this is not a contradiction in reality; rather, it is in agreement with them, since each of those rulings is true relative to its own age and includes the wisdom upon which the purpose of the Law revolves. There is nothing in the earlier (Books) that indicates the perpetuity of their rulings which have been abrogated (mansukha), such that the later abrogating (nasikh) ruling would contradict them. The earlier (Books) only indicate their legitimacy absolutely, without addressing their continuation or cessation. Rather, we say: it speaks explicitly of their cessation, because affirming the validity of that which abrogates them is a statement of their abrogation and cessation.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿of the Book﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of "what," and the definite article is for the genus, since what is meant is the heavenly Book, which under this title is a genus in itself, even though in itself it is a specific type within the meaning of the word "Book." On this basis they said the definite article is for previous reference (al-ʿahd), except that this does not terminate in the specificity of individuality, but in the specificity of type, which is more specific than the general "Book." This is evident. And (it is) of the heavenly Book as well, since it has been specified as distinct from everything other than the Qur'an.

﴿And a guardian over it﴾: that is, a watcher over all the other Books, which are preserved from alteration, because it bears witness to their soundness and stability, affirms the principles of their laws, and what of their branches endures permanently, specifies their abrogated rulings by clarifying the end of the legitimacy of those rulings derived from those Books, and the expiry of the time for acting upon them. There is no doubt that distinguishing its rulings that remain legitimate forever from those whose time of legitimacy has ended and which have passed out of it is among the rulings of its being a guardian over it.

It has been read: (*muhaymanan ʿalayhi*), with the passive form: that is, it has been guarded over and preserved from alteration and change, as in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾. The Guardian is either from His part, exalted is He, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾, or the guardians in every age and every land.

The *fa'* in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So judge between them﴾ is for the consequence of what follows upon what precedes it, since the status of the Mighty Qur'an being the truth, confirming what came before it of the Books sent down to the nations, and being a guardian over them, necessitates the judgment commanded: that is, if the Qur'an is as has been mentioned, then judge between the People of the two Books when they come to you for judgment.

﴿by what God has sent down﴾: that is, by what He has sent down to you, for it comprises all the legal rulings that remain in the Divine Books. The placement of "between them" first is for the concern of explaining that the ruling applies to them all. Placing the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun is to alert to the causal status of what is within the relative clause for the ruling, and the shift to the explicit noun of the Majestic Name is to cultivate awe and to signal the cause of the ruling.

﴿And do not follow their desires﴾, the deviant ones,

﴿away from the truth that has come to you﴾, which cannot be deviated from. "Away from" (*ʿan*) is connected to "do not follow," with the implication (*tadmin*) of the meaning of deviating or the like, as if it were said: "And do not deviate from the truth that has come to you by following their desires." It has been said it is connected to an omitted element that occupies the position of a circumstantial clause relating to its subject: that is, do not follow their desires while deviating from what has come to you. In this there is the point that what occupies the position of a circumstantial clause must necessarily be a general verb. The placement of the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun of the first relative is to allude, by what is in the relative clause, to the arrival of the truth, to that which necessitates complete avoidance of following desires.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ is a resumed statement (*istinaf*) brought in to lead the People of the two Books among his contemporaries (ﷺ) to submit to his judgment by what has been sent down to him of the Noble Qur'an, by explaining that it is the one they were commanded to act upon, to the exclusion of the other two Books. Those who were commanded to act upon the two (earlier Books) were only those among the earlier nations who lived before their abrogation. The address is by way of shifting (*taljin*) and turning (*iltifat*) to people in general, but not only to those present, rather also to those who passed before, by way of prevalence (*taghlib*). The *lam* is connected to "We have made," which is transitive to one object, and it is a report of a past making, not a performative utterance (*insha'*), and its placement before it is for specification. "Among you" is connected to an omitted element that occupies the position of an attributive modifier to what the nunation of *kull* stands in for. There is no harm in placing "We have made" between the modifier and the modified, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Shall I take other than God as a protector, the Originator of the heavens and the earth?﴾ ... etc. The meaning is: for every nation among you, O nations that remain and those that have passed, We have made, that is, We have appointed and established, a law (*shir'a*) and a way (*minhaj*) specific to that nation, such that no nation can overstep the law appointed for it. Thus the nation that existed from the mission of Moses to the mission of Jesus, peace be upon them both, had the Torah as its law, and the nation that existed from the mission of Jesus to the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) had the Gospel as its law. As for you, O present ones, your law is the Qur'an alone, so believe in it and act upon what is in it. The *shir'a* and *shari'a* are the path to water; the religion has been likened to it because it is a connected path to what is the cause of eternal life, just as water is the cause of transient life. The *minhaj* is the clear path in religion, from *nahaja al-amr*, when it became clear.

It has been read: (*shar'atan*) with a fatha on the *shin*. It has been said: in this is evidence that we are not bound to the laws of those before us. The verified position is that we are bound by their remaining rulings, insofar as they are rulings of our law, not insofar as they are the law of the earlier people.

﴿And had God willed, He would have made you one nation﴾ agreed upon one religion in all ages, without difference between you and those before you among the nations in any of the religious rulings, and without abrogation or alteration. The object of the will is omitted, relying on the indication of the conditional clause upon it: that is, "And had God willed that He make you one nation, He would have made you..." etc. It has been said the meaning is: had God willed your gathering upon Islam, He would have compelled you to it.

﴿But that He may try you﴾ is connected to an omitted element that the context requires: that is, "But He did not will that," namely, to make you one nation; rather He willed what the Divine Practice (*sunna*) that operates among the nations requires, so that He may deal with you as one who tests you.

﴿in what He has given you﴾, of the diverse laws suited to their ages and centuries: whether you will act upon them, submitting to them, believing that their difference is in accordance with the Divine Will founded upon the basis of profound wisdoms and beneficial interests for you in your livelihood and your afterlife; or whether you will deviate from the truth and follow desire, exchanging harm for benefit, and buying error for guidance? By this it becomes clear that the basis for the non-willing mentioned is not merely testing, but the principal matter in that is what has been pointed out: that difference encompasses what contains their interest in livelihood and afterlife.

As His saying, mighty and majestic is He, indicates: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾: that is, since the matter is as has been mentioned, then hasten to what is better for you in both abodes, of true beliefs and righteous deeds included in the Noble Qur'an, and seize them, taking advantage of the opportunity and securing precedence in virtue and advancement. In this there is of emphasizing the encouragement to submit to the truth and intensifying the warning against deviation what is not hidden.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To God is your return﴾ is a resumed statement, brought as a justification for racing to good deeds, with the promise and threat it contains.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿all together﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun of address, and its governing element is either the verbal noun resolved into a verbal particle and a verb in the active or passive, or the implicit stability within the preposition-phrase.

﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to differ about﴾: that is, He will do to you, of the recompense that separates the righteous from the falsifier, what leaves you no trace of doubt, regarding what you used to differ about in this world. He expressed it by what has been mentioned because it takes the place of removing the difference, which is the function of information.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 49:

﴿And judge between them by what God has revealed, and do not follow their desires﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "the Book"; that is, We sent down to you the Book and the judgment according to what it contains. The mention of the title of His sending it down (inzal) is to emphasize the obligation to comply with the command. Alternatively, it is coordinated with "the truth"; that is, We sent it down with the truth and [sent down] "and judge."

The narration of the sending down of the command to this judgment, after the explicit command to this effect that has already passed, is an affirmation of it and a preparation for what follows it, the words of the Exalted: ﴿And beware of them, lest they tempt you away from some of what God has revealed to you﴾; that is, they divert you away from part of it, even if it is the smallest amount, by presenting falsehood in the form of truth. The mention of the Glorious Name (the Divine Name) is to emphasize the matter by magnifying the gravity of the affair. The particle "an" with its complement is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition, a substitute that includes its referent) for the pronoun in "them"; that is, beware of their temptation. Or it is a maf'ul lahu (object of purpose, a accusative of reason); that is, beware of them for fear that they will tempt you. The repetition of "what God has revealed" is to emphasize the warning by magnifying the gravity of the affair.

It is narrated that "the rabbis of the Jews said: Come, let us go to Muhammad, perhaps we can tempt him away from his religion. So they went to him (ﷺ) and said: O Abu al-Qasim, you know that we are rabbis of the Jews, and that if we follow you, all the Jews will follow us, and that there is a dispute between us and our people, so we will bring it to you for judgment, and you will rule in our favor against them, and we will believe in you and affirm you. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) refused that, and so it was revealed."

﴿But if they turn away﴾; that is, they turn away from judgment by what God the Exalted has revealed and desire other than it.

﴿Know that God only intends to afflict them for some of their sins﴾; that is, for the sin of their turning away from the judgment of God, Mighty and Majestic. He expressed it in this way to signal that they have many sins, and that one of them alone is of great enormity. In this vagueness there is a magnification of turning away, as in the verse of Labid:

"Or some souls are bound to their death (ḥimām)"

He means by it himself; that is, a great soul, and a soul of whatever kind.

﴿And indeed many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾; that is, they are rebellious in disbelief, persistent in it, and exceed the known limits. This is a tadhyil (concluding parenthetical statement) that confirms the content of what came before it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 50:

﴿Do they desire the judgement of the Jahiliyya?﴾ This is a denunciation and an expression of astonishment at their condition, and a rebuke to them. The particle *fa'* (ف) here is for coordination with an implied antecedent that the context requires; that is, they turn away from your judgement and so they desire the judgement of the *Jahiliyya* (the Age of Ignorance). The fronting of the object (*taqdim al-maf'ul*) serves restriction (*takhsis*), which conveys emphasis on the denunciation and astonishment, because turning away from the judgement of the Messenger (ﷺ) and seeking another judgement is a strange and reprehensible matter, while seeking the judgement of the *Jahiliyya* is even more vile and more astonishing. By *al-Jahiliyya* is meant either: the ignorant creed, which is the following of desire that necessitates inclination and flattery in judgements, so that it is a reproach to the Jews that, despite being People of the Book and of knowledge, they seek the judgement of the *Jahiliyya*, which is desire and ignorance, which does not proceed from a Book nor return to revelation; or: the people of the *Jahiliyya* and their judgement, which was what they practised of differentiating between the slain (*al-tafadul bayna al-qatla*). It is narrated that when the Banu al-Nadir had recourse to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in a dispute over a killing that occurred between them and the Banu Qurayza, they asked him (ﷺ) to judge between them by what the people of the *Jahiliyya* had practised of differentiation, and he (ﷺ) said: "The slain are equal." The Banu al-Nadir said: "We are not content with that." Thereupon it was revealed.

It is read with *al-hukmu* in the nominative (*raf' al-hukm*), as a subject (*mubtada'*), with *yabghun* as its predicate, and the returning pronoun (*al-raji'*) is omitted, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ (25:41). This has been considered weak outside of poetry.

It is also read with the second-person *ta'* (تاء الخطاب), either by *iltifat* (shift of address) to intensify the rebuke, or by implying a verb of saying, meaning: say to them, "Do you desire the judgement of…" etc. It is also read with *fath* on the *ha'* and *kaf* (حُكّامًا), meaning: "Do they desire rulers like the rulers of the *Jahiliyya*?"

﴿And who is better in judgement than God?﴾ This is a denial that anyone's judgement should be better than the judgement of God, exalted is He, or equal to it, although the apparent construction does not expressly address the negation of equality or its denial. Its detailed explanation has already passed in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God﴾ (4:125).

﴿for a people who have certainty﴾; that is, with them. The *lam* is as in *hayta laka* (هَيْتَ لَكَ, "come, I am at your disposal"), meaning: this question is for them, for they are the ones who reflect upon matters with their insight, and so they know with certainty that the judgement of God, mighty and majestic is He, is the best of judgements and the most just of them.

﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ خِطابٌ يَعُمُّ حُكْمُهُ كافَّةَ المُؤْمِنِينَ مِنَ المُخْلِصِينَ وغَيْرِهِمْ، وإنْ كانَ سَبَبُ وُرُودِهِ بَعْضًا مِنهم كَما سَيَأْتِي. (p-48)

[The address ﴿O you who have believed﴾ is a general address whose ruling encompasses all believers, sincere and otherwise, even though the cause of its revelation concerned some of them, as will come.]

وَوَصْفُهم بِعُنْوانِ الإيمانِ لِحَمْلِهِمْ مِن أوَّلِ الأمْرِ عَلى الِانْزِجارِ عَمّا نُهُوا عَنْهُ بِقَوْلِهِ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿لا تَتَّخِذُوا اليَهُودَ والنَّصارى أوْلِياءَ﴾ فَإنَّ تَذْكِيرَ اتِّصافِهِمْ بِضِدِّ صِفاتِ الفَرِيقَيْنِ مِن أقْوى الزَّواجِرِ عَنْ مُوالاتِهِما؛ أيْ: لا يَتَّخِذْ أحَدٌ مِنكم أحَدًا مِنهم ولِيًّا، بِمَعْنى: لا تُصافُوهم ولا تُعاشِرُوهم مُصافاةَ الأحْبابِ ومُعاشَرَتَهم، لا بِمَعْنى: لا تَجْعَلُوهم أوْلِياءَ لَكم حَقِيقَةً، فَإنَّهُ أمْرٌ مُمْتَنِعٌ في نَفْسِهِ لا يَتَعَلَّقُ بِهِ النَّهْيُ.

[Describing them with the title of faith is because, from the outset, it moves them to refrain from what they have been forbidden, by His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾. For reminding them of their being characterized by the opposite of the attributes of the two groups is among the strongest deterrents from allying with them. That is: none of you should take any of them as an ally (walī), in the sense of: do not be companions to them or associate with them in the friendship and close company of loved ones; not in the sense of: do not make them your allies in reality, for that is in itself an impossibility to which a prohibition does not apply.]

﴿بَعْضُهم أوْلِياءُ بَعْضٍ﴾؛ أيْ: بَعْضُ كُلِّ فَرِيقٍ مِن ذَيْنِكَ الفَرِيقَيْنِ أوْلِياءُ بَعْضٍ آخَرَ مِن ذَلِكَ الفَرِيقِ، لا مِنَ الفَرِيقِ الآخَرِ، وإنَّما أُوثِرَ الإجْمالُ في البَيانِ؛ تَعْوِيلًا عَلى ظُهُورِ المُرادِ لِوُضُوحِ انْتِفاءِ المُوالاةِ بَيْنَ فَرِيقَيِ اليَهُودِ والنَّصارى رَأْسًا. والجُمْلَةُ مُسْتَأْنَفَةٌ مَسُوقَةٌ؛ لِتَعْلِيلِ النَّهْيِ وتَأْكِيدِ إيجابِ الِاجْتِنابِ عَنِ المَنهِيِّ عَنْهُ؛ أيْ: بَعْضُهم أوْلِياءُ بَعْضٍ مُتَّفِقُونَ عَلى كَلِمَةٍ واحِدَةٍ في كُلِّ ما يَأْتُونَ وما يَذَرُونَ، ومِن ضَرُورَتِهِ إجْماعُ الكُلِّ عَلى مُضادَّتِكم ومُضارَّتِكم، بِحَيْثُ يَسُومُونَكُمُ السُّوءَ ويَبْغُونَكُمُ الغَوائِلَ، فَكَيْفَ يُتَصَوَّرُ بَيْنَكم وبَيْنَهم مُوالاةٌ.

[﴿Some of them are allies of others﴾; that is: some of each of those two groups are allies of some other of that same group, not of the other group. The statement was given in general terms (ijmal) rather than explicitly, relying on the clarity of the intended meaning, since the absence of alliance between the Jews and the Christians is entirely evident. The sentence is a resumed (mustaʼnafah) clause, given to provide the reason for the prohibition and to emphasize the obligation of avoiding what is forbidden. That is: some of them are allies of others, agreed upon one word in all that they do and forgo; and it follows from this that all of them are united in opposition to you and in harming you, such that they inflict evil upon you and seek your ruin, so how could any alliance between you and them be conceived?]

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَمَن يَتَوَلَّهم مِنكم فَإنَّهُ مِنهُمْ﴾ حُكْمٌ مُسْتَنْتَجٌ مِنهُ، فَإنَّ انْحِصارَ المُوالاةِ فِيما بَيْنَهم يَسْتَدْعِي كَوْنَ مَن يُوالِيهِمْ مِنهم ضَرُورَةَ أنَّ الِاتِّحادَ في الدِّينِ الَّذِي عَلَيْهِ يَدُورُ أمْرُ المُوالاةِ، حَيْثُ لَمْ يَكُنْ بِكَوْنِهِمْ مِمَّنْ يُوالِيهِمْ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ تَعَيَّنَ أنْ يَكُونَ ذَلِكَ بِكَوْنِ مَن يُوالِيهِمْ مِنهم، وفِيهِ زَجْرٌ شَدِيدٌ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ عَنْ إظْهارِ صُورَةِ المُوالاةِ لَهم، وإنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ مُوالاةً في الحَقِيقَةِ.

[﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is indeed one of them﴾ is a ruling deduced from what precedes it. For the confinement of alliance to occurring among themselves requires that whoever allies with them is one of them, since necessarily the unity in religion, upon which the matter of alliance turns, is what is in question; and since their being allies of the believers is not possible, it is determined that it must be by his allying with them that he becomes one of them. In this there is a severe warning to the believers against displaying the appearance of alliance with them, even if it is not alliance in reality.]

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَهْدِي القَوْمَ الظّالِمِينَ﴾ تَعْلِيلٌ لِكَوْنِ مَن يَتَوَلّاهم مِنهم؛ أيْ: لا يَهْدِيهِمْ إلى الإيمانِ، بَلْ يُخَلِّيهِمْ وشَأْنَهم، فَيَقَعُونَ في الكُفْرِ والضَّلالَةِ، وإنَّما وُضِعَ المُظْهَرُ مَوْضِعَ ضَمِيرِ هم؛ تَنْبِيهًا عَلى أنَّ تَوَلِّيَهم ظُلْمٌ، لِما أنَّهُ تَعْرِيضٌ لِأنْفُسِهِمْ لِلْعَذابِ الخالِدِ، ووَضْعٌ لِلشَّيْءِ في غَيْرِ مَوْضِعِهِ.

[﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a reason for his being one of them who allies with them; that is: He does not guide them to faith, but leaves them to themselves, so they fall into disbelief and misguidance. The explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun "them" to alert that allying with them is wrongdoing, because it exposes themselves to everlasting punishment, and it is placing a thing in other than its proper place.]

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 52:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ is an explanation of the manner of their turning away, and an indication of its cause and of what their affair will lead to. The fa' (fa) is for signalling that this is consequent upon their not being guided. The address is either to the Messenger ﷺ by way of tilwin (shifting of address), or to everyone who is qualified to receive it, and in it there is an increase in censure upon censure; that is: He does not guide them, but leaves them to themselves, so you see them ... etc. It was placed in the position of the relative pronoun so as to indicate, through what is within the scope of its relative clause, that their turning away was due to the disease of hypocrisy in their hearts and the looseness of the bond in religion.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿hastening into them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the relative pronoun, and the seeing is visual. It has been said that it is a second object and the seeing is of the heart, but the first is more suitable given the manifestness of their hypocrisy; that is: you see them hastening in their alliance with them. It was said "fihim" (into them), for emphasis in showing their eagerness for it and their fervent craving for it. The choice of the word fi (in) over ila (to) serves to indicate that they are firmly settled in alliance, and that their hastening is only from one of its degrees to another of its degrees, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those hasten to the good things﴾, not that they are outside it and turning towards it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a garden﴾.

It is also read: (fa-yurī) with the ya' of the third person, on the basis that the pronoun refers to God, glorified is He. It has been said: it refers to whoever is capable of seeing. It has been said: the subject is the relative pronoun and the object is the clause, with the omission of the verbal particle an (that), and the seeing is of the heart; that is: "and those in whose hearts is a disease will see that they hasten into them." Since an was omitted, the verb became marfu' (nominative), as in the saying of one who said:

"Hey you, the one who restrains me from attending the battle"

By them is meant: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his like, who used to hasten into friendship with the Jews and the Christians of Najran, and who used to excuse themselves to the believers by saying that they did not feel safe from the vicissitudes of time.

That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They say: "We fear that a reverse may befall us."﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "they hasten", and "reverse" (da'ira) is among the predominant attributes which are not mentioned together with the thing they qualify; that is: a reversal of the times revolves around us, and a turn of its turns, by which the matter is overturned and the dominion becomes for the disbelievers. It has been said: we fear that some disagreeable thing of the disagreeable things of the age may befall us, such as drought and famine, so they will not give us provisions and loans.

It is related that 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "I have many allies among the Jews, numerous in number, and I disavow to Allah and His Messenger their alliance, and I take Allah and His Messenger as allies." 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said: "I am a man who fears reversals, and I will not disavow the alliance of my allies, who are the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa'." Perhaps he was showing the believers that he meant by "reversals" the latter meaning, while concealing in himself the former meaning.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So perhaps Allah will bring a conquest﴾ is a response from Allah, exalted is He, to their false pretexts, and a cutting off of their vain hopes, and good tidings to the believers of victory. For "perhaps" (asa) from Him, glorified is He, is an inevitable promise, since the generous, when he raises hopes, certainly gives; so what do you think of the most generous of the generous. The "an" (that) of "yaʾtiya" is in the accusative position, either as the predicate of "asa", which is the opinion of al-Akhfash, or as its object, which is the opinion of Sibawayh, so as to avoid predicating the entity of an event, as in your saying: "Zayd perhaps will stand." The conquest intended is the conquest of Mecca, said by al-Kalbi and al-Suddi. Al-Dahhak said: the conquest of the Jewish villages of Khaybar and Fadak. Qatada and Muqatil said: it is the decisive judgment through His granting victory to His Messenger ﷺ over whoever opposed him, and the strengthening of the religion.

﴿Or a command from Him﴾, by the uprooting of the root of the Jews through killing and expulsion.

﴿And they will become﴾; that is, those hypocrites who make excuses with what has been mentioned. It is a conjunction upon "yaʾtiya", included together with it within the scope of the predicate of "asa"; and although there is no pronoun in it referring back to its subject, the fa' of causation suffices for that, since it makes the two clauses a single clause.

﴿regretful for what they had concealed within themselves﴾, which is what they used to hide within themselves of disbelief and doubt concerning his affair ﷺ. The regret is attached to this, and not to what they used to display of allegiance to disbelief, because it is what used to drive them to alliance and incite them towards it. This indicates their regret over it in its root and its cause.

﴿And those who believe will say﴾: this is a new sentence (kalam mubtada'), brought to show the full extent of the wretched condition of the group mentioned. It is also read without the conjunction "wa," on the basis that it is an answer to a question arising from what preceded, as if it were said: "What then will the believers say at that time?" It is also read as ﴿wa-yaqula﴾ in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿yusbihu﴾ ("they will become"). It was said that it is coordinated with ﴿ya'ti﴾ ("comes") in terms of meaning, as if it were said: "So perhaps God will bring the victory, and those who believe will say." The first reading is more correct, because this statement is only issued by the believers when the hypocrites' remorse becomes evident, not merely at the arrival of victory. The meaning is: those who believe will say, addressing the Jews and pointing to the hypocrites who used to befriend them, hoping for their rule, and showing them the utmost love and inseparability from them in prosperity and adversity, when they witness the failure of their hopes and the reversal of their calculations by the occurrence of the opposite of what they were awaiting, and making excuses for it, marveling at the addressees on account of their condition and reproaching them indirectly. (p-50)

﴿Are these the ones who swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?﴾ That is: in support and assistance, as they said in what is related of them: ﴿And if you are fought, we will surely support you.﴾ The demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) is the subject (mubtada'), and what follows it is its predicate (khabar). The meaning is a denunciation of what they did, a declaration of its improbability, and a rebuke of them for it. Or some believers say to one another, pointing also to the hypocrites: "Are these the ones who swore to the disbelievers that they were with them?" The address in ﴿ma'akum﴾ ("with you") is to the Jews under both interpretations, except that under the first it is from the side of the believers, and under the second from the side of those who swore.
