This sentence has no grammatical position (la mahalla laha min al-i'rab), because it is an explanation and a narration of the meaning of "they swore," but not in their own words, for otherwise it would have said "innā ma'akum" ("we are with you"). "Jahd al-aymān" means the most severe of oaths; it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), and its accusative is a circumstantial state (hal), on the assumption of: "and they swore by God, exerting themselves to the utmost in their oaths," so the verb was deleted and the verbal noun put in its place. Its definiteness in form is disregarded, because it is interpreted as indefinite; that is, "striving in their oaths." Or it is an absolute object (masdar): that is, "they swore with the swearing of striving in the oath."

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their deeds have become void, and they have become losers﴾ is either a resumed sentence (jumlah mustaanifah), brought from His side, to show the outcome of what they did, of claiming friendship and swearing to being together in ease and hardship, following the indication of its nullity through the rhetorical question of denunciation. Or it is a second predicate of the subject, according to whoever permits it to be a sentence, as in His saying: ﴿So behold, it is a snake, moving swiftly﴾. Or it is the predicate, and the relative pronoun together with what is in its relative clause is an attribute of the demonstrative noun; the interrogation is then for affirmation (taqrir), and it contains the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "How void their deeds are, and how great their loss!" The meaning: their deeds that they performed concerning your friendship became void, and they strove in that with eloquent striving, since you had no dominion, so that they might benefit from the efforts they made, and bore the hardships of toil; and in this is what is clear of mockery of the hypocrites and rebuke of the addressees.

It was also said: one of the believers said it addressing another, marveling at the bad condition of the hypocrites and rejoicing in what God, exalted is He, bestowed upon themselves of success in sincerity: "Are these the ones who swore to you with the most severe oaths that they were your allies and your supporters against the disbelievers? Their deeds, which they used to strain at in the view of people's eyes, have become void." You know well that this statement from the believers is only fitting if the hypocrites had then displayed the opposite of what they claimed and swore to concerning the allegiance to the believers and their support against the disbelievers, so that their lie became apparent and they were disgraced thereby before the eyes of the witnesses, and their deeds which they strained at in the view of the believers' eyes became void. And there is no doubt that on that day they are far more insistent in claiming and more abundant in swearing than they were before that, let alone displaying the opposite of that. What appears from them is only remorse for what they did, and that is not a clear sign of their disbelief and lying in their claim, for they claim that their remorse is only over what they had shown of allegiance to the disbelievers, out of fear that a misfortune would befall them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 54:

﴿O you who believe, whoever among you turns back from his religion﴾ It is also read (yartaddid) with the unassimilated form (fakk), according to the dialect of the Hijaz; the assimilated form (idgham) is the dialect of Tamim. When what precedes forbade allying with the Jews and the Christians, and it was made clear that allying with them leads to apostasy from the religion, and the fate of those among the hypocrites who ally with them was spelled out, he began to explain the state of apostates in general. This is among the unseen matters that the Qur'an reported before they occurred.

It is narrated that eleven groups apostatized from Islam. Three of them were in the time of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him: the Banu Mudlij and their chief Dhu al-Khimar, who was al-Aswad al-'Ansi. He was a soothsayer who claimed prophethood in Yemen and seized control of its lands, and he expelled the governors of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from it. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, wrote to Mu'adh ibn Jabal and to the leaders of Yemen, and God the Exalted destroyed him at the hands of Fayruz al-Daylami, who attacked him by night and killed him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was informed of his killing on the night he was killed, so the Muslims rejoiced at it, and the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was taken (in death) the next day. The news of it reached (Medina) at the end of the month of Rabi' al-Awwal.

And the Banu Hanifa, the people of Musaylima al-Kadhdhab (the Liar), who claimed prophethood and wrote to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "From Musaylima, the Messenger of God, to Muhammad, the Messenger of God: To proceed, the earth is half mine and half yours." He, peace and blessings be upon him, replied: "From Muhammad, the Messenger of God, to Musaylima the Liar: To proceed, the earth belongs to God; He bequeaths it to whomever He wills of His servants, and the final outcome is for the God-fearing." Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, fought him with the armies of the Muslims, and he was killed at the hands of Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza, may God be pleased with him. Wahshi used to say: "I killed the best of people in my jahiliyya, and the worst of people in my Islam."

And the Banu Asad, the people of Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid, who claimed prophethood. Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, sent Khalid ibn al-Walid against him, and he fled after the fighting to Syria, then embraced Islam and his Islam was good.

And seven groups in the time of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him: Fazara, the people of Uyayna ibn Hisn; Ghatafan, the people of Qurra ibn Salama al-Qushayri; Banu Sulaym, the people of al-Fujja'a ibn Abd Yalil; Banu Yarbu', the people of Malik ibn Nuwayra; part of Tamim, the people of Sajah bint al-Mundhir, the female claimant to prophethood who married herself to Musaylima the Liar. Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri says of her in the book "Istaghfir wa-Istaghfiri":

Sajah has gone astray, and Musaylima has followed her,
a liar among the worldly tribes, and a liar.

Kinda, the people of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays; and Banu Bakr ibn Wa'il in Bahrain, the people of al-Hutam ibn Zayd. God the Exalted sufficed their affair at the hand of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him.

And one group in the time of Umar, may God be pleased with him: Ghassan, the people of Jabala ibn al-Ayham. The slap (of Umar) turned him back, and he was sent to the lands of the Romans, and his story is well known.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then God will bring forth⦆ — it is the answer to the conditional, and the returning pronoun to the conditional noun is omitted; that is: then God will bring forth in their place (a people), after their destruction.

﴿a people He loves⦆; that is: He intends for them the good of both this world and the Hereafter. The clause's position is in the genitive, as it is an attribute of "a people."

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and who love Him⦆; that is: they desire His obedience and guard themselves against His disobedience. It is conjoined to the preceding clause and falls under its judgment. It was said: they are the people of Yemen, based on the report that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, pointed to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and said: "These are his people." It was also said: they are the Ansar, may God be pleased with them. It was also said: they are the Persians, based on the report that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about them, so he struck with his noble hand upon the shoulder of Salman, may God be pleased with him, and said: "This one and his kin," then said: "If faith were suspended from the Pleiades, men from the sons of Persia would reach it." It was also said: they are two thousand from al-Nakha', five thousand from Kinda, and three thousand from the scattered people, who fought on the day of al-Qadisiyya.

﴿humble toward the believers⦆ is the plural of dhalil, not dhalul; its plural is dhulul; that is: gentle, merciful, lowly and humble toward them. Its construction with "ala" is either to imply the meaning of kindness and tenderness, or to alert that they, despite their high rank and superiority over the believers, lower their wings to them.

Or it is to preserve the antithesis between it and what is in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿mighty toward the disbelievers⦆; that is: stern and dominant over them, from 'azza-hu, meaning he overcame him, as in His saying, Mighty and Exalted: ﴿stern against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves⦆. These are two further attributes of a people, between which the conjunction is omitted to indicate that each is independently characterized by them. In this there is evidence for the validity of placing a pure attribute after non-pure attributes (a clause or prepositional phrase), as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and this is a blessed Book which We have sent down⦆, and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿there does not come to them any reminder from their Lord, newly revealed⦆, and His saying, the Exalted: (p-52) ﴿there does not come to them any reminder from the Merciful, newly revealed⦆.

As for what was held by one who does not permit it, that His saying, the Exalted, "He loves them and they love Him," is a parenthetical clause, and that "blessed" is a predicate after a predicate, or a predicate of an omitted subject, and that "from their Lord" and "from the Merciful" are two fronted circumstantial phrases of the pronoun in "newly revealed," it is an artificial view that is not hidden. It was read: (adhillatan), (a'izzatan) with the accusative, as circumstantial states of "a people," since it is specified by the attribute.

﴿they strive in the way of God⦆ is another attribute of a people, consequent upon what precedes it, and it is joined with what follows it to explain the manner of their might; or it is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "mighty."

﴿and they do not fear the blame of any blamer⦆ is conjoined to "they strive," meaning: they combine striving in the way of God with firmness in religion. In it there is an allusion to the hypocrites, for when they went out with the army of the Muslims they feared their Jewish allies, so they hardly did anything that would bring upon them blame from them. It was said: it is a circumstantial state of the subject of "they strive," meaning: they strive while their condition is contrary to the condition of the hypocrites. This was objected to on the ground that they stated that the negated present tense with la or ma, like the affirmed, does not permit the waw of circumstance to precede it. "Blame" (lawma) is the single instance of blame, and in it and in the indefiniteness of "blamer" there is an exaggeration that is not hidden.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the noble attributes mentioned earlier, and the sense of distance in it is to signal the distance of their rank in excellence.

﴿is the bounty of God⦆; that is: His kindness and benevolence, not that they are independent in possessing them.

﴿He gives it to whomever He wills⦆: giving it to him, and enabling him to earn and attain it, as wisdom and benefit require.

﴿And God is Vast⦆: abundant in bounties and kindnesses.

﴿All-Knowing⦆: exceedingly knowing of all things, among which is who is worthy of bounty and success. The clause is a parenthetical concluding statement confirming what precedes it, and the mention of the noble Name is to signal the cause and to emphasize the independence of the parenthetical clause.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 55:

﴿Your only walī (guardian, protecting friend) is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who believe﴾ When Allah, Exalted and Majestic, had forbidden them from taking the disbelievers as walī (muwalah), and gave as the reason that some of them are awliyā' (protectors) of others, such that their walāyah over the believers cannot be conceived, and made clear that whoever takes them as walī becomes one of them, He here specified who their walī is, by way of restricting walāyah to him, as if it were said: Do not take them as awliyā', because some of them are awliyā' of others, and they are not your awliyā'. Rather, your awliyā' are Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. So single them out for walāyah and do not pass over them to others. The word walī is given in the singular despite its plurality (in the sense of the verse's meaning) to indicate that walāyah belongs primarily to Allah, Exalted is He, and that His walāyah extends to him (peace be upon him); likewise, the walāyah of the believers is by way of following His walāyah, Exalted and Majestic.

﴿who establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾ This is a ṣifah (qualifying description) of "those who believe," since it functions as a noun; or it is a badal (substitute) of it; or it is in the accusative (naṣb) by way of praise (madḥ); or in the nominative (raf') by way of praise.

﴿and they bow in ruku'﴾ This is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) with respect to the doer of the two verbs; that is, they perform what was mentioned of establishing the prayer and giving zakah, while being humble and submissive before Allah, Exalted is He. It was also said: it is a ḥāl specifically tied to the giving of zakah, and ruku' is the ruku' of prayer; the purpose being to show the completeness of their eagerness for good deeds and their hastening toward them. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, when a beggar asked him while he was bowing (in ruku'), so he tossed his ring to him, as if he had made a gesture with his little finger, without needing in its removal to much action that would lead to the invalidation of the prayer. The use of the plural form in this case serves to encourage people to imitate his action, may Allah be pleased with him. And in it is an indication that voluntary charity is called zakah.

﴿And whoever takes as allies Allah and His Messenger and those who believe﴾. The explicit mention (*al-izhar*, repeating the noun instead of using a pronoun) was preferred over saying "and whoever takes them as allies" (*wa-man yatawallahum*). This preserves the subtle point mentioned earlier, that guardianship (*al-wilayah*) belongs originally to Him, Exalted is He, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Indeed, the party of Allah, they are the victorious﴾. Here the party (*hizb*) is attributed to Him, Exalted is He, specifically. This is also an instance of placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun referring back to "whoever" (*man*). That is: indeed they are the victorious. But they were called "the party of Allah, Exalted is He" to honour them and to establish their victory by way of demonstrative proof (*al-tariq al-burhani*), as if it were said: whoever takes these as allies, then indeed they are the party of Allah, and the party of Allah are the victorious.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 57:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take those who have taken your religion as ridicule and play, from among those who were given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers, as allies; and fear Allah, if you are believers.﴾ It is narrated that Rifa'ah ibn Zayd and Suwayd ibn al-Harith declared Islam and then became hypocrites, and some of the believers were friendly with them, so they were forbidden from allying with them. The prohibition was attached to a description that encompasses them and others, generalizing the ruling, drawing attention to the cause ('illah, underlying reason), and signalling that one of this character is worthy of enmity, let alone alliance.

﴿from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ is an explanation of "those who ridicule," and the mention of the title "given the Scripture" serves to show the full extent of their vileness and the utmost of their error, since being given the Scripture is a restraint preventing them from mocking a religion founded upon the Scripture that confirms their own Scripture.

﴿nor the disbelievers﴾; i.e., the polytheists. They are singled out for mention because of the multiplication of their disbelief. It is a conjunction with the first relative clause, and it implies that they are not among the mockers, as is indicated by the restriction of the address to the People of the Scripture in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Scripture, do you resent us...﴾ (Qur'an 5:59), and so on. It has also been read in the genitive case as a conjunction with the last relative clause, and this is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "and from among the disbelievers," and the reading of Abdullah: "and from among those who associated partners," so they too are among the mockers.

﴿allies﴾; and keep away from them entirely.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in this matter by abandoning their alliance, or by abandoning the forbidden things in general, in which case abandoning their alliance enters primarily.

﴿if you are believers﴾; i.e., truly, for the requirement of faith necessitates fearing Allah without doubt.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 58:

﴿And when you call to the prayer (salah), they take it as mockery and play.﴾ That is, the prayer (al-salah) or the calling (al-munadah); in this there is an indication of the legitimacy of the call to prayer (adhan).

﴿Mockery and play﴾ is a specification of their ridicule of a particular ruling of the religion after the statement of their ridicule of the religion in general, to show the completeness of their wretchedness. It is related that a Christian in Medina, whenever he heard the muezzin say, "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God (ﷺ)," would say, "May God burn the liar." Then one night his servant came in with a fire while his family were asleep, and a spark flew from it into the house, and it burned him and his family all together.

﴿That﴾; that is, the aforementioned mockery, ﴿because﴾ on account of the fact that they,

﴿are a people who do not reason﴾, for foolishness leads to ignorance of the excellences of the truth and to mocking it. Had they possessed any intellect at all, they would not have dared to commit such a grave offence.

﴿Say﴾: a command to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), in the form of a shift in address, after the prohibition on the believers from taking as allies those who mock. He is to address them, make clear that the religion is free of anything that would justify what they uttered of mockery, reveal to them the cause of what they committed, and silence them with proof. That is, say to those wicked people.

﴿O People of the Book﴾: they are described by their possession of the Book, as a preparation for what follows of their rebuke and of the charge that their disbelief contradicts their own Book.

﴿Do you find fault with us﴾: from naqama minhu kadhā, meaning he found fault with it, disapproved of it, denied it and disliked it; it is conjugated as yanqimu from the pattern daraba. It is also read with a fatha on the qaf, from the pattern 'alima, and this too is a dialect form. That is: what do you blame in us and what do you deny in us?

﴿Except that we believe in God and in what has been sent down to us﴾: the noble Qur'an.

﴿and in what was sent down before﴾: that is, before its revelation, the Torah and the Gospel which were sent down to you, and the rest of the divine Books.

﴿and that most of you are defiant﴾: that is, rebellious and outside belief in what has been mentioned. For disbelief in the Qur'an necessarily entails disbelief in what confirms it. This is coordinated with "that we believe", as an object of cause for "you find fault", and the object which is the religion is omitted, being well known, since what precedes and follows clearly indicates it. For taking the religion as mockery and play is itself the same as finding fault with it and denying it, and belief in what has been detailed is itself the same as the religion they found fault with. Except that it is presented in the position of the cause of their fault-finding, as a recording against them of complete obstinacy and inversion, in that they made it the reason for their censure, although in itself it is the reason for its acceptance and approval. Thus the exception is from the most general of causes: you find fault with our religion for no cause except that we believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us and what was sent down before from your Books, and because most of you are rebellious, not believing in any one of what has been mentioned, even if you were believers in your Book, which speaks of the truth of our Book, you would have believed in it.

The attribution of defiance to most of them is because they are the ones who lead their followers into rebellion and obstinacy. It has been said: it is coordinated with it as an object of "you find fault with us", but not on the basis that the exception is the combination of the two coordinated items, rather it is what their combination entails of opposition, as if it were said: you find fault with us only because of your opposition, in that we entered belief while you are outside it. It has been said: it is on the omission of the opposite, that is, and the belief that most of you are defiant. It has been said: it is coordinated with "what" (ma), that is: you find fault with us only that we believe in God and in what has been sent down to us, and that you are defiant. It has been said: it is coordinated with an omitted cause, that is: because of the scarcity of your fairness, and because most of you are defiant.

It has been said: the "wa" means "with", that is: you find fault with us only the belief together with the fact that most of you... etc. It has been said: it is governed by a verb understood, indicated by what has been mentioned, that is: you do not find fault that most of you are defiant. It has been said: it is nominative, as a beginning, with the predicate omitted, that is: and your defiance is known, that is established, and the clause is circumstantial or parenthetical. It has been read with the kasra on "inna" (إنّ), and the clause is then resumptive, explaining that most of them are defiant and rebellious.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 60:

﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from Allah?﴾ When the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to confront them and rebuke them by explaining that the basis of their resentment toward the religion lies only in its containing what would make it deserving of approval even in their own eyes, and that their disbelief is in that which they themselves accept, he (ﷺ) was then commanded to rebuke them further by explaining that what truly deserves resentment and blame is the distorted religion they follow. In the course of this explanation he also denounces their crimes and the consequences and punishments that befell them, in the manner of allusion, lest a direct statement drive them to persist in obstinacy and stubbornness. He addresses them before the explanation with something that indicates the great importance of what is to be explained, and that calls for their attentive reception of it, through the interrogative sentence that arouses longing for the information to be given, and through the announcement that signals it is a momentous matter, because the naba' (tidings, a report of significance and weight) is news that has importance and gravity. Since the ground of resentment is the evil of the one resented, in reality or in belief, and mere resentment does not at all establish its evil, it was said: "something worse than that" and not "something more resented than that," in order to affirm the evil of what will be mentioned and to add emphasis to it.

It has also been said that this was said because of its occurrence in the words of the addressees, when "a group of Jews came and asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about his religion, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us…' up to His saying: '…and we are Muslims to Him'; when they heard the mention of 'Isa (peace be upon him) they said: We know of no worse religion than yours." The evil was attributed in relation to religion, though religion is wholly free of any trace of evil, in deference to them according to their false belief that is fixed upon its complete evil, so as to establish that their religion is worse than every evil; that is: "Shall I inform you of what is in reality worse than what you believe to be evil, even though in itself it is pure good?"

﴿Mathubatan 'inda Allah﴾; that is: a reward established in His judgment. It was also read as (mathwabatan), which is a dialect form of it, like mashurah and mashwarah; it is specific to good, just as punishment (ʿuqubah) is specific to evil, and it has been placed here in its position following the manner of the poet's saying:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

Its accusative is as a specification (tamyiz) from "evil" (bi-sharrin).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, with an implied genitive construction before it corresponding to what is indicated by the word "that"; that is: the religion of whoever Allah has cursed… etc. Or with an implied genitive construction before "that" corresponding to "whoever"; that is: worse than the people of that. The sentence under both estimates is a resumptive clause answering a question arising from the interrogative sentence; either as it stands, which is the apparent reading and suits the context of the noble text, or in consideration of the implied element within it. So it is as if it were said: "What is worse than that?" and it was answered: "It is the religion of whom Allah has cursed… etc." Or it was said in the question: "Who is the one worse than the people of that?" and it was answered: "It is whoever Allah has cursed."

Placing the noble Name in the place of the pronoun serves to cultivate awe, to instill dread, and to magnify the matter of the curse and what follows from it. The relative clause refers to the addressees, whom Allah has removed far from His mercy and against whom He became angry because of their disbelief and their immersion in sins after the clarity of the signs and the manifestation of the proofs.

﴿And made from them apes and swine﴾; that is: He transformed some of them into apes, namely the People of the Sabbath, and some of them into swine, namely the disbelievers of the table of 'Isa (peace be upon him). It has been said that both transformations were among the People of the Sabbath: their young men were transformed into apes and their elders into swine. The plural of the pronoun returning to the relative clause in "from them" is according to its meaning, just as the singular of the first two pronouns is according to its wording; and the choice of placing it in the position of the appropriate second-person pronoun "we inform you" is for the purpose of establishing the evil through what is enumerated within the scope of its clause of momentous matters that necessitate it, in a demonstrative manner, together with what it contains of avoiding stirring up their obstinacy.

﴿And served the Taghut﴾ is coordinated with the clause of "whoever" (man), and the singular of the pronoun is for the reason already given. Likewise (ʿubida al-taghut) on the reading with passive voice and the taghut raised, and likewise (ʿabada al-taghut) in the sense of: became an object of worship. The returning pronoun to the relative clause is thus omitted on both readings; that is: it was worshipped among them or between them. The placing of their mentioned attributes ahead of their characteristic of serving the taghut, in order to establish the evil of their religion, though serving the taghut is the origin that entails them in existence, and because its indication of the evil of their religion is in itself, since serving the taghut is the very essence of their religion, which is manifestly false; and its indication of it is by way of inference from the evil of the effects to the evil of what necessitates them of belief and action. This is either for the purpose of rebuking them from the outset by describing them with what they have no way to deny, not with the evil and monstrousness of it, nor with their being characterized by it; or to signal that each of the preceding and the following independently indicates the evil mentioned, even if the order of existence were observed.

It has been said: "Whoever served the taghut, and whom Allah cursed and with whom He became angry…" etc., might lead one to understand that the cause of the evil is the whole combined, and it was read as (ʿabid al-taghut), and likewise (ʿabid al-taghut) with the genitive construction as an adjective, like fatin and yaqiz; and likewise (ʿabadat al-taghut); and likewise (ʿabad al-taghut) with the genitive construction as the plural of ʿabid, like khadam, or on the basis that its original form was ʿabadat, its ta' being dropped for the genitive construction; all in the accusative, coordinated with "the apes and swine."

It was read as (ʿabadi al-taghut) in the genitive, coordinated with "whoever," on the basis that it is genitive by an implied genitive construction. It has also been said that "whoever" is genitive as a substitute for "evil" on one of the two aspects of the implied genitive construction mentioned. You know that this, along with its requiring that the noble text be emptied entirely of the aforementioned excellences, is certainly not a possible course; for the primary intended purpose is not the content of the interrogative sentence, but rather, as has passed, it is a preface placed before the intended meaning, to mock the addressees and to direct their minds toward receiving what is cast to them immediately after it in a declarative sentence corresponding in manner to the question arising from it, and that is the meaning intended to be conveyed; and upon it revolves that censure and rebuke as explained. So if the relative clause with what is within its scope is made part of the interrogative sentence, where is the answer cast to them immediately after it, responding to the question arising from it, so that censure and rebuke might be achieved thereby?

As for the following sentence, it is far from being fit as an answer, how could it be, since it must correspond in manner to the question arising from the interrogative sentence? And you have understood that the question arising from it demands that the evil be part of what is reported about, not a predicate, as in the sentence mentioned; and this will become clearer, God willing.

By the taghut is meant the calf. It has been said: it is the soothsayers and everyone they obeyed in disobedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; so the ruling includes the religion of the Christians as well. The reason for placing the mention of their worship after the punishments mentioned becomes clear: for had it been placed before them, it might have been supposed that both groups share those punishments. Since what has been mentioned, in the context of rebuke, amounts to this: that what is worse than what they resented is their religion, or that whoever is worse than the people of what they resented is themselves, according to the genitive constructions estimated, and since the evil on both aspects is part of the subject matter and not intended to be established for their religion or for themselves right after that, it was established for them in a manner that suggests the causality of the vices mentioned, by a separate sentence brought from His Glory, as testimony against them of complete wickedness and misguidance, or as one falling under the command, for emphasis of the censure and intensification of the rebuke.

So it was said: ﴿Those are worse in place﴾; the demonstrative refers to those whose wicked attributes were mentioned, and the sense of distance in it signals the far remove of their rank in wickedness; that is: those described with those vices and disgraces. "Worse in place" means: their place was made worse, so that it would be more emphatic in indicating their wickedness. It has also been said: "worse in place" means: in status.

﴿And further astray from the right way﴾ is coordinated with "worse," confirming it; that is: more astray from the straight path. In it is an indication that their religion is pure evil, far from the truth; for what they follow of the way is their religion, so when they are more astray, their religion is manifest error with no beyond. The comparative form in both places is for absolute increase, not by comparison with those who share with them the basic wickedness and misguidance.

"And when they come to you, they say, 'We believe,'" This was revealed concerning some of the Jews who used to enter upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and display belief to him out of hypocrisy. Thus the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the plural is for magnification (ta'zim), or it is addressed to him together with those Muslims who are with him; that is: when they come to you, they show Islam.

"And they had entered with disbelief and they had left with it" means: they leave from your presence still bound to disbelief just as they entered; what they heard from you had no effect on them. The two clauses are circumstantial (hal) clauses relating to the subject of "they say." "With disbelief" and "with it" are circumstantial phrases relating to the subject of "entered" and "left." Although "qad" (indeed/already) has entered here to bring the past close to the present, so that it may be correctly used as a circumstantial state, it also conveys, through the sense of expectation it carries, that the signs of hypocrisy were evident, and that the Messenger (ﷺ) was suspecting this and expecting that God Most High would expose it. Therefore it is said: "And God knows best what they were concealing," that is, of disbelief; and in this there is a severe warning (wa'id) for them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 62:**

﴿And you see﴾ is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to be addressed, and the seeing is visual (baṣariyya).

﴿Many of them﴾: from among the Jews and the hypocrites.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿they hasten into sin﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "kathīran" (many). It has been said that it is a second object, and that the seeing is of the heart (qalbiyya). But the first is more fitting to their condition and the manifestation of their hypocrisy. Al-musāraʿa (hastening) is to hurry toward a thing and to engage in it swiftly. The choice of the word "fī" (in) over "ilā" (to), which occurs in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and hasten to forgiveness﴾ ... etc., is due to what was mentioned in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿so you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening among them﴾.

By ﴿sin (al-ithm)﴾ is meant lying in general. It has been said: the forbidden. It has been said: the word of polytheism, and their saying: "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah." It has been said: it is the sins specific to them.

﴿and transgression (al-ʿudwān)﴾; that is, injustice that oversteps onto others, or exceeding the limit in acts of disobedience.

﴿and their consuming of unlawful gain (al-suḥt)﴾; that is, the forbidden. He singled it out for mention, although it is included within sin, for emphasis in condemning it.

﴿Evil is what they used to do﴾; that is, evil is the thing they were doing. The combining of the past and present verb forms is to indicate continuity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 63:

﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them﴾ al-Hasan said: "al-Rabbaniyyun (the rabbinic masters) are the scholars of the Gospel, and al-Ahbar (the scholars of the law) are the scholars of the Torah." It was also said: "All of them are among the Jews." This is an exhortation to those whom their elders take as models, and who know the ugliness of what they are engaged in and its evil outcome, to forbid their inferiors from that, together with a rebuke to them for abandoning it.

﴿from their saying sinful words and their consuming of unlawful gain﴾ Even though they know the ugliness of both and see them practiced by them.

﴿Evil indeed is what they used to do.﴾ This is more emphatic than what was said about their common people, because an act does not reach the level of "workmanship" (sun') unless its doer has trained in it and attained complete skill. For this reason, their elite were censured with it. Also, abandoning a good deed is uglier than committing a sin, because the self takes pleasure in sin and inclines towards it, whereas abstaining from condemning it does not have this quality. Thus it deserves the most emphatic censure. It also contains, in what it implies about the scholars' laxity in forbidding evil deeds, a point that is quite evident. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it is the most severe verse in the Qur'an. It is reported from al-Dahhak: "There is no verse in the Qur'an that I find more frightening than this one."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 64:

﴿And the Jews said﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: Allah, exalted is He, had expanded provision upon the Jews, so that they were among the most wealthy of people and the most fertile in their region. When they disobeyed Allah, may He be glorified, by disbelieving in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and denying him, He withheld from them what He had expanded upon them. At that point Finhas ibn 'Azura said: ﴿The hand of Allah is chained up﴾. Since the others did not object to him and approved of it, that monstrous statement was attributed to all of them, as one says: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," when in fact only one of them was the killer. By this they intended, may Allah curse them, that He, exalted is He, is withholding and restricting provision. Indeed, both "chaining the hand" (ghall al-yad) and "extending the hand" (bast) are metaphors for sheer miserliness and generosity, without any intention thereby to affirm an actual hand or chain or extension. Do you not see that they use it in places where such a meaning cannot be conceived, as in his saying:

Generosity of the sanctuary, the extension of two hands with a downpour, whose plains and valleys gave thanks for his bounty.

Labid also followed this sound path when he said:

And a morning of wind, of which I witnessed, and cold, when the North Wind had its reins in hand.

He only intended by this to affirm the complete power of the North Wind to direct the cold as it wishes, in the manner of metaphor, without it ever occurring to him to attribute to it a hand or to the cold a rein. Its origin is a kinaya (allusion) concerning one to whom the literal meaning may be intended, as passed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ in Surat Al 'Imran. It has also been said: they meant what is reported of them in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the saying of those who said: Allah is poor and we are rich﴾.

﴿Their hands are chained up﴾: a supplication against them with blameworthy miserliness and humiliation, or with poverty and wretchedness, or with the literal chaining of their hands, that they be prisoners in chains in this world and be dragged to the Fire with their shackles in the Hereafter. In that case the correspondence (mutabaqa) is then in terms of the wording and the consideration of the original meaning, as in: "He cursed me, may Allah cut off his progeny (sabba-ni sabba Allahu dabirahu)."

﴿And they are cursed﴾ is conjoined to the first supplication; that is, they are distanced from the mercy of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿For what they said﴾; that is, because of the shameful utterance they uttered. It has also been said that both are predicates.

﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ is conjoined to an implied element required by the context; that is: No, it is not so, rather He is at the utmost degree of generosity. To this was alluded by the dual form of "hand," for the highest that the aspirations of the generous reach is that they give what they give with both their hands. It has also been said: the dual is to draw attention to His bestowal of the two blessings of this world and the Hereafter. It has also been said: [it refers] to His giving as honour and His giving as gradual deception (istidraj).

﴿He spends as He wills﴾ is an independent sentence coming to emphasize the perfection of His generosity, and to draw attention to the secret of the affliction they suffered from the constriction, which they took, out of the extremity of their ignorance and error, as a pretext for audacity against that great disbelief. The meaning: that this is not due to deficiency in His overflowing, but because His spending follows His will, which is based on the wisdoms upon which the matters of livelihood and the Hereafter revolve. Wisdom has required, because of what is among them of the evil of sins, that provision be constricted for them, as is indicated by what will come of His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And if they had established the Torah and the Gospel﴾ to the end of the verse. "How" (kayfa) is an adverbial of "He wills," and the sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "He spends"; that is: He spends being in whatever state He wills; that is: being in accordance with His will; that is: willing. Omitting mention of what He spends is for the purpose of generalization.

﴿And surely many of them will increase﴾, and they are their scholars and their leaders.

﴿What has been sent down to you﴾, of the Qur'an comprising these verses. The placing of the object first is for the sake of giving it attention, and the restriction of "many of them" to this judgment is because some of them are not like that.

﴿from your Lord﴾ is connected to "sent down," just as "to you" is. Its being placed after it, although the rule is that the origin precedes the terminus, is because the context requires attention to the explanation of the terminus, for the focus of the increase is the descent to him, peace be upon him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sent down for you water from the sky﴾. The mention of the title of Lordship with its attribution to his pronoun, peace be upon him, is to honour him, peace be upon him.

﴿Transgression and disbelief﴾ is the second object of "increase"; that is: surely He will increase them in transgression upon their former transgression, and disbelief upon their former disbelief, either in terms of intensity and extremity, or in terms of quantity and multiplicity; for whenever a verse is sent down they disbelieve in it, so their transgression and disbelief increase in proportion to its measure, just as food suitable for the healthy increases the sick in sickness.

﴿And We have cast among them﴾; that is, among the Jews, for some of them are Jabriyya, some Qadariyya, some Murji'a, and some Mushabbiha.

﴿Enmity and hatred﴾; so their hearts scarcely agree, nor do their sayings correspond. The sentence is a new clause (mubtada') brought to remove what might be suspected from the mention of their transgression and disbelief, namely their gathering upon a matter that would lead to harm to the Muslims. It has been said: enmity is more specific than hatred, for every enemy is a hater, but not conversely in a universal sense.

﴿Until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is connected to "We have cast"; it has also been said: to "hatred."

﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it﴾ is an explicit statement of what was alluded to regarding the non-arrival of the calamity of what they are in to the Muslims; that is: whenever they intend to fight the Messenger (ﷺ), arrange its beginnings, and ride in that every rough and smooth path, Allah, exalted is He, repels them and subdues them; or: whenever they intend to fight anyone, they are defeated. For when they opposed the judgment of the Torah, Allah, exalted is He, gave power over them to Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar); then they corrupted, so Allah gave power over them to Futrus the Roman; then they corrupted, so Allah gave power over them the Magians; then they corrupted, so Allah gave power over them the Muslims. "For war" (li-l-harb) is either an complement of "kindled," or is connected to an omitted element that stands as an attribute of "a fire"; that is: being for war.

﴿And they strive in the land for corruption﴾; that is: they strive hard in plotting against Islam and its people, and in stirring up evil and sedition among themselves, which differs from what was expressed by kindling the fire of war. "Corruption" (fasad) is either an object of purpose, or in the position of a verbal noun; that is: they strive for corruption, or they strive a striving of corruption.

﴿And Allah does not love the corrupters﴾. Therefore He extinguished the blaze of their corruption. The definite article may be generic, in which case they enter it primarily, or it may be for a specific reference. The placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun is for the sake of causation and to show that they are firmly established in corruption.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 65:

﴿And if the People of the Book had believed﴾; that is, the Jews and the Christians, on the understanding that by "the Book" is meant the genus encompassing the Torah and the Gospel. They were mentioned with this designation to emphasize the reproach, for the very status of being People of the Book necessarily entails their belief in it and their upholding of it. Thus their disbelief in it and their failure to uphold it, while they are its people, is more ugly than every ugliness and more shameful than every shameful act.

The object of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿had believed﴾ is omitted, relying on its being evident from what preceded it, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you blame us for nothing except that we believed in Allah and in what was revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?﴾ (5:59), and what follows it, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah﴾ ... and so on. That is: and if they, despite what has proceeded from them of the various kinds of crimes, in word and deed, had believed in what they were denied belief in, then within it falls the obligation of their believing in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. As for the intention that they believe in him ﷺ specifically, the context rejects it, because what was mentioned before and after of their disbelief in him ﷺ was mentioned coupled with their disbelief in their own Book as well, aiming at censure and rebuke by showing that disbelief in him ﷺ entails disbelief in their Book. Therefore, restricting the belief here to belief in him ﷺ alone disrupts the correspondence of the parts of the noble composition.

﴿And had been mindful of Allah﴾ regarding what We have enumerated of their sins, among which is opposing their Book.

﴿We would have removed from them their misdeeds﴾ which they committed, however great they were in magnitude and extreme in number, and We would not have punished them for them; ﴿and We would have admitted them﴾ in addition to that

﴿to Gardens of Bliss﴾. The repetition of the lam is for emphasizing the promise, and in it is an alert to the perfection of the greatness of their sins and the abundance of their transgressions, and that Islam effaces what came before it of misdeeds, however grand they are and however they exceed every known limit.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 66:

﴿And if they had truly upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾ by observing (p-60) what is in them of rulings, among which are the signs of the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ and the good tidings of his mission. For establishing them is only by that, not by observing all that is in them of rulings, since some of them were abrogated (insikh) by the revelation of the Qur'an. So observing the whole is not, in any way, part of establishing them.

﴿And what has been sent down to them from their Lord﴾: that is, the glorious Qur'an, which confirms their books. Its being mentioned with this designation serves to signal the obligation to uphold it upon them, since it was sent down to them, and to state explicitly the falsity of what they claimed, namely that it had not been sent down to the Children of Israel. The placing of "to them" earlier is due to what has passed before, and the attribution of "Lord" to the pronoun "them" conveys extra gentleness towards them in the call to establishing it. It has been said: what is meant by "what has been sent down to them" is the books of the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as the Book of Isaiah (Sha'ya'), the Book of Habakkuk (Hanquq), and the Book of Daniel (Daniyal), for these are full of good tidings of his sending ﷺ.

﴿They would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾; that is, He would have widened their provision by pouring upon them the blessings of heaven and earth, or by increasing the fruits of the trees and the produce of the crops, or by granting them gardens laden with ripe fruit, so that they would pick what hangs down from the tops of the trees and gather what has fallen from them onto the ground.

It has been said: what is meant is an emphasis on describing abundance and fertility, not a specifying of the two directions, as if it were said: "they would have eaten from every direction." The object of "eaten" is omitted for the purpose of generality, or for the purpose of focusing on the act itself, as in the saying: "So-and-so gives and withholds." And "from" in both places indicates the starting point. In these two conditional clauses there is an exhortation to what has been mentioned of faith and piety, and to upholding them with the promise of attaining the happiness of both abodes, and a warning against neglecting what has been mentioned, by explaining that it leads to deprivation of these, and an alert to them that what has befallen them of hardship and constriction is only from the evil consequences of their misdeeds, and not due to any shortfall in the bounty of the Bountiful, which is not hidden.

﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾: a new sentence, built upon a question arising from the content of the two clauses introduced by the particle of impossibility, which indicate the absence of faith and piety and of upholding the books revealed to the People of the Book. It is as if it were said: "Are all of them thus, persisting in not believing...?" So it was said: "Among them is a moderate community." This is either on the basis that "among them" is a subject in terms of its meaning, i.e., some of them are a community, or by supposing an omitted qualified noun, i.e., some who are from among them, as was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God"﴾ and so on; i.e., a moderate group, and they are the believers among them, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and his like, and forty-eight of the Christians. It has been said: a community whose condition is that of nations in enmity to the Messenger of God ﷺ.

﴿And many of them﴾ is a subject, being specified by the description, whose predicate is ﴿evil is what they do﴾; i.e., this statement is said concerning them: how evil is what they do. It carries the sense of wonder: how bad their deeds are, of obstinacy and stubbornness, distortion of the truth and turning away from it, and excess in enmity. They are the coarse and fanatical, such as Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his like, and the Romans.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 67:

﴿O Messenger!﴾ He was addressed (ﷺ) by the title of Messengership, as an honour to him and as an indication that it necessitates doing what he was commanded, namely conveying what was revealed to him.

﴿Convey what has been sent down to you﴾; that is: all of what has been sent down to you of rulings and what relates to them, whatever it may be.

In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from your Lord﴾; that is: the Owner of your affairs, and the One who brings you to the perfection befitting you, is an implicit promise of His protection and safeguarding of him (ﷺ); that is: convey it without watching anyone in that matter, and without fearing that any harm will ever reach you.

﴿And if you do not do so﴾, meaning, if you do not do what you were commanded of conveying all of it in the sense mentioned.

As His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿then you have not conveyed His message﴾, for what the rulings do not relate to at all (p-61) of the hidden secrets is not something whose conveyance to people is intended. That is: you have not conveyed any part of His message, and you have entirely stripped yourself of the title of Messengership with which you were honoured, since some of it is not more deserving of delivery than others. So if you do not deliver some of it, it is as if you had neglected delivering all of it. Just as whoever does not believe in some of it is like one who does not believe in all of it, since each part conveys what the others convey, and they are therefore in the ruling of one thing. There is no doubt that one who is a conveyor of one part and not a conveyor of another, or who believes in one part and not in another, is not a true believer. Also, concealing some of it is a waste of what has been delivered of it, like omitting some pillars of the prayer, for the purpose of the call is thereby defeated.

It has been said: "then it is as if you had conveyed none of it," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿it is as if he had slain all of mankind﴾, in that concealing a part or the whole is equal in heinousness and in attracting punishment.

It has been read: (فَما بَلَّغْتَ رِسالاتِي) ("then you have not conveyed My messages"). And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "If you conceal a single verse, you have not conveyed My messages." And it is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Allah sent me with His messages, and I was distressed by them, so Allah revealed to me: 'If you do not convey My messages, I will punish you,' and He guaranteed me protection, so I grew strong." That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. For this, as you see, is a generous promise of His protecting him from the harm of the people reaching his noble soul, which moves him to earnestness in fulfilling what he was commanded of conveyance, without caring for their enmity and their plotting. And from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: that he (ﷺ) used to be guarded until this was revealed, then he put his head out of a leather tent and said: "Disperse, O people, for Allah has protected me from the people."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ is a reason for His protection of him (ﷺ); that is: He does not enable them to do what they intend to you of harm. The placement of this noble verse amid the verses concerning the People of the Book is because all of them are thunderbolts whose hearing distresses the disbelievers, and it is hard for the Messenger (ﷺ) to address them with them, especially the text that follows, which censures them for the completeness of their misguidance.

And for this reason the command is repeated, so it is said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 68:

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything﴾, addressing both groups.

﴿You are not upon anything﴾; that is, no religion that is held in regard and that deserves to be called "anything," because its falsehood is manifest and its corruption is clear. In this expression there is a degree of belittling and diminishing beyond which there is no further limit.

﴿Until you establish the Torah and the Gospel﴾; that is, you observe them and preserve what is in them of matters, among which are the proofs of the Messenger's mission (ﷺ) and the signs of his prophethood, for their establishment is only through that. As for observing their rulings that have been abrogated (naskh), this is not part of establishing them in any way; rather it is a nullifying of them and a rejection of their testimony, because they bear witness to the abrogation of those rulings and to the end of the time for acting by them. For their testimony to the soundness of what abrogates them is a testimony to its abrogation and to its leaving the category of their rulings, and that their rulings are what the Prophet (ﷺ) established, the one whose coming they gave good news of, and whose attributes are mentioned within them. Thus, establishing them is the clarification of the signs of prophethood and acting by what the Sharia has established of rulings.

As He, the Exalted, expresses in His saying: ﴿and what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾; that is, the glorious Qur'an, by believing in it, for the establishment of all of them is not achieved without that. The mention of establishing the two Books before establishing it, although it is the primary aim for the sake of observing the right of testimony and bringing them down from the rank of opposition, and presenting it under the heading of being sent down to them, is because of what has passed of the explicit statement that they are commanded to establish it and believe in it, not as they claim, that it is restricted to the Arabs.

In the attribution of "the Lord" to the pronoun "them" there is what has been pointed out of gentleness in the invitation. It has been said: what is meant by ﴿what has been sent down to them﴾ is the books of the prophets of the Children of Israel, as has passed. It has also been said: the divine books, for all of them command belief in one whom the miracle has confirmed, and declare the obligation of obedience to him.

It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: that a group of the Jews said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you not recite that the Torah is true, from Allah, the Exalted?" He (ﷺ) said: "Yes." They said: "Then we believe in it and do not believe in anything other than it." So it was revealed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And what has been sent down to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief﴾ is a resumed sentence explaining the severity of their obstinacy, their excess in arrogance and enmity, and that conveying the message does not benefit them. Its opening with an oath is to emphasize its content and confirm its meaning. By "the many" mentioned is meant their scholars and their leaders. The attribution of the sending down to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), together with its attribution to them earlier, is to indicate their detachment from that attribution.

﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾; that is, do not be sorrowful or grieved over them, because of their excess in transgression and disbelief in what you convey to them, for its harm returns to them, and its consequence encompasses them and does not pass them by. And among the believers there is room for you away from them. Placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is to record upon them their firmness in disbelief.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 69:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), brought to encourage those other than those previously mentioned to believe and to do righteous deeds. That is: those who believe only with their tongues, and they are the hypocrites. It has been said: the phrase is more general, covering those whose hearts do not first agree with their tongues.

﴿And those who are Jews﴾: that is, those who entered Judaism (al-Yahudiyya).

﴿And the Sabians and the Christians﴾: "Nasara" is the plural of "Nasran," and its detailed explanation has already passed in surah al-Baqara. The words of the Exalted, "﴿And the Sabians﴾," are in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted, and the intention is that it is delayed beyond what falls within the scope of "inna" (indeed). The estimated meaning is: indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Christians, their ruling is such-and-such, and the Sabians likewise, as in the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I and Qayyar in it are strangers"

And in the saying of another:

"Otherwise know that we and you are transgressors, so long as we remain in dissension"

Except that it has been placed between the subject of "inna" and its predicate, to show that the Sabians, despite the clarity of their error and their deviation from all religions, their repentance is accepted if they truly attain faith and righteous deeds, so others are more deserving of this. It has also been said: the following clause is the predicate of the mentioned subject, and the predicate of "inna" is omitted, as in the saying of the poet:

"We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, though opinions differ"

It has also been said: "al-Nasara" is in the nominative case as a subject, and the words of the Exalted, "﴿and the Sabians﴾," are coordinated with it, and it, together with its predicate, is coordinated with the clause introduced by "inna." There is no way to coordinate it alone with the place (mahall) of "inna" and its subject, because that requires the completion of the predicate; otherwise the predicate would be in the nominative by both "inna" and the subject together. It has been answered that this applies when the mentioned word is the predicate of both, but when the predicate of the coordinated word is omitted, there is no objection. Nor is it coordinated with the pronoun in "hadu" (they were Jews), because there is no emphasis and no separation, and because that would imply that the Sabians are Jews.

It was read as "wal-Sabiyyun" with a clear "ya'" and with the hamza eased. It was read as "wal-Sabbun," which is from "saba, yasbu," because they inclined (saba) toward following desire and lusts in their religion. It was read as "wal-Sabi'in." It was read as: "Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu wal-ladhina hadu wal-Sabi'un."

The words of the Exalted, "﴿whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds﴾," are either in the place of nominative case, as a subject whose predicate is "﴿then no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾," and the "fa'" (then) is because the subject includes the meaning of a conditional; the plural of the final pronouns is considered in light of the meaning of the relative pronoun, just as the singular of what is in its relative clause is considered in light of its wording. The clause is the predicate of "inna," and the returning pronoun to its subject is omitted, meaning: whoever among them believes. Or it is in the place of accusative case, as a substitute (badal) for the subject of "inna" and what is coordinated with it, and the predicate is the words of the Exalted, "﴿then no fear﴾," and the "fa'" is as in the words of the Exalted, Mighty and Sublime: "﴿Indeed, those who persecute the believing men and believing women and then do not repent will have the punishment of Hell﴾," etc. So the meaning, on the supposition that what is meant by "those who believe" is the hypocrites, which is the more evident: whoever among these groups newly brings about sincere faith in the origin (of creation) and the return (to God) in the proper manner, not as the People of the Book claim, for that is far from being faith in them, and does a righteous deed as faith in them requires, then there is no fear for them when the disbelievers fear punishment, nor shall they grieve when those who fell short grieve over wasting their lives and missing the reward. The purpose is to show the continuity of the negation of these two, not the negation of their continuity, as might be suggested by the predicate in the second clause being in the present tense, as has been explained many times; because negation, even when it enters upon the present tense itself, indicates continuity and persistence according to context. As for the supposition that what is meant by "those who believe" is every adherent of the religion of Islam, sincere and hypocritical alike, then what is meant by "whoever believes" is whoever among them is characterized by sincere faith in the origin and the return in general, whether by way of steadfastness and persistence in it, as is the case of the sincere, or by way of initiating and creating it, as is the case of the hypocrites and the rest of the groups.

The benefit of generalizing to include the sincere is to strongly encourage the others to faith, by showing that their delay in attaining it does not prevent them from being exemplars like those early distinguished leaders. As for what has been said, that the meaning is: whoever among them, in his religion before it was abrogated (nasakh), believed in his heart in the origin and the return and acted according to the requirements of his law, this is something that has no way at all, as its detailed explanation has passed in surah al-Baqara.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 70:

﴿Indeed, We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ This is an independent statement, brought to explain another of their crimes, which calls for the exclusion of faith from them. That is: by Allah, We indeed took their covenant concerning monotheism and all the laws and rulings prescribed for them in the Torah.

﴿And We sent to them messengers﴾ of great number and of weighty standing, so that they would hold them to observing the rights of the covenant, inform them of what they must do and what they must refrain from in their religion, and keep them under admonition and reminder.

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Every time there came to them a messenger with what their souls did not desire﴾ is a conditional sentence, introduced as a new statement, which came as an answer to a question arising from the report of the taking of the covenant and the sending of the messengers. The apodosis of the condition is omitted, as if it were said: "What did they do to the messengers?" Then it was said: "Every time there came to them a messenger from those messengers with what their souls, absorbed in wealth and corruption, did not love, of the true rulings and laws, they disobeyed him and showed hostility to him."

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿A party they denied, and a party they killed﴾ is a new answer to an inquiry about the manner of the opposition they displayed, which is understood from the conditional sentence, given in summary form, as if it were said: "How did they treat them?" Then it was said: a party of them denied them without going further to inflict any other harm, and another party of them did not content themselves with denying them, but killed them as well. The present tense was chosen over the past tense in narrating a past situation in order to bring its dreadful image to mind so as to marvel at it, to alert to the fact that this was their constant habit, and to preserve the rhyme endings of the noble verses.

The fronting of "a party" in both places is for the sake of emphasis on it and to arouse the listener's eagerness toward what they did to it, not for restriction. As for making the conditional clause a description of "messengers," as the majority have held, the context does not support it at all, since when a declarative sentence is made a description or a relative clause, the ruling within it is cancelled, and it becomes a title for the described noun, a complement to it in establishing another matter concerning it.

For this reason, the description must be known to the listener as belonging to the described noun before it is made a description of it. Hence they said: descriptions before knowledge of them are reports, and reports after knowledge of them are descriptions. And there is no doubt that what the composition was brought to convey is only the explanation that they made every one who came to them from the messengers of Allah, the Exalted, a target for killing or denial, as its meaning indicates, making it a new statement in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, to explain that He, the Exalted, sent to them messengers described by each of them being of this kind, as the intent of making it a description would require.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 71:**

﴿And they thought there would be no trial﴾; that is: the Children of Israel thought that they would not be struck by God, the Exalted, for what they had committed of the great calamity (al-dahya' al-dahya'), and the vile scheme (al-khutta al-shan'a), by way of affliction and punishment.

It is recited as ﴿لا تكونُ﴾ (*la takūnu*, "there is not") with the *raf'* (nominative) ending, on the basis that ﴿أنْ﴾ (*an*) is the lightened form (*al-mukhaffafa*) of ﴿أنَّ﴾ (*inna*), and its noun is the omitted pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*, the pronoun referring to the situation). Its original form is: "that there is not a trial." The verb of thinking (*fi'l al-husban*) is suspended (*ta'līq*) by it, and *an* here is for affirmation (*lil-tahqīq*), placing the verb in the position of knowledge because of its great strength. And *anna* with what follows it fills the place of its two objects.

﴿So they became blind﴾ is coordinated with "they thought," and the *fa'* (fa) indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it; that is: they felt secure from the might of God, the Exalted, so they persisted in all kinds of error and corruption, and became blind to the religion after the messengers had guided them to its clear signposts and made its evident paths plain to them.

﴿And they became deaf﴾ to hearing the truth that was cast upon them. For this reason they did to them what they did. This refers to the first of the two occasions of corruption by the Children of Israel, when they opposed the rulings of the Torah, committed the forbidden acts, and killed Sha'ya (Isaiah), peace be upon him. It was also said that they imprisoned Irmiya (Jeremiah), peace be upon them both, not that they worshipped the calf as has been said. For although that was a great sin arising from complete blindness and deafness, it occurred in the time of Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, and has no connection with what is related of them regarding what they did to the messengers who came after him, peace be upon him, by many ages.

﴿Then God turned to them﴾ when they repented and returned from the corruption they had been in, after they had been in Babylon for a long time under the domination of Bukht Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar), as captives in the utmost humiliation and abasement. God, the Mighty and Majestic, then sent a great king of the kings of Persia to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to rebuild it. He rescued the remnants of the Children of Israel from the captivity of Bukht Nasr after his death, returned them to their homeland, and those among them who had scattered into the regions returned and rebuilt it for thirty years. They multiplied and became as good as they had ever been.

It was also said: when Bahman ibn Isfandiyar inherited the kingdom from his grandfather Kastasp (Kay Gushtasp), God, the Mighty and Majestic, placed compassion for them in his heart. He returned them to al-Sham (Greater Syria) and appointed Daniel (Dāniyāl), peace be upon him, as their ruler. They then took control over those who were there from among the followers of Bukht Nasr, and the prophets rose among them, so they returned to the best condition they had been in. This is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Then We gave you back your turn over them﴾.

As for what has been said, that the intended meaning is the acceptance of their repentance from worshipping the calf, you have known that this has no connection with the context. He did not attribute the repentance to them, as He did with their other states of thinking, blindness and deafness, in order to avoid explicitly attributing good to them. It is only indicated within the statement of God's turning to them in repentance, as a preparation for the explanation of their breaking of it, in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Then they became blind and deaf﴾. This refers to the last of the two occasions of their corruption, which was their audacity in killing Zakariyya (Zechariah) and Yahya (John), and their intention to kill Isa (Jesus), peace be upon them. It does not refer to their asking to see God, as has been said, for reasons you have come to know. The varieties of crimes committed by them are almost endless. Yet the restriction of what is related of them here to two occasions, and its being ordered after the narration of what they did to the messengers, peace be upon them, requires that the intended meaning is what we have mentioned. And God knows the Book best.

﴿They became blind﴾ and ﴿they became deaf﴾ are also recited with a *ḍamma* (u-vowel): ﴿عُمُوا وصُمُّوا﴾, on the assumption that God blinded them and deafened them; that is, He struck them with blindness and deafness, just as one says *nazaktuhu* when one strikes him with a *nayzak* (a spear), and *rakibtuhu* when one strikes him with one's knee.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿many of them﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in the two verbs. It was also said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*); that is: "those are many of them."

﴿And God is Seeing of what they do﴾; that is: of what they did. The use of the present tense (*ṣīghat al-muḍāriʿ*) is to narrate a past situation so as to bring its dreadful image before the mind and to observe the verse-endings (*fawāṣil*). The sentence is a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*), by which is indicated the falsity of their presumption mentioned above, and the occurrence of punishment from where they did not expect it. This is a general indication, sufficed for by relying on what was explained in some detail in Surat Bani Isra'il. The meaning is: they thought that no punishment would befall them, so they committed the great crimes that deserve the severest punishments, and God is Seeing of their details. How then would He not take them to account for them? And from where did they get that false presumption?

This did indeed happen the first time, when God gave power over them to Bukht Nasr, the agent of Lohrasp over Babylon. It was also said that it was Jalut al-Jaziri (Goliath) or Sanjarib (Sennacherib) of the people of Nineveh. The first is the more apparent. He then took control of Bayt al-Maqdis and killed from its people forty thousand of those who read the Torah, and took the rest away to his land. They remained there in the utmost humiliation and misery until they made a sound repentance. God, the Mighty and Majestic, then returned them to the good condition described above. Then they went back to the last occasion of corruption, and God sent the Persians against them. The king of Babylon, one of the kings of the Tawa'if (the Parthian dynasties), named Khaydarud, or it was said Khaydarus, attacked them and did to them what he did.

It was said: the commander of the army entered the place where they sacrificed their offerings and found blood boiling in it. He asked them about it, and they said: it is the blood of an offering that was not accepted from us. He said: you have not told me the truth. So he killed thousands of them upon it. Then he said: if you do not tell me the truth, I will leave none of you alive. They said: it is the blood of Yahya, peace be upon him. He said: with the like of this God, the Exalted, takes revenge upon you. Then he said: O Yahya, my Lord and your Lord knows what has befallen your people because of you; so calm down, by God's leave, before I leave none of them alive. And it calmed down.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 72:**

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾ This begins the detailing of the abominations of the Christians, and the refutation of their corrupt statements after the detailing of the abominations of the Jews. These are the ones who said that Mary gave birth to a god. It was said: they are the Malkaniyya (Melkites) and, among them, the Ya'qubiyya (Jacobites). It was also said: they are specifically the Ya'qubiyya. They said: the meaning of this is that Allah, exalted is He, indwelled the essence of Jesus and united with his essence, exalted is He above that by a great exaltation.

﴿And the Messiah said﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "they said," with a implicit "qad" (indeed) that conveys the intensification of the ugliness of their condition, by showing that they denied the Messiah and did not desist from what they persisted in, despite what he had threatened them with. That is, they said this.

The Messiah had indeed said, addressing them: ﴿O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.﴾ Indeed I am a servant nourished (by Allah) like you, so worship my Creator and your Creator. ﴿Indeed, He﴾, that is, the matter is that:

﴿whoever associates others with Allah﴾, that is, associates anything in His worship, or in what is specific to Him of the attributes of divinity.

﴿Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾, so he will never enter it, just as the one who is forbidden cannot reach the forbidden thing (?), for it is the abode of the monotheists. The mention of the Exalted Name in place of the pronoun serves to magnify the matter and to instill awe.

﴿And his refuge is the Fire﴾, for it is what is prepared for the polytheists. This is an explanation of their being afflicted with punishment after the explanation of their being deprived of reward.

﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, that is, they have no one who helps them by rescuing them from the Fire, either by way of overpowering (the punishment) or by way of intercession. The plural is used to correspond with the contrast with "the wrongdoers." The definite article is either for specification (al-'ahd), with the plural in view of the sense of "min" (whoever), just as the singular in the three pronouns is in view of its wording; or it is for the category (al-jins), and they are included in it in the primary sense. Placing it, on the first view, in the position of a pronoun serves to record against them that they wronged themselves by associating partners with Allah and deviated from the path of truth.

The sentence is a concluding clause (tadhyil) confirming what precedes it. It may be part of the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, or it may be an address from Allah, exalted is He, to the statement of Jesus, peace be upon him, confirming its content.
