It has been said that it is from the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with the meaning that they wronged and deviated from the way of truth in what they fabricated about Jesus, peace be upon him; therefore He did not support them in it, did not help their statement, rejected and denied it, even though they were exalting him thereby and raising his station; or it is from the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, with the meaning: no one will help you in what you say, nor will anyone support you in it, because it is impossible and far from reason.

You know well that the expression of what is related from him, peace be upon him, opposing their false statement with explicit rejection and denial, and the threat of being deprived of Paradise and entering the Fire merely for not supporting him in that, and the negation of his help for him, while being devoid of benefit, is a depiction of the strong in the image of the weak, and a diminishing of the gravity of the matter from the station of its awesomeness. Indeed, this may give the apparent impression of what is not fitting for his dignity, peace be upon him, namely the imagining of support and help, especially with the observation of his words: "And even though they were exalting him..." etc. Unless the statement is taken as sarcasm toward them. Likewise the circumstantial clause, on the assumption that it is part of the speech of him, peace be upon him: his admonishing them, peace be upon him, against their corrupt statement by mentioning the absence of any helper or supporter, after his admonishing them with what has passed of the emphatic rejection and the severe threat, is of no benefit or effect. There is no way here except to excuse it as sarcasm.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 73:

﴿Certainly those who say, "Indeed Allah is the third of three," have disbelieved.﴾ This begins the explanation of the disbelief of another group among them. The meaning of their saying "third of three" and "fourth of four" and the like is that one of these numbers is absolute, not specifically the third or the fourth. For this reason the majority (al-Jumhur) prohibited putting the noun that follows in the accusative, as in saying "thaalithu thalathatin" and "raabi'u arba'atin." Rather, the accusative is used only when what follows is one rank below, as in your saying "'ashiru tis'atan" (tenth of nine) and "taasi'u thamaniyatan" (ninth of eight).

It has been said: they say that divinity is shared between Allah, glorified and exalted be He, Jesus, and Mary, and each one of these is a god. This is reinforced by the words of Allah, exalted be He, to the Messiah: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ So His saying, exalted be He, "third of three" means: one of three gods.

This is what is immediately apparent from the outward meaning of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿There is no god except one God.﴾ That is, the state of affairs is that there exists in existence no being that is necessary, deserving of worship, in that it is the origin of all existent things, except a God described by oneness, exalted above accepting partnership. And "min" (in "min ilahin") is extra, for the sake of generalization (istighraq).

It has also been said: they say, "Allah is one substance (jawhar) of three hypostases (aqanim): the hypostasis of the Father, the hypostasis of the Son, and the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit." They mean by the first the essence (dhat), and it has been said existence (wujud); by the second, knowledge (ilm); and by the third, life (hayat). So the meaning of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿There is no god except one God﴾ is: no god except one God in essence, free from any trace of plurality in any respect whatsoever.

﴿And if they do not desist from what they say﴾ of the monstrous disbelief and do not affirm the oneness of God.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Those who disbelieve among them will surely be touched﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, which takes the place of the answer to the condition; that is: and by God, if they do not desist, they will surely be touched. It was placed in the position of the pronoun "hum" (they) of the relative clause, in order to repeat the testimony against them regarding disbelief.

The "min" in His saying ﴿among them﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyya), or, if it refers to those among them who remained upon the disbelief they were on, then "min" is partitive (tab'idiyya). The verb used, which indicates occurrence (huduth), was employed to alert that persisting in it after the arrival of what abrogates it by the decisive text of Jesus, peace be upon him, and others, is a new disbelief and an excess of extremism beyond the original disbelief they were already in.

﴿A painful punishment﴾; that is, a kind of punishment of severe pain.

The interrogative hamzah in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness?﴾ is for denouncing and deeming improbable what has occurred, not for denying its occurrence. It expresses amazement at their persistence. The fa' is for coordination with an implied antecedent that the context requires; that is: "Will they not desist from those deviant beliefs and false sayings, so that they repent to Allah, exalted is He, and seek His forgiveness by affirming His oneness and declaring Him free of what they have attributed to Him of incarnation and indwelling?" Thus the focus of the denunciation and amazement is both non-desistence and non-repentance together. Alternatively, it means: "Do they hear these repeated testimonies and firm warnings, and yet not repent immediately afterwards?" Thus the focus of both is the failure to repent after the realization of what necessitates it, namely hearing those mighty admonitions.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ form a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) relating to the subject of "yastaghfirunahu" (they seek His forgiveness). It reinforces the denunciation and amazement at their persistence in disbelief and their failure to hasten to seek forgiveness. That is: while the state is that He, exalted is He, is abundant in forgiveness, so He forgives them when they seek forgiveness and bestows upon them of His grace.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 75:

﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to establish the truth from which there is no deviation, and to explain the true reality of his state, peace be upon him, and the state of his mother. It points first to the most noble of the attributes of perfection that they possess, by which they became among the foremost of the most perfect individuals of the human species, and lastly to the attribute they share with all individuals of mankind, indeed with all individuals of animals, so as to bring them down gradually from the rank of persistence in what they have fabricated about them, and to guide them to repentance and seeking forgiveness. That is: he is restricted to the messengership and hardly transcends it.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Messengers had passed away before him﴾ is an attribute of "messenger," indicating that he is characterized by what contradicts divinity. For the passing away of the earlier messengers, peace be upon them, is a warning of his own passing away, which necessitates the impossibility of his divinity. That is: he is no more than a messenger like the messengers who passed away before him. God Most High singled him out with some of the signs, just as He singled out each of them with some other signs. If he brought the dead back to life through his hand, then Moses, peace be upon him, turned the staff in his hand into a moving serpent, and that is more wondrous than it. If he was created without a father, then Adam was created without father or mother, and that is more remarkable than it. All of this is from His presence, Mighty and Majestic. Moses and Jesus are only manifestations of His affairs and acts.

﴿And his mother was a truthful woman﴾; that is: his mother too is not unlike the rest of women who persist in truthfulness or in believing, and who exceed in being characterized by it. Their rank is no more than the rank of two humans, one of whom is a prophet and the other a companion (sahabi). So from where do you derive for them attributes that are not ascribed to the rest of the prophets and their elect?

﴿They both used to eat food﴾ is a resumptive statement explaining what was alluded to, namely that they are like the rest of the individuals of mankind in needing what every individual of them needs, indeed like the individuals of animals.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them﴾ is an expression of wonder at the state of those who claim divinity for them both, and who do not desist from that after the reality of their state has been made clear to them with a clarity around which no trace of doubt hovers. "How" (kayfa) is an object of "We make clear" (nubayyinu), and the clause, being in the place of accusative, is suspended for "look" (unzur); that is: look how We make the dazzling signs clear to them, which proclaim the falsehood of what they have fabricated about them, a proclamation that nearly makes the deaf mountains hear it.

﴿Then look how they are turned away﴾; that is: how they are diverted from listening to them and reflecting upon them. The discussion regarding it is as in what precedes it. The repetition of the command to look is for emphasis in expressing wonder, and "then" (thumma) is to show the disparity between the two wonders; that is: Our making the signs clear is a matter wondrous in its kind, reaching the furthest extremes of verification and clarification, while their turning away from them, despite the complete absence of anything that justifies it, and the convergence of what necessitates their acceptance, is more wondrous and more marvellous.

Say, [O Muhammad, as a command to him, peace be upon him, to hold them to account and rebuke them, following His expressing wonder at their conditions.]

﴿Do you worship, besides Allah,﴾ that is, going beyond Him. Placing ﴿what has no power to harm you or benefit you﴾ before the phrase "Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing" follows the principle, repeated many times, of giving prominence to what is placed first and creating anticipation for what comes later. The relative pronoun refers to Jesus, peace be upon him. Its use instead of the word "man" (who) serves to establish what is intended: that he is entirely outside divinity, by showing that he, peace be upon him, is included among the things that have no power over anything at all. Although he, peace be upon him, possesses such power through Allah's granting it to him, he does not possess it of himself, nor does he possess the like of what Allah Most High can inflict upon people of tribulations and calamities, or what He can benefit them with of health.

The mention of harm before benefit is because guarding against harm is more important than seeking benefit, and because the lowest degree of influence is averting evil, then bringing good.

His statement, Most High, ﴿And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "Do you worship" (ataʿbudūna), emphasizing the denunciation and rebuke and establishing the argument and reproach. The linking element is the waw (and); that is: "Do you associate with Allah, Most High, that which has no power over any of your harm or benefit, while Allah Most High is the One exclusively encompassing with complete knowledge all that is heard and known, of which is what you hold of false statements, deviant beliefs, and evil deeds, and with overwhelming power over all things within capability, of which is your harm and your benefit in this world and the Hereafter."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 77:**

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture!"﴾ This is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab) and a turning of the address (tawjih) toward the two groups of the People of the Scripture, by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), spoken on the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ) after the refutation of the path of each of them. This is for the sake of intensifying their rebuke for the false path they have followed, and for guiding them to the nations that came before them (al-umam al-munta'ah).

﴿Do not go to excess in your religion﴾: that is, do not transgress the limit. This is a prohibition addressed to the Christians against elevating Jesus above the rank of messenger to what they have fabricated concerning him of greatness, and addressed to the Jews against lowering him, peace be upon him, from his exalted rank to what they have fabricated about him of the vile utterance. It is also said that it is specific to the Christians, as in Surah al-Nisa', so He reminded them by the title of "People of the Scripture" to remind them that (p-69) the Gospel also forbids them from excess (ghuluw).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿other than the truth﴾ is in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar); that is: do not go to excess in your religion, an excess other than the truth, that is, false excess. Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject pronoun; that is: do not go to excess, transgressing the truth. Or it is a circumstantial clause from "your religion"; that is: do not go to excess in your religion while it is false. It is also said that it is in the accusative as an exception of the contiguous type (istithna' muttasil), and it is also said as an exception of the disconnected type (istithna' munqati').

﴿And do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before, and led many astray, and strayed from the sound way﴾: they are their forefathers and their leaders who had gone astray from both groups, or, according to both opinions, from the Christians, before the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission, in their own law.

﴿And led many astray﴾: that is, a great many people who joined them in deviation and misguidance, or a great leading-astray; the object is omitted.

﴿And strayed﴾ at the time of the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission, and at the clarification of the clear path of truth and the explanation of the methods of Islam.

﴿from the sound way﴾ when they denied him, envied him, and rebelled against him. It is also said: the first (is) an indication of their straying from the requirement of reason, and the second: to their straying from what the Sharia brought.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 5, verse 78:**

﴿Those who disbelieved were cursed﴾. That is, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cursed them. The verb is built in the passive form (*bina' al-fi'l lil-maf'ul*) to follow the manner of divine majesty.

﴿from among the Children of Israel﴾: *min Bani Isra'il* is related to an omitted element (*muta'allaq bi-mahdhuf*, a dependent phrase whose verb is understood) that serves as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*). Alternatively, it is related to the subject of *kafaru* (the doer of the disbelieving).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿upon the tongue of Dawud and Isa, son of Maryam﴾. This phrase is related to *lu'ina* (was cursed). That is, Allah the Exalted cursed them in the Zabur (Psalms) and the Injil (Gospel) through the tongues of the two of them. It has been said that when the people of Ayla transgressed on the Sabbath (*al-Sabt*), Dawud, peace be upon him, invoked a curse upon them and said: "O Allah, curse them and make them a sign." So Allah transformed them into apes. And when the companions of the Table (*Ashab al-Ma'idah*) disbelieved, Isa, peace be upon him, said: "O Allah, punish whoever disbelieved after eating from the Table with a punishment You have not inflicted upon anyone among the worlds, and curse them as You cursed the companions of the Sabbath." So they became swine. They numbered five thousand men, among whom there was no woman and no child.

﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the aforementioned curse. Choosing the demonstrative noun rather than a pronoun serves to draw attention to its complete manifestness, its distinction from similar things, and its incorporation, by virtue of it, into the category of visible matters. The sense of distance it carries signals the extreme heinousness of the curse and the great degree of its horror and dreadfulness. It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is Allah's statement: ﴿because they disobeyed and were transgressing﴾, *bima 'asaw wa-kanu ya'tadun*. The sentence is a resumptive clause (*jumlah musta'nafah*) occupying the position of an answer to what arises from the preceding speech, as if it were said: "For what reason did that occur?" And it was answered: that dreadful, terrible curse was due to their persistent disobedience and transgression, as the combination of the past and present forms (*sighatay al-madi wa-al-mustaqbal*) indicates.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 79:

What points to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They did not forbid one another from any wrongful deed they committed﴾. This is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) which, by its wording, conveys the continuity of the failure to forbid wrongdoing. This continuity cannot be realized except through the continuous commission of wrongful deeds. The meaning of "forbidding one another" (al-tanahi) is not that each of them forbids the other from the wrongdoing he commits, which is the well-known meaning of the verbal form of the reciprocal (tafaʿul) pattern. Rather, it is merely the issuing of a prohibition from multiple persons, without requiring that each of them be both forbidder and forbidden at once, as in "they saw the crescent" (taraʾaw al-hilal).

It has also been said that tanahi means intihaʾ (cessation). One says: "tanaha ʿan al-amr" and "intaha ʿanhu," when one abstains from it and leaves it. In that case the sentence explains what precedes it, namely the disobedience and transgression, and conveys the continuity of both explicitly. According to the first view, it conveys the continuity of the absence of forbidding wrongdoing, such that there is never found among them anyone who undertakes it at any time, and by necessity the continuity of committing the wrong follows, as already stated. In every case, the unity implied by the indefinite noun "munkar" (wrongful deed) is a unity of type (nawʿiyya), not of a specific individual. Therefore, describing it with the past tense verb does not detract from the prohibition's application to it, since the object of the verb is only one instance of what the prohibition applies to, and the abstaining from wrongdoing in general is realized through any of its instances whatsoever. Moreover, the past tense considered in the description refers to the time of revelation, not to the time of the prohibition, so that it would not follow that the prohibition came after the act. Hence there is no need to posit repetition (muʿawada), or a hypothetical example (mathal), or to take the verb as an expression for intention (irada). Furthermore, repetition, like prohibition, does not apply to a wrongful deed already committed, so one must resort to one of the two aspects mentioned, or to positing a hypothetical example, or to taking the verb as an expression for intending it. All of these involve evident forced interpretation.

﴿Certainly evil is what they used to do﴾: this is a condemnation of their evil deeds and an expression of astonishment at them, through emphasis by oath. How could it not be so, when it led them to the great curse explained above? The fact that they were the cause of that does not indicate that their disbelief falls outside causation, given the indication of its causality in the earlier words of His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed﴾. For the application of the judgment to the relative pronoun signals that what is in the clause following it is the cause of it, since what was mentioned in the sphere of causation also includes their disbelief.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 80:

﴿You see many of them﴾; that is, of the People of the Book, such as Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his likes, when they went out to the polytheists of Makkah in order to agree together on fighting the Prophet (ﷺ). The seeing here is visual (basariyyah).

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿turning in friendship to those who disbelieve﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "many" (kathiran), because it is qualified; that is, they take the polytheists as allies out of hatred for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers. It has been said: they are from among the hypocrites of the People of the Book who take the Jews as allies; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujahid, and al-Hasan. It has also been said: they take the polytheists as allies and maintain friendly relations with them.

﴿Evil is what their own souls have sent forward for them﴾: an evil thing they sent forward, to be confronted with it on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿That Allah has become wrathful towards them﴾ is the subject of the blame (al-makhsus bi-al-dhamm), with the omission of the qualified noun (al-mudaf) and the placing of the noun it is attached to (al-mudaf ilayh) in its place, to draw attention to the complete connection and bond between the two, as if they were one thing, and for emphasis in blame; that is, what necessitates His wrath, the Exalted. Its position is nominative (raf') as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and the clause before it is its predicate (khabar). The connecting pronoun, according to those who require it, is the generality (al-'umum), or there is no need for it, because the clause is itself the subject. Or it is a predicate of an omitted subject indicated by the preceding clause, as if it were said: "What is it, or what thing is it?" and it was answered: "It is that Allah has become wrathful towards them." It has also been said: the subject of blame is omitted, and "ma" is a complete, definite noun in the nominative position as the agent of the verb of blame; "what their own souls have sent forward for them" is a clause in the nominative position, functioning as a qualifier of the omitted subject of blame standing in its place. The sense is: "Evil is the thing that their own souls have sent forward for them," so His saying, the Exalted: "﴿that Allah has become wrathful towards them﴾" is an apposition (badal) to the omitted "thing" (shay'), and this is the view of Sibawayh.

﴿And in the punishment﴾; that is, the punishment of Hell.

﴿They will abide therein﴾ forever and ever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 81:

﴿And if they had believed in Allah and the Prophet﴾; i.e., those who take the polytheists as allies from among the People of the Book.

﴿and what was revealed to him﴾; i.e., their Prophet.

﴿and what was revealed to him﴾ of the Book, or: if the hypocrites believed in Allah and our Prophet with a sound faith.

﴿they would not have taken them﴾; i.e., the polytheists or the Jews.

﴿as allies﴾, for belief in what has been mentioned is definitively a restraint from taking them as allies.

﴿but many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾: they have gone outside the religion, and of belief in Allah, their Prophet, and their Book; or they are rebellious in hypocrisy, exceeding its bounds in it.(p-71)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 82:

﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believe to be the Jews and those who associate partners with God﴾. This is a resumed clause (jumla mustaʾnafa), brought to affirm what precedes it of the ugly deeds of the Jews and their deep-rootedness in disbelief, and their other shameful conditions, of which their allying with the polytheists is one. It is emphasized with an oath-based emphasis (al-tawkid al-qasami), out of concern for making clear the certainty of its content. The address is either to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone suitable for it; signaling that their condition is not hidden from anyone among the people.

Wijdan (finding) is transitive to two objects: the first is "the most intense of people," and the second is "the Jews" and what is conjoined to it. It was said: the reverse, because they are in origin a subject and predicate, and the point of the benefit lies in the predicate, not the subject. There is no harm in fronting and postponing when evidence indicates the order, and here there is clear evidence for it, namely that the intended meaning is to explain that the two groups are the most intense of people in enmity toward the believers, not that the most intense of them in enmity toward them are the two groups mentioned.

You know well that this is far from indicating that. How could it not be, since the benefit in the second form is more complete and perfect, free from the strain of fronting and postponing; for the meaning is that if you intend to know who is the most intense of people in enmity toward the believers, and you follow the conditions of all the groups, and encompass what they possess in knowledge, and strive to know their apparent and hidden conditions, and endeavor to seek out what they have of manifest and concealed matters, you will surely find the most intense of them to be those two groups and no others. So reflect.

The lam that enters upon the relative pronoun is attached to "enmity" (ʿadawa), strengthening its governance. It does not harm that it is feminine by the tā’ and built upon it, as in the verse: "wa-rahbatan ʿiqabaka" (out of fear of your punishment).

It was also said: it is attached to an omitted element which is an attribute of "enmity," meaning: "existing for those who believe." God, exalted, described them with this because of the severity of their obstinacy, the multiplication of their disbelief, their immersion in following desire, their closeness to blind imitation, their distance from verification, their habituation to rebellion and defiance against the prophets, and their audacity in denying them and opposing them.

In placing the Jews before the polytheists, after binding them in one sequence, there is an indication of their precedence over them in enmity, just as their being placed before them in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And you will surely find them the most greedy of people for life, and of those who associate partners﴾, signaling their precedence over them in greed.

﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe﴾. The relative pronoun is repeated with its relative clause in order to increase clarification and explanation.

﴿Those who say, "We are Christians"﴾. He expressed them thus, indicating the nearness of their affection, since they claim that they are the helpers of God and friends of the people of truth, even if they do not show belief in the truth of Islam. On this nuance rests the second view in the interpretation of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And from those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant﴾.

The discussion concerning the two objects of "you will find" and the attachment of the lam is as previously mentioned. The shift away from making the item of difference between the two groups one thing in which they differ by intensity and weakness, or by nearness and distance, such as saying at the end: "you will surely find the weakest of them in enmity..." etc., or saying first: "you will surely find the farthest of people in affection..." etc.; is to signal the complete contrast of the difference between the two groups, by showing that one of them is at the extreme of one of the two opposites, and the other is at the nearest degree of the other opposite.

﴿That﴾; i.e., their being nearest in affection to the believers, ﴿is because among them﴾, by reason that among them.

﴿Priests (qissisin)﴾, who are the scholars of the Christians, their worshippers and their leaders. Qissis is an intensive form from taqassasa al-shayʾ: when one tracks and seeks something at night. They were so named for their intensity in tracking knowledge, as said by al-Raghib. It was said: al-qass with a fatha on the qaf means tracking a thing, and from it the scholar of the Christians was called qissis, for his tracking of knowledge. It was said: qassa al-athar and qassahu have the same meaning. It was said: (p-72) it is non-Arabic.

Qutrub said: al-qiss and al-qissis: the scholar in the language of the Romans. It was said: the Christians lost the Gospel and what is in it, and there remained among them a man called Qissisa, who did not alter his religion; so whoever follows his guidance and religion is called qissis.

﴿And monks (ruhban)﴾, which is the plural of rahib, like rakib and rukban, and faris and fursan. It was said: it is used for the singular and the plural, and there was recited in it the verse of one who said:

"Were he to see the monks of a monastery upon a height, the monks would come running and descend."

Al-tarahhub: worship in a hermitage. Al-Raghib said: al-rahbaniyya: excess in bearing worship out of extreme fear. The indefinite form is for the sake of conveying abundance, and it is necessary to consider it also in the qissisin; for it is that which indicates the affection of the Christian kind toward the believers, since the attribution of a quality to many individuals of a kind is an indication of the kind's possessing it. Otherwise, among the Jews too there are rightly-guided people; do you not see ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his like? God, exalted, said: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a upright community who recite the verses of God in the hours of the night while they prostrate﴾ ... etc. But since they were not in number like those among the Christians, their ruling did not extend to the kind of Jews.

﴿And that they are not arrogant﴾, a conjunction upon "that among them"; i.e., and because they are not arrogant toward accepting the truth when they understand it, and they are humble and not proud like the Jews. This quality includes all individuals of the kind, so its being the cause of their nearness in affection to the believers is clear. In it is evidence that humility, devotion to knowledge and action, and turning away from base desires are praiseworthy, even if that comes from a disbeliever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 83:

﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with "they are not arrogant" (lā yastakbirūn); that is, this is because they are not arrogant, and because their eyes overflow with tears upon hearing the Qur'an. This is an explanation of the tenderness of their hearts, the intensity of their fear, their hastening to accept the truth, and their not refusing it.

﴿You see their eyes overflowing with tears﴾; that is, they are filled with tears. Thus the word "overflowing" (fayḍ), which is the pouring out from fullness, is used metaphorically for it, for emphasis. Or, their eyes, because of the excess of weeping, are made as though they overflow by themselves.

﴿from what they have recognized of the truth﴾. The first "min" (from) indicates the starting point (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), and the second "min" explains the relative pronoun (li-tabyīn al-mawṣūl). That is: the overflowing began and arose from the knowledge of the truth, and came about because of it and by reason of it. It is also possible that the second "min" is partitive (tabʿīḍiyya), because what they recognized is only part of the truth. And since that moved them to weep, what would your opinion of them be if they recognized all of it, read the Qur'an, and comprehended the Sunnah? It was also read as "turā aʿyunuhum" (with the verb in the passive voice).

﴿They say﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf) built upon a question arising from the description of their state upon hearing the Qur'an, as if it were said: "What do they say?" So it was said: "They say."

﴿Our Lord, we have believed﴾ in this, or in the one to whom this was sent down, or in both. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "they recognized", or from the pronoun in the genitive in "their eyes", since the thing added is a part of it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will remove whatever is in their breasts of resentment, as brothers﴾.

﴿So write us among the witnesses﴾; that is, those who testified that it is the truth, or to his prophethood, or among his community (ummah), who are witnesses over the nations on the Day of Resurrection. They said this only because they found their mention in the Gospel as such.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 84:

﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we should not believe in Allah and in what has come to us of the truth?﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustani'af), uttered by them to affirm their faith and to establish it by denying the cause of its absence and negating it entirely, on the basis that the phrase ﴿we do not believe﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿for us﴾, with the governing element (al-'amil) being the sense of stability (al-istiqrar) contained in it; that is: what has happened to us, while we are not believers, given the direction of the denial.

The negation applies to both the cause and the effect together, as in His saying, ﴿And what is [the matter] with me that I should not worship He who originated me?﴾ and its like; not to the cause alone while the effect is established, as in His saying, ﴿So what is [the matter] with them that they do not believe?﴾ and its like. For the interrogative hamza, just as it is sometimes for denying the occurrence (inkar al-waqi') as in: "Do you strike your father?", it is other times for denying the occurrence itself (inkar al-wuqu') as in: "Shall I strike my father?"

Likewise, the interrogative ma (ma al-istifhamiyyah) may be for denying the cause of the occurrence and negating it alone, as in the second verse, and His saying, ﴿What is [the matter] with you that you do not hope for dignity from Allah?﴾ Thus the content of the circumstantial clause is established, since both the non-belief and the non-hope are a certain matter whose cause has been denied and negated. And the denial may be the cause of the occurrence and its negation, so that they also extend to the effect, as in the first verse, whereby the content of the circumstantial clause is definitely assumed, since the absence of worship is a matter that is absolutely required.

His saying, ﴿And we hope that our Lord will admit us along with the righteous people﴾ is another circumstantial clause from the mentioned pronoun, with an implied subject (mubtada'), and the governing element in it is the same governing element as in the first, restricted by it; that is: what has happened to us while we are not believers, and we hope for the companionship of the righteous. Or it is from the pronoun in "we do not believe", in the sense that they denied upon themselves their non-belief, while they hope for the companionship of the believers. It has also been said: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "we believe", in the sense of: what is [the matter] with us that we combine abandoning faith with the aforementioned hope?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 85:

﴿So Allah rewarded them for what they said﴾; that is, sincerely, from your saying: "This is the saying (qawl) of so-and-so," meaning his belief (mu'taqad). It is also read: (fa-ataahumu Allahu) ["so Allah gave them"].

﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the recompense of the good-doers﴾; that is, those who did well in their reflection and their deeds, or those who habitually do good in affairs. It is narrated that the four verses were revealed concerning al-Najashi and his companions. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him his letter, and he read it. Then he summoned Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and the Muhajirun with him, and he brought in the priests (qissisin) and the monks (ruhban). He ordered Ja'far to recite the Qur'an to them, so he recited Surah Maryam, and they wept and believed in the Qur'an. It is also said that they were revealed concerning thirty or seventy men from his people who came as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited Surah Maryam to them, and they wept and believed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 86:

﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ The denial of Allah's signs is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with disbelief (kufr) even though it is a kind of it, because the purpose is to describe the state of those who deny and to mention them in contrast with those who affirm them as true, combining encouragement (targhib) and warning (tarhib).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 87:

﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that God has made lawful for you﴾; that is, what is good and pleasant of them. It is as if, since the preceding verses contained praise of the Christians for monasticism, they encouraged the believers to subdue the self and reject desires, and so this was followed by a prohibition against excess in this matter. That is: do not withhold them from yourselves as prohibition would, or do not say, "We have made them unlawful for ourselves," out of exaggerated determination on your part to abandon them, in asceticism and self-denial.

It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) once described the Resurrection to his Companions, and he went to great lengths and elaborated greatly in warning. They were moved and gathered in the house of Uthman ibn Maz'un, and they agreed that they would not cease fasting and standing in prayer, that they would not sleep on beds, that they would not eat meat or fat, that they would not approach women or perfume, that they would renounce the world, wear hair shirts, wander about the earth, and castrate themselves. When this reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he said to them: "I was not commanded to do that. Your selves have a right over you. So fast and break your fast, stand in prayer and sleep, for I stand in prayer and I sleep, I fast and I break my fast, I eat meat and fat, and I approach women. Whoever turns away from my sunnah (the Prophet's normative practice) is not of me." Then the verse was revealed.

﴿And do not transgress﴾; that is, do not exceed the limits of what has been made lawful for you to what has been made unlawful for you. Or: do not be extravagant in partaking of the good things. Or: the forbidding of good things is made a transgression and an injustice, so He prohibited transgression in general, so that the prohibition against forbidding them would be included under it by way of priority, since it came right after it. Or it is intended: do not transgress in that matter.

﴿Indeed God does not love the transgressors﴾ is a reason for what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 88:

﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good﴾; that is: what is lawful for you and good, of what Allah has provided for you. So "ḥalālan" (lawful) is the object (maf'ūl) of "kulū" (eat), and "mimmā razaqakum" (of what He has provided for you) is either a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of it, placed before it because it is indefinite (nakira), or it is attached to "kulū" (eat). The "min" (mimmā) is either partitive-initial (ibtidā'iyya), or it is the object itself, and "ḥalālan" is a circumstantial qualifier of the relative pronoun (mawṣūl), or of its omitted resumptive pronoun ('ā'id), or it is an attributive qualifier of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar); that is: eating that is lawful. In all these readings, if the provision did not fall upon the forbidden, the mention of the lawful would have no additional benefit.

﴿And fear Allah, in whom you are believers﴾: an emphasis on the admonition to what He has commanded, for belief in Him, exalted is He, necessitates excessive piety and abstaining from what He has forbidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 89:

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths.﴾ Al-laghw (idle, or unintended, oath) in an oath is that which falls away and to which no ruling attaches. According to us, it is to swear to something one believes to be so, when it is not as one believes. This is the view of Mujahid. It has been said: they had sworn to forbid the good things, believing this to be an act of devotion. When the prohibition was revealed, they said: "What about our oaths?" Then this verse was revealed. According to al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him): it is what escapes a person without intent, such as his saying: "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah." This is also the view of 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her). The phrase ﴿in your oaths﴾ is related either to ﴿will hold you accountable﴾ or to al-laghw, since it is a verbal noun, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it.

﴿But He will hold you accountable for what you have solemnly confirmed by oaths﴾: that is, for your solemn confirmation of oaths and your binding them with intention and resolve. The meaning is: but He will hold you accountable for what you have confirmed by oath when you break it, or for breaking what you have solemnly confirmed. The object has been omitted because it is known. It has been read with the lighter form (ʿaqqadtum with tashdid removed), and it has been read ʿāqadtum, meaning ʿaqadtum.

﴿Then its expiation﴾: that is, then the expiation for breaking it, which is the act that is capable of atoning for the offence and covering it. Its apparent meaning has been used as evidence for the permissibility of making expiation before breaking the oath. According to us, this is not permissible, because of his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else to be better, let him do what is better and then make expiation for his oath."

﴿Feeding ten needy persons from the middle [standard] of what you feed your families﴾: that is, from the most moderate of it in kind or quantity. It is half a ṣāʿ of wheat for each needy person. Its grammatical position is accusative, because it is an attribute of an omitted object, the intended sense being: that you feed ten needy persons with food that is of the middle standard of what you feed your families. Or it is nominative, being a substitute (badal) for ʾiṭʿām (feeding).

Ahlūna is the plural of ahl (family), like arḍūna being the plural of arḍ (earth). It has been read ahālīkum, with the yāʾ made quiescent, according to the dialect of those who make it quiescent in all three cases, like the alif. This is also the plural of ahl, as al-arāḍī is the plural of arḍ and al-layālī is the plural of layl. It has been said that it is the plural of ahlāh.

﴿Or clothing them﴾: this is coordinated with ʾiṭʿām (feeding), or with the position of ﴿from the middle standard﴾, on the assumption that it is a substitute for feeding. Clothing is a garment that covers the private parts. It has been said: a comprehensive garment, a shirt, a cloak, or a wrap. It has been read with a ḍamma on the kāf (kuswa), which is a dialect form, like qidwa for qudwa and iswa for uswa. It has also been read ﴿or like their clothing﴾ (ka-usvatihim), with the kāf in the nominative position, the sense being: or their feeding is like their clothing, meaning: or like the manner in which you feed your families, with extravagance or stinginess, you share with them, and between them if you do not feed them the middle standard.

﴿Or freeing a slave﴾: that is, or freeing a human being of any kind. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) stipulated faith in this case, by analogy with the expiation for killing. The meaning of ﴿or﴾ is the obligation of one of the options without restriction, and the choice among them belongs to the responsible person.

﴿But whoever does not find﴾: that is, any of the matters mentioned above.

﴿Then fasting﴾: that is, then his expiation is fasting.

﴿Three days.﴾ Consecutiveness is a condition according to us, on the basis of the reading "three consecutive days." Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) does not regard irregular readings (shādh) as evidence.

﴿That﴾: that is, what has been mentioned.

﴿Is the expiation of your oaths when you swear﴾: that is, and break them.

﴿And guard your oaths﴾: by holding them dear and not casting them away carelessly, as His saying ﴿when you swear﴾ indicates. It has been said: by fulfilling them as far as you can, and by not forgoing good through them, or by expiating them when you break them. It has been said: guard them in whatever way you swear by them, and do not forget them out of disregard for them.

﴿Thus﴾ refers to the verbal noun of the verb that follows, not to another clarification understood from what preceded. The kāf is inserted to emphasise the grandeur that the demonstrative noun conveys. Its original position is accusative, as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun. The underlying sense is: Allah clarifies with a clarification like that clarification. Thus it was placed before the verb to convey restriction, and the kāf was treated as inserted for the reason mentioned. So it became the verbal noun itself, not an attribute of it. Its detailed explanation has passed in His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾; that is, that wonderful clarification.

﴿Allah makes clear to you His signs﴾: the markers of His law and His rulings, not a clarification lesser than that. The placing of ﴿to you﴾ before the object is for the reason that has passed many times.

﴿That perhaps you may be thankful﴾ for His blessing in what He teaches you and what He makes the way out easy for you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 90:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan.﴾ That is, al-anṣāb (stone alters): the idols set up for worship.

﴿And divining arrows﴾: its explanation has already passed at the beginning of the noble surah.

﴿Defilement﴾: filth from which the intellects recoil. It is singular because it is the predicate of al-khamr (intoxicants), and the predicate of the items conjoined to it is omitted, relying on what has been mentioned; or the genitive-modified noun is omitted, meaning: the matter of intoxicants and gambling... and so on.

﴿Defilement from the work of Satan﴾: it is in the position of nominative (raf') as an attribute of rijs (defilement); that is, it is originating from his work, because it is caused by his enticement and adornment.

﴿So avoid it﴾: that is, the defilement, or what has been mentioned.

﴿That you may be successful﴾: that is, hoping for your success. It has also been said: so that you may succeed by abstaining from it. Its verification has passed in the explanation of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿that you may be mindful [of Allah]﴾. The prohibition of intoxicants and gambling has been emphasized in this noble verse with various forms of emphasis: the sentence is introduced with innamā (indeed, only), they are paired with idols and divining arrows, and they are called "defilement from the work of Satan," as an alert that indulging in them is pure evil; and avoidance of their very substance is commanded, and that avoidance is made a means through which success is hoped for, so that committing them is loss and deprivation.

Then the explanation of the corrupting effects of the two, both worldly and religious, which necessitate their prohibition, was established. It is said: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through intoxicants and gambling﴾. This points to their worldly corruptions.

﴿And to prevent you from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer﴾ points to their religious corruptions. Singling out the two by repeating the mention and explaining the harm they contain serves to alert that the aim is to clarify their condition. Mentioning idols and divining arrows indicates that the two are like them in prohibition and evil, due to his saying ﷺ: "The drinker of wine is like the worshipper of an idol."

The singling out of the prayer by its separate mention, despite its inclusion in the remembrance, is for exaltation and to convey that one who turns people away from it is like one who turns people away from faith, since it is its pillar.

Then the exhortation to desist was repeated in the form of a question, arranged upon the preceding kinds of deterrents, so it is said: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ This signifies that the matter of warning, cautioning, and exposing the corruptions and evils they contain has reached its utmost limit, and that excuses have been entirely cut off.

Translation:

﴿And obey Allah, and obey the Messenger﴾: a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "avoid it" (ijtanibūhu); that is, obey both of them in everything they have commanded and forbidden.

﴿And beware﴾: that is, beware of opposing them in that. Opposing their command and prohibition regarding wine (khamr) and gambling (maysir) enters into this in the first instance.

﴿But if you turn away﴾: that is, you turn away from complying with what you were commanded regarding avoiding wine and gambling, and from obeying Allah the Exalted and obeying His Messenger (ﷺ), and from guarding against opposing the two of them.

﴿Then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾: he has done that to the utmost, has fully discharged the responsibility of the Message, and the proof has been established against you, the excuses have ended, and the pretexts have been cut off. Nothing remains after that except punishment, and in this there is a great degree of threat and severity of warning that is not hidden.

As for what has been said, that the meaning is: "Know that you do not harm [Allah or the Messenger] by your turning away, because he was only charged with the clear conveyance of the verses, and he has done it; rather, you harm yourselves when you turn away from what you were charged with," this does not fit the context, since it is not conceivable from them that they claim that by turning away they harm him (ﷺ), so that it would be answered by saying they do not harm him but only harm themselves.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 93:

﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾; i.e., sin and fault.

﴿for what they have eaten﴾; i.e., what they have consumed as food or drink, for its use for drink is also widespread. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever does not taste it, then he is of me﴾.

It is said: When God Almighty revealed the prohibition of wine after the Battle of the Confederates (Ghazwat al-Ahzab), some men among the Companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "So-and-so was killed on the Day of Badr, and so-and-so on the Day of Uhud, and they used to drink it, and we testify that they are in Paradise." In another narration: When the prohibition of wine and gambling (maysir) was revealed, the Companions, may God be pleased with them, said: "O Messenger of God, what of our brothers who died while they were drinking wine and consuming gambling (maysir)?" (p-77)

In another narration, Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of God, what of our brothers who died, having drunk wine and engaged in gambling (qimar)?" Then this was revealed.

The word "ma" in "ma taima'u" (what they have eaten) is not a reference to permissible things only; otherwise, the permission would have to be restricted by avoiding whatever else is forbidden, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿when they fear God﴾, and the necessary consequence is absolutely invalid. Rather, it is a general expression in its generality, whether it is a relative or a descriptive construction, and it has only been specified by that subsequent condition that applies to it. The meaning is: there is no blame upon them for what they have consumed of food and drink, whatever it may be, provided they avoid that there be in it any of the forbidden things; otherwise the removal of blame would not apply to everything they ate, but only to some of it, and there is no objection to this, since the necessary consequence of that would be restricting the permission of the whole, so that nothing in it is forbidden, and the permission of a part is not restricted by avoiding another part of it, as is the necessary consequence of the first.

﴿and believe and do righteous deeds﴾; i.e., and they persist in faith and righteous deeds.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿then fear God﴾ is a conjunction (ataf) upon "ittaqaw" (they feared God), included with it within the scope of the condition; i.e., they fear God regarding what becomes forbidden to them after that, although it had been permissible before.

﴿and believe﴾; i.e., in its prohibition and in placing taqwa (fear of God) before it; either for the sake of giving it attention, or because it is what indicates the newly introduced prohibition, which is what is believed in, or they persist in faith.

﴿then fear God﴾; i.e., regarding what becomes forbidden to them after that, of what had been permissible before, on the basis that what is conditioned upon taqwa each time is the permissibility of everything they ate at that time, not the permissibility of everything they ate before it, because the permissibility of some of it had been abrogated at that time.

﴿and do good﴾; i.e., they performed the good, beautiful deeds encompassing all of the deeds mentioned, both of the heart and of the outward body. The mention of these instances is not for the purpose of restricting the ruling to them, but to show multiplicity and repetition, however far it may reach. The meaning is: when they avoid the forbidden things and persist in the faith and righteous deeds they have, and are in obedience to God, observing His commands and prohibitions, such that whenever something from the permissible is forbidden to them they avoid it, again and again, then there is no blame upon them for what they have eaten of foods and drinks each time, since there is nothing forbidden in them at the time of eating.

You should know that apart from avoiding the forbidden things, the other beautiful attributes mentioned have no bearing on the removal of blame. They are mentioned in a context that is a testimony to the attributes of those about whom the question was asked, and a praise of them for that, and a commendation of their conditions. This has been indicated, since those attributes were made to follow taqwa each time, to distinguish them from what has a bearing on the ruling. The manner of the noble composition, by way of expression, though it is for describing the state of those characterized by what was mentioned of qualities in what follows, by virtue of the phrase "idha ma", nonetheless it has been brought out in the form of an answer about the state of those who passed away, to establish the ruling regarding them within the framework of general legislation in the demonstrative manner, by way of the indication of the text, based on their complete fame for being characterized by these. It is as if it were said: There is no blame upon them for what they have eaten, if they are in obedience to Him, exalted is He, together with the praiseworthy attributes they possess, such that whenever they are commanded with something they receive it with compliance. They only used to indulge in wine and gambling during their lives because these had not been prohibited at that time; had they been prohibited in their era, they would have avoided them entirely.

This, and it has been said: the repetition is with regard to three times, or with regard to three states: a person's use of taqwa between himself and himself, between himself and people, and between himself and God, the Mighty and Majestic; and for this reason "ihsan" (doing good) was brought in the third instance in place of "iman" (faith), as an indication of what he, peace be upon him, said in its explanation. Or it is with regard to three levels: the beginning, the middle, and the end. Or it is with regard to what is to be guarded against: one should abandon the forbidden things out of fear of punishment, the doubtful things out of fear of falling into the unlawful, and some of the permissible things in order to preserve the soul from baseness and to refine it from the defilement of nature.

It has also been said: the repetition is merely for emphasis, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Nay, you will come to know﴾ ﴿Then nay, you will come to know﴾ and its like. It has been said: what is meant by the first is avoiding disbelief (kufr), by the second avoiding the major sins (kaba'ir), and by the third avoiding the minor sins (saghair). There is no doubt that these considerations have no connection to the present context, so reflect well.

﴿And God loves the good-doers﴾: a concluding statement that confirms the content of what precedes it in the most eloquent confirmation.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 5, verse 94:**

﴿O you who believe, Allah will surely test you﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath. That is: "By Allah, He will certainly deal with you in the manner of one who tests you, in order to learn your circumstances."

﴿with something from the game﴾: that is, from the game of the land, whether edible or not, excluding the exempted harmful creatures (al-mustathnayat min al-fawasiq). The definite article in al-sayd is the lam of al-'ahd (the definite article referring to something already known). It was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyya. Allah tested them with game while they were in ihram (the state of ritual consecration for pilgrimage). The wild animals would come upon them in their encampments, so that they were able to catch them by hand and to spear them with their lances.

That is His saying: ﴿Your hands and your lances can reach it﴾. So they resolved to take them, and this verse was revealed. It is narrated that a wild ass appeared to them, and Abu al-Yasar ibn 'Amr charged at it, stabbed it with his lance, and killed it. He was told: "You killed it while you are in ihram!" So he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked him about that, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed the verse.

The oath-emphasis in ﴿He will surely test you﴾ serves only to affirm that what occurred, namely the game not fleeing from them, is nothing but a test for them. It does not serve to affirm the occurrence of the thing by which they are tested, as would have been the case had the revelation come before the test. The indefinite noun shay' ("thing") is used for belittlement, indicating that this is not among the great trials in which the feet of the firm slip, such as being tested by the killing of souls and the destruction of property. Rather, it is of the kind by which the people of Ayla were tested with the game of the sea. Its benefit is to alert that whoever is not steadfast in such a matter, how will he be steadfast in the severe ordeals?

The min in ﴿from the game﴾ is definitively explicative (bayaniyya, indicating what the thing is); that is, "with a thing that is base, namely game." To take it as partitive (tab'idiyya, indicating a part of a whole) would require considering its paucity and baseness relative to all game, not relative to the great calamities, and the statement would then be stripped of the alert mentioned above.

﴿That Allah may know who fears Him in the unseen﴾: that is, that the one who fears His punishment in the Hereafter, while He is unseen and awaited, may be distinguished, owing to the strength of his faith, so that he does not approach the game. And [that He may distinguish] the one who does not fear Him, owing to the weakness of his faith, so that he proceeds to it. This was expressed in terms of Allah's knowledge, which is a necessary consequence of it, as an indication that reward and punishment revolve around it, for this is more effective in compelling them to fear.

It is said: the meaning is that His knowledge should attach to the one who fears Him in fact. His knowledge that he will fear Him, though it attaches to him before his fear, its attachment to him as one who actually fears, on which the matter of reward turns, occurs only upon the actual realization of fear.

It is said: there is an omitted mudaf (a noun governed in a possessive construction that is dropped), and the estimate is: "that the friends of Allah may know." It was also read as لِيُعْلِمَ (liyu'lima, with a damma on the yā' and the form of the causative), from the causative of knowing (al-i'lam), with the first object omitted; that is, "that Allah may inform His servants..." etc. Knowledge, in both readings, is transitive to one object. The mention of the noble Name in place of the pronoun is to cultivate awe and to instill a sense of dread.

﴿So whoever transgresses after that﴾: that is, after the explanation that what occurred was a trial from Him, exalted is He, for the wisdom mentioned. It is not "after the prohibition" as some have said, since prohibition and forbidding is not a newly occurring matter upon which a conditional introduced by fa' (then) would be consequent. Nor is it "after the trial" as others have chosen, since the trial itself is not fit to be the basis for intensifying the punishment; rather, it might be imagined to be an excuse justifying its lightening. What necessitates intensification is the explanation that it is a trial, because transgression after that is blatant obstinacy, indifference to Allah's providence, departure from His obedience, and complete severance from His fear and dread. That is: whoever approaches the game after we have explained that the abundance of the game and its not fleeing from them is a trial leading to the distinction of the obedient from the disobedient.

﴿then for him is a painful punishment﴾: for what was mentioned, that it is pure obstinacy; and because whoever does not control his own soul and does not observe Allah's command in such trivial trials will hardly observe it in great matters of slipping. What is meant by "painful punishment" is the punishment of both abodes. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "His back and belly will be widened by flogging, and his garments will be stripped off."

﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ O you who have believed. This begins the explanation of the rulings by which the transgression is to be made good, following the explanation of the punishment that befalls it.

The explicit prohibition in His saying, ﴿لا تَقْتُلُوا الصَّيْدَ وأنْتُمْ حُرُمٌ﴾ (Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram), although it is already known, especially from His saying, ﴿غَيْرَ مُحِلِّي الصَّيْدِ وأنْتُمْ حُرُمٌ﴾ (not violating the sanctity of game while you are in the state of ihram), is for the emphasis of the sanctity and for establishing what follows from it. The alif-lam in ﴿الصَّيْدَ﴾ is for the specific reference (al-'ahd), as has preceded. Ḥurum is the plural of ḥarām, meaning one in ihram even if he is in the non-sacred area (al-ḥill), and one in the sacred area (al-ḥaram) is in its ruling even if he is not in ihram, like ruduḥ, the plural of radāḥ. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "do not kill," meaning: do not kill it while you are in ihram.

﴿وَمَن قَتَلَهُ﴾ And whoever kills it, meaning the known game. The mention of killing in both places, rather than slaughtering, is to signal that it is in the ruling of carrion.

﴿مِنكُمْ﴾ (from among you) is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "killed," meaning: being one of you.

﴿مُتَعَمِّدًا﴾ (intentionally) is also a circumstantial clause from him, meaning: remembering his ihram and knowing the sanctity of killing what he kills. The restriction to intentional action, although the prohibitions of ihram are equal in intentional and unintentional cases, is because the verse was revealed concerning the intentional killer, as has passed in the story of Abu al-Yasar, and because the primary case is the intentional act, while the unintentional one is attached to it for severity.

It is related from al-Zuhri (may Allah have mercy on him): The Book was revealed concerning the intentional act, and the Sunnah (the prophetic practice) came concerning the unintentional act. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr (may Allah be pleased with him): I see nothing in the case of an unintentional killing, taking as proof the condition of intention stated in the verse. This is the view of Dawud (al-Zahiri). It is related from Mujahid and al-Hasan that the intended meaning of intention is: intentionally killing while forgetting that one is in ihram. As for one who kills it intentionally while remembering that he is in ihram, there is no ruling upon him, and his affair is with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because that is too great a matter to have an expiation.

﴿فَجَزاءٌ مِثْلُ ما قَتَلَ﴾ then a recompense equal to what he killed, with both read in the nominative. That is: upon him is a recompense equivalent to what he killed. It is read with the first in the nominative and the second in the accusative, by making the verbal noun operative. It is read with the second in the genitive, by its being annexed to its object. It is read: ﴿فَجَزاؤُهُ مِثْلُ ما قَتَلَ﴾ (then its recompense is equal to what he killed), as an inchoative and predicate. It is read with both in the accusative, on the assumption: then let him give a recompense, or: upon him is that he should give a recompense equal to what he killed.

What is meant by it, according to Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf (may Allah be pleased with them both), is equivalence in value: it is valued on the day of the hunting at the place where it was hunted, or at the nearest places to it. If its value reaches the value of a sacrificial animal (hady), the offender is given the choice between buying with it what is worth the value of the game and sacrificing it to the Sacred House (al-Ḥaram), or buying with it food and giving to each poor person half a ṣā' of wheat or a ṣā' of other grain, or fasting for each poor person's food a day. If what remains does not reach the food of one poor person, he gives it in charity, or fasts a full day for it, since fasting less than a day is not known in the Sharia.

Thus His saying ﴿مِنَ النَّعَمِ﴾ (from the livestock) is an explanation of the sacrificial animal bought with value, according to one of the forms of choice, since whoever does this is truly said to have recompensed with an equivalent of what he killed from the livestock.

According to Malik and al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on them both) and those who hold their view, it is equivalence in form and appearance, because Allah, Exalted, required an equivalent of the killed animal restricted to livestock. Therefore whoever considers equivalence by value has opposed the text.

It is related from the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) that they required for an ostrich a camel (badana), for a gazelle a sheep, for a wild ass a cow, and for a hare a female kid (ʿanāq). It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The hyena is game, and in it is a sheep if the one in ihram kills it." Our argument is that the text required equivalence, and equivalence, whether absolutely in the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus of the community (ijma', the scholarly agreement) and reason, is meant either as equivalence in form and meaning, or as equivalence in form without meaning. The latter has no consideration at all in the Sharia. When the first is impossible by consensus, the second is determined, because it is known in the Sharia, as in the rights of people. Do you not see that equivalence among individuals of one species, though it is in the utmost strength and clarity, has not been considered by the Sharia, and it did not make the animal, when destroyed, guaranteed by another individual of its species equivalent to it in most attributes, but guaranteed by its value? Yet what is stated concerning its like is only equivalence. He, Exalted, said: ﴿فاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ بِمِثْلِ ما اعْتَدى عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (so retaliate against him in the same manner as he has transgressed against you). Since that powerful equivalence was not considered, though it is easy to know and to observe, then, lest equivalence be considered between individuals of different kinds, which is weak and hidden, with the difficulty of its source and the hardship of preserving it, is all the more fitting and proper. Also, value has been intended in what has no counterpart by consensus, so nothing else remains intended, since the shared term has no generality in affirmative contexts.

What is meant by the transmitted report is the requirement of a counterpart by value, not by the thing itself. Then the original obligation for the offence and the equivalent recompense for the killed is actually its value, but not in the sense that the offender intends it and spends it on its objects directly. Rather it is in the sense that he makes it a standard by which he determines one of the three options and so puts it in its place. So His saying ﴿مِثْلُ ما قَتَلَ﴾ (equal to what he killed) is a necessary attribute of the recompense, never separated from it in any state. As for His saying ﴿مِنَ النَّعَمِ﴾ (from the livestock), it is an attribute of it considered in the second state, based on its first attribute, which is the standard for it and for what follows of food and fasting. So its rightful place is to be conjoined with the separable attribute, not with the necessary attribute, let alone with the thing described, as will come, God willing.

Among what guides you to the fact that equivalence means value is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿يَحْكُمُ بِهِ﴾ (by which two just persons judge), meaning: by the equivalent of what he killed.

﴿ذَوا عَدْلٍ مِنكُمْ﴾ (two persons of justice from among you), meaning: two just judges from among the Muslims. But this is not because valuation requires reflection and effort from the just, unlike visible things which every person knows equally. That would arise from heedlessness of what they intended by the equivalence. Rather, what they made the basis of equivalence between game and livestock is a kind of resemblance and analogy in some attributes and forms, while the difference between them in the rest of the states is certain. This is not reached by the pillars of the leading imams of ijtihad (independent reasoning) and the chieftains of guidance and right direction, except those supported with holy power. Do you not see that Imam al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) required a sheep for killing a dove, on the basis of what he established as equivalence between them, namely that each of them coos and cries out, though the relation between them in all other respects is like that between a lizard (ḍabb) and a fish-eater? How then could knowledge of such subtle and difficult details be entrusted to the opinion of two just persons from ordinary people? Moreover, this ruling in this sense concerns kinds, not individuals. After one kind of game is matched with one kind of livestock the ruling is complete, and when the particulars of events occur there remains no need for a judgment at all.

It is also read: ﴿يَحْكُمُ بِهِ ذُو عَدْلٍ﴾ (by which one just person judges), meaning the class of the just rather than the singular. It is also said: rather, it is meant as the imam (ruler). The clause is a qualifier of ﴿جَزاءٌ﴾ (recompense), or a circumstantial clause from it, because it is specified by the qualifier.

His saying ﴿هَدْيًا﴾ (as an offering) is a qualified circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "by it," or from ﴿جَزاءٌ﴾ for the reason mentioned, that it is specified by the qualifier. Or it is a substitute for ﴿مِثْلُ﴾ (equal) for the one who read it in the accusative, or from its place for the one who read it in the genitive, or an accusative of the verbal noun, meaning: he offers it as an offering. The clause is another qualifier of ﴿جَزاءٌ﴾.

﴿بالِغَ الكَعْبَةِ﴾ (reaching the Ka'bah) is a qualifier of ﴿هَدْيًا﴾, because the annexation is not genuine.

﴿أوْ كَفّارَةٌ﴾ (or an expiation) is conjoined to the position of ﴿مِنَ النَّعَمِ﴾, as a predicate of an omitted subject. The clause is a second qualifier of ﴿جَزاءٌ﴾, as has been indicated.

His saying ﴿طَعامُ مَساكِينَ﴾ (the feeding of needy persons) is an explanatory apposition to ﴿كَفّارَةٌ﴾ according to one who does not restrict it to the definite, or a substitute from it, or a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is the feeding of needy persons.

His saying ﴿أوْ عَدْلُ ذَلِكَ صِيامًا﴾ (or the equivalent of that in fasting) is conjoined to ﴿طَعامُ﴾, and so on. It is as if it were said: upon him is a recompense equal to the one he killed, which is of the livestock, or the feeding of needy persons, or fasting days equal to their number. In that case equivalence is a necessary attribute of the recompense, by which the sacrificial animal, the food and the fasting are measured. The first two are without intermediary, while the third is through the second. So the offender chooses each of them in place of the other two.

Having said this, it has been said: His saying ﴿أوْ كَفّارَةٌ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿جَزاءٌ﴾, so then there remains in the noble arrangement nothing by which the food and the fasting are measured, and resorting to analogy with the sacrificial animal is an artificial stretch that is not hidden. This is on the reading ﴿جَزاءٌ﴾ in the nominative and on all the other readings.

So His saying ﴿أوْ كَفّارَةٌ﴾ is a predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is conjoined to the clause "it is of the livestock." It is also read: ﴿أوْ كَفّارَةُ طَعامُ مَساكِينَ﴾ with annexation, to specify the kind of expiation.

It is also read: ﴿طَعامُ مِسْكِينٍ﴾ (the feeding of a needy person), on the basis that the specification is achieved by the singular which indicates the class. It is also read: ﴿أوْ عِدْلُ﴾ with a kasra on the ʿayn. The difference between them is that ʿadl (with fatha) of a thing is what equals it of a different kind, such as fasting and feeding, while ʿidl (with kasra) is what it is equated with in quantity. It is as if the fatha is a naming by the verbal noun, and the kasra is in the sense of the passive participle. That refers to the food. ﴿صِيامًا﴾ (in fasting) is a specification for ʿadl. The choice in this matter belongs to the offender according to Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf (may Allah have mercy on them both), and to the two judges according to Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him).

﴿لِيَذُوقَ وبالَ أمْرِهِ﴾ (that he may taste the consequence of his affair) is connected to what is settled in the prepositional phrase, meaning: upon him is a recompense in order that he may taste... and so on. It is also said: it is connected to a verb indicated by the speech, as if it were said: this was prescribed for him so that he might taste the consequence of his affair, meaning the evil result of violating the sanctity of ihram. The word wabal originally means what is disliked, and the harm that is reached in the outcome from a bad deed because of its heaviness. From it is His saying: ﴿فَأخَذْناهُ أخْذًا وبِيلا﴾ (so We seized him with a heavy seizing). And from it is: "a wabil food," which is food the stomach does not digest.

﴿عَفا اللَّهُ عَمّا سَلَفَ﴾ (Allah has pardoned what has passed) refers to whoever killed game while in ihram before they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is also said: "what has passed" refers to what he did in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah), because they were bound by the laws of those before them, and game was forbidden in them.

﴿وَمَن عادَ﴾ (and whoever returns) means returning to killing game after the prohibition against it while in ihram.

﴿فَيَنْتَقِمُ اللَّهُ مِنهُ﴾ (then Allah will take retribution from him) is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: so he is one from whom Allah takes retribution. That is why the fa' entered, as in His saying: ﴿فَمَن يُؤْمِن بِرَبِّهِ فَلا يَخافُ بَخْسًا ولا رَهَقًا﴾ (so whoever believes in his Lord does not fear any loss or burden), meaning: so that one does not fear... and so on. And His saying: ﴿وَمَن كَفَرَ فَأُمَتِّعُهُ﴾ (and whoever disbelieves, I will let him enjoy briefly), meaning: so I will let him enjoy briefly. The intended meaning of retribution is punishment in the Hereafter. As for expiation, it is related from ʿAta', Ibrahim, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan that it is obligatory upon the one who returns. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and Shurayh that there is no expiation upon him, holding to the apparent wording.

﴿واللَّهُ عَزِيزٌ﴾ (And Allah is Mighty) meaning: Victorious, who is not overcome.

﴿ذُو انْتِقامٍ﴾ (Owner of retribution) meaning: severe, so He takes retribution from whoever persists in disobedience and transgression.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 96:

﴿Lawful for you﴾: the address is to those in the state of ihram (ihram: the sacred state of pilgrimage).

﴿The game of the sea﴾: that is, what is hunted in all waters, whether sea, river, or pond, namely that which cannot live except in water, whether edible or inedible.

﴿And its food﴾: that is, what is fed from its game. This is a specification after a generalization. The meaning is: lawful for you is the pursuit of everything that is hunted in the waters and the benefiting from it, and the eating of what is eaten from it, which is fish according to us. According to Ibn Abi Layla, it is everything that is hunted in it. On his reading, the meaning of the verse is: lawful for you is the hunting of the animals of the sea and feeding them (to others). It was also read as (p-82) (wa-ta'mahu). It is said: "the game of the sea" is what is caught in it, and "its food" is what it casts up or what recedes from it (leaves behind when the water ebbs).

﴿A provision for you﴾: it is in the accusative as an object of purpose, specific to the food, just as "a gift" (nafilah) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as a gift﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier specific to Jacob, peace be upon him. That is: lawful for you is its food, as an enjoyment for those of you who are residents, who eat it fresh.

﴿And for the traveller﴾ among you, who take it as provision dried. It is also said: it is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun of an implied verb, meaning: He has granted you enjoyment of it as an enjoyment. It is also said: it emphasizes the meaning of "lawful for you", for it is in the sense of "He has granted you enjoyment of it", like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Book of God, which is prescribed for you﴾.

﴿But forbidden to you is the game of the land﴾. It was also read with the verb in the active voice and with "the game of the land" in the accusative. It refers to what is bred on land, even if it lives in water at some times, such as the water bird.

﴿As long as you are in the state of ihram﴾: that is, in the state of ihram. It was also read with the vowel of the dal broken (dumtum), from the verb daama yadaamu.
