Its apparent meaning requires the prohibition, for the one in ihram, of what a non-pilgrim has hunted, even if he had no part in it. This is the view of Umar and Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them. Related from Abu Hurayrah, Ata', Mujahid, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may God be pleased with them: it is lawful for him to eat what a non-pilgrim has hunted, even if it was hunted for his sake, provided he did not point to it or guide to it. Likewise, what was slaughtered before he entered ihram. This is the position of Abu Hanifah, since the address is to those in ihram; it is as if it were said: "forbidden to you is what you hunt on land," so the game of others is excluded from it. According to Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad: what is hunted for him is not permitted.

﴿And fear God﴾ in what He has forbidden you, or in all acts of disobedience, of which this is one.

﴿To whom you will be gathered﴾: not to anyone else, so that one might imagine escape from His seizing by seeking refuge in other than Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 97:

﴿Allah made the Ka'bah﴾ Mujahid said: it was called Ka'bah because it is cubical (muka''abah) and square (murabba'ah). It was also said: because it stands apart (infiradiha) from other buildings. And it was said: because of its height above the ground and its protrusion (nutu'ihā).

His words, exalted is He: ﴿the Sacred House﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) by way of praise (madh) rather than clarification (tawdih), just as an adjective comes in that manner. It was also said that it is a second object (maf'ul thani) of ja'ala (made).

His words, exalted is He: ﴿a means of support for the people﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). This is refuted by the conjunction of what follows it to the first object, as will come, rather this is the second object. It was also said that ja'l (making) here means initiation and creation (inshaʾ wa-khalq), and then it is a circumstantial state as has passed. The meaning of it being a support for them is that it is the pivot (madar) upon which the affairs of their religion and their worldly life are sustained; for it is a cause of their revival in the matters of their livelihood and their hereafter. The one who fears seeks refuge in it, the weak find safety in it, the merchants profit in it, and the pilgrims and visitors (ʿumar) turn toward it. It was also read as qiyaman (qiyam), being a verbal noun (masdar) on the pattern of shibaʿ, whose middle radical was altered by the same alteration as in its verb.

﴿and the Sacred Month﴾; that is, the one in which the Hajj is performed, which is Dhu al-Hijjah. It was also said: the category of the Sacred Months, and it and what follows it are conjoined to the Ka'bah, so the second object is omitted, relying on what has passed; that is: and the Sacred Month was made [a means of support].

﴿and the offering animals and the garlanded ones﴾ likewise [are] a means of support for them. By "the garlanded ones" is meant those bearing garlands, namely the camels (al-budn), which are singled out for mention because the reward in them is greater and the splendor of the Hajj is more manifest through them.

﴿That﴾ is a reference either to the aforementioned making alone, or together with what was mentioned of the command to observe the sanctity of the state of ihram and other matters. Its place is the accusative by a verb understood from the context, which is the governing agent of the lam after it; that is: that was legislated.

﴿so that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾ For the legislating of these laws, which entail the averting of religious and worldly harms before they occur and the bringing of primary and ultimate benefits, is among the clearest proofs of the Lawgiver's wisdom and of the fact that nothing lies outside His all-encompassing knowledge.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿and that Allah is Knowing of everything﴾ is a generalization after a specification, for emphasis. It is also permissible that by "what is in the heavens and the earth" is meant the existent entities within them, and by "everything" the matters related to those existents, such as accidents and states, which belong to the category of meanings (ma'ani).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 98:**

﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ is a warning for whoever violates His sanctities, or persists in that.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ is a promise for whoever guards the observance of His sacred prohibitions, or desists from violating them after having engaged in them. The reason for placing the warning first is evident.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 99:

﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey (the message).﴾ This is an emphatic statement of the obligation to carry out what he was commanded to do; that is: the Messenger has indeed done what was incumbent upon him of conveying (the message) completely, leaving nothing more to be added, the proof has been established against you, obedience has become binding upon you, and so you have no excuse thereafter for neglect.

﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾, so He will call you to account for that, (even) for a speck (naqir) or a trifle (qitmir).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 100:

﴿Say: The wicked and the good are not equal.﴾ This is a general ruling affirming that, in the sight of God Most High, there is no equality between the inferior among persons, deeds and wealth and the excellent among them. It is intended to encourage the excellent of each of these and to warn against their inferior, even though the occasion of revelation was Shurayh ibn Dubay'a al-Bakri, whose story has passed in the explanation of God's words: ﴿O you who believe, do not make lawful the rites of God﴾ ... etc.

It is also said: it was revealed concerning "a man who asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'Wine was my trade, and I have acquired wealth from selling it. Will that wealth benefit me if I spend it in obedience to God Most High?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'If you spend it on pilgrimage, or on holy war, or on charity, it will not equal the wing of a gnat. Indeed God accepts only the good.'" 'Ata' and al-Hasan (may God be pleased with them both) said: "the wicked and the good" means the forbidden and the lawful.

The mention of "the wicked" first serves to indicate from the outset that the deficiency which the non-equality reveals lies in it, and not in its opposite. The concept of non-equality between two things that differ in excess and deficiency, although it may be considered in terms of the excess of the greater, is more evidently considered in terms of the deficiency of the lesser, as in God's words: ﴿Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ and so on. As for God's words: ﴿Are those who know and those who do not know equal?﴾, the preceding of the superior there is perhaps because its attribute is a disposition whose counterpart is the attribute of the inferior.

﴿And even if the abundance of the wicked pleases you﴾; that is, even if its abundance delights you. The address is to each one of those whom the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to address, and the "waw" links the conditional clause to a similar one that is implied. It is also said that the "waw" is for the circumstantial (hal), and this has passed; that is: whether or not the abundance of the wicked pleases you, and whether or not it pleases you. Both clauses are in the position of a circumstance relative to the subject of "is not equal"; that is, they are not equal, existing under every supposed condition, as in your saying: "Be good to so-and-so even if he wrongs you"; that is: be good to him if he does not wrong you, and even if he wrongs you; that is, existing under every supposed condition. The first has been omitted by a regular elision, since the second indicates it clearly, for when a thing is realized in the presence of an opposing factor, it is all the more realized without it. On this secret turns the emphasis and stress of the concessive "law" and "in" (even if), and the answer of "law" is omitted in both clauses because what precedes them indicates it. The full verification of this will come in many places, God willing, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿So fear God, O people of understanding﴾; that is: in seeking out the wicked even if it is abundant, and prefer over it the good even if it is scant, for the criterion of consideration is quality and inferiority, not abundance and scarcity. Thus the praiseworthy few is better than the blameworthy many, and indeed, the more the wicked multiplies, the more wicked it becomes.

﴿That you may prosper﴾, hoping that you will attain success.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 101:

﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things﴾ *ashya'* is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) according to the view of al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and the majority of the Basrans, like *tarfa'* and *qasba'*. Its original form was *shi'a'*, with two hamzas separated by an alif. The word then underwent metathesis, with its final radical (*lam*) moved before its first radical (*fa'*), so its pattern became *lf'a'*. It is not declined (*manu'a al-sarf*) because of the extended feminine alif (*alif al-ta'nith al-mamdudah*).

It is also said that it is the plural of *shay'*, as a lightened form of *shayyi'*, just as *hayn* is a lightened form of *hayyin*. The original form would then be *ashy'i'a'*, on the pattern *af'ila'*, like *ahwina'*. Two hamzas came together: the radical of the word and the hamza of the feminine alif, since the alif is like a hamza. The word was lightened by changing the first hamza into a *ya'* because the letter before it was kasra. It became *ashyiya'*, and two *ya's* came together, the first of which was the radical of the word, so it was deleted for lightness, becoming *ashya'*. Its pattern is *af'ila'*, and it is not declined because of the feminine alif.

It is also said that what was deleted from *ashiya'* was the *ya'* that resulted from changing the hamza which was the *lam* of the word. The kasra on the remaining *ya'* was changed to a fatha so that the alif of the plural would be preserved. Its pattern is then *af'a'*.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If it is shown to you, it will distress you﴾, is an attributive clause (*sifah*) modifying *ashya'*, which calls for refraining from asking about them. Since the distress in this conditional clause is connected to their being disclosed and not to asking about them, another conditional clause follows it, which states that asking about them necessarily entails their disclosure, which definitely leads to what is to be avoided.

It is said: ﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, it will be shown to you﴾; that is, those things that cause distress will be disclosed through revelation, as the restriction of the question to the time of revelation indicates. What is meant by them is what is burdensome and distressing to them from difficult obligations that they cannot bear, and hidden secrets by which they would be disgraced when they are revealed, and similar things that contain no good. Just as asking about events that have occurred entails their disclosure, asking about those obligations entails imposing them upon them as a punishment, because they have violated proper conduct, dared to question and to dispute, and exceeded what befits them of submission to the command of Allah, mighty and majestic, without investigating it or examining its nature and quantity. That is: do not ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) excessively about what does not concern you, such as burdensome obligations. If he gives you a ruling on them and imposes them on you, as he was revealed to do, you will not be able to bear them, such as some hidden matters whose disclosure you would dislike.

This is like what was reported from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us, praised Allah the Most High and extolled Him, and then said: 'Indeed Allah the Most High has prescribed for you the Hajj.' A man from the Banu Asad, called 'Ukkasha ibn Mihsan (it is also said that he was Suraqa ibn Malik), stood up and said: 'Every year, O Messenger of Allah?' He turned away from him until he repeated his question three times. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Woe to you! What makes you sure that I would not say yes? By Allah, if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and if it had become obligatory, you would not have been able to do it. If you had left it, you would have disbelieved. So leave me as I have left you, for those before you were destroyed by their excessive questioning and their disputing with their prophets. When I command you with something, take from it what you are able to do, and when I forbid you from something, avoid it.'"

Similar to this is what was reported from Anas and Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the people asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about things until they pressed him with questions. The Messenger (ﷺ) stood up angrily to deliver a sermon, (p-85) praised Allah the Most High and extolled Him, and said: "Ask me. By Allah, you will not ask me about anything as long as I am standing in this place except that I will explain it to you." The Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) feared that something was about to happen. Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I began to look to the right and to the left, and I found no man except that he had covered his head with his garment, weeping. A man from Quraysh, from the Banu Sahm, called 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafa, stood up. He was someone who, when he quarrelled with men, was called by someone other than his father, and he said: 'O Prophet of Allah, who is my father?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Your father is Hudhafa ibn Qays al-Zuhri.' Another man stood up and said: 'Where is my father?' He (ﷺ) said: 'In the Fire.' Then 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) stood up and said: 'We are pleased with Allah the Most High as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Messenger and Prophet. We seek refuge with Allah the Most High from trials. Indeed we are people recently come from the age of ignorance and polytheism, so pardon us, O Messenger of Allah.' Then the anger of the Prophet (ﷺ) subsided."

﴿Allah has pardoned it﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) brought to clarify that their prohibition from it was not merely for protecting them from distress, but because it is itself a disobedience that entails accountability, and Allah has pardoned it. In this is an urging to them to earnestly refrain from it, which is clear.

The pronoun in ﴿'anha﴾ ("about it") refers to the question implied by "do not ask." That is: Allah the Most High has pardoned your past questions, in that He did not impose the Hajj on you every year as a retribution for your question, and He overlooked your punishment in the Hereafter for all your questions. So do not return to their like.

As for taking it as another attributive clause for *ashya'*, with the pronoun *ha* meaning: "Do not ask about things that Allah has pardoned and did not impose upon you," this is absolutely impossible, because it implies that the Hajj was first obligatory every year and then abrogated by way of pardon, and that this was known to the addressees. The necessary condition of a description is that it must be known to the addressee to be true of the described thing before it is made a description of it, and both of these are definitely impossible. Moreover, it would require restricting the prohibition to the question of the Hajj and similar matters, if we assume that such questions occurred. Yet the noble wording is explicit that it is directed at the prohibition of asking about things whose disclosure would distress them, whether they are of the kind of rulings and obligations that cause them distress by their establishment and imposition as a result of the question, as a punishment and a tightening, like the question about the Hajj were it not for Allah's pardon of it, or of the kind of matters that occurred before the question and whose disclosure causes distress through being reported, like the question of the one who said: "Where is my father?"

If you say: those things do not necessarily cause distress at all, but may also cause joy. For if their being disclosed is because of their existence, then from the perspective of their non-existence they certainly cause the other (joy). Neither of the two aspects is established for the questioner, and his purpose in asking is only to make them manifest however they are, or indeed to make them manifest in the aspect of causing joy. Therefore they are not described in terms of causing distress.

We say: this is to establish the thing forbidden, as you will know, along with what it contains of emphasizing and intensifying the prohibition. For that aspect is what necessitates stopping and restraint, not the aspect of their causing joy, nor the aspect of their being uncertain between the two causes.

If it is said: the second conditional clause explicitly states that asking about those things that cause distress necessarily entails their disclosure, as has passed. Then why did the disclosure fail to follow the question in the matter of the Hajj, since it was not imposed every year? We say: because the question occurred before the prohibition was revealed, and what is mentioned in the conditional clause is only the question that occurs after its revelation, since that is what necessitates severity and intensification, and there is no failure in it.

If it is said: what you have mentioned only applies when the question concerns matters that are uncertain between occurring and not occurring, as with the burdensome obligations mentioned. But if it concerns matters that occurred before it, it can hardly hold, because what the disclosure concerns is what has occurred in reality, and it cannot be averted, whether the question was before or after the prohibition. Sometimes what has occurred is something that causes joy, as in the matter of 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafa, so it is what the disclosure concerns and not anything else, and thus failure is necessarily determined.

We say: there is no possibility of failure, let alone its being determined. For what is forbidden in reality is only asking about things that cause distress and that have occurred in reality before the question, like the question of the one who said: "Where is my father?" It is not asking about what encompasses them and other things that have not occurred but that might occur for the responsible persons, so that failure would have to occur in the case where they do not occur.

The sum of the matter is that the meaning of the noble wording, by way of its explicit expression, is only the prohibition of asking about things whose disclosure definitely causes distress. Either these things are of the kind that might occur, so that they are disclosed when asked about by way of establishment, as a punishment and intensification, as is the case when they are of the kind of burdensome obligations. Or they are things that have occurred in reality before the question, so that they are disclosed at the time of the question by way of reporting them. Thus failure is impossible in both cases together. The origin of the illusion of failure is the failure to distinguish between what is forbidden and other matters, on the basis that what exists is not distinguished, or that the existence of those things in reality is accidental, and what is not so for the responsible persons, who consider each of them with the possibility of existence and non-existence. The benefit of this vagueness is to refrain from asking about those things absolutely, out of fear of disclosing what is disliked.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾ is a concluding interjection that confirms His pardon, exalted is He. That is: He is abundant in forgiving sins and overlooking disobedience. For this reason He pardoned you and did not hold you accountable with punishment for what you committed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 102:

﴿Indeed, a people before you asked such questions⦆; that is, they asked this very kind of question, but not the same question itself, rather one like it in being forbidden and in bringing about ruin. The absence of an explicit mention of "like it" is for the sake of emphasis in warning.

﴿Before you﴾ is connected to ﴿asked﴾.

﴿Then they became disbelievers because of them﴾; that is, because of their cause, or by their consequence.

﴿Disbelievers﴾: for the Children of Israel used to seek rulings (istifta', seeking legal opinion) from their prophets concerning matters, and when they were commanded to do them they abandoned them, and so they perished.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 103:

﴿Allah has not instituted any bahira, nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham.﴾ This is a refutation and nullification of what the people of the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance) had innovated, for when a she-camel gave birth to five young ones, the last of which was a male, they would slit her ear (bahara udhunaha), i.e., split it, and they would forbid her to be ridden or her milk to be drunk, and she was not to be driven away from water or pasture. A man would say: "If I return from my journey, or recover from my illness, then my she-camel is a sa'iba (freed)," and he would make her like the bahira in forbidding any benefit from her. It was also said: when a man freed a slave, he would say, "He is a sa'iba," so there would be no blood-money (aql) nor inheritance between them.

And when a ewe gave birth to a female, it was for them; if it gave birth to a male, it was for their gods; and if it gave birth to a male and a female, they said, "It has joined (wasalat) its brother," so they would not slaughter the male for their gods. And when ten young ones were born from the loins of a stallion, they said, "He has protected his back (ham zahrahu)," so he would not be ridden, nor carried upon, nor prevented from water or pasture.

The meaning of "ma ja'ala" is: "ma shara'a wa-ma wada'a" (what He legislated and what He instituted); for this reason it is transitive to one object only, namely bahira and what is conjoined to it.

The "min" is redundant (mazida) for the emphasis of negation, for just as the creative "ja'l" sometimes comes transitive to two objects and sometimes to one, so too the legislative "ja'l" sometimes comes transitive to two objects, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah made the Ka'ba, the Sacred House, a means of standing for mankind﴾, and sometimes to one, as in this noble verse.

﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah﴾, in that they do what they do and say, "Allah commanded us with this," and their leader is 'Amr ibn Luhayy, for he was the first to do these vain deeds. This is the matter of their leaders and great ones.

﴿And most of them﴾, namely their lowly ones who follow them from among the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as the context of the noble arrangement indicates.

﴿do not reason﴾ that it is a vain fabrication, until they oppose them and find the truth by themselves, so they remain in the captivity of imitation (taqlid). This is an explanation of the deficiency of their intellects and their inability to be guided by themselves.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 104:

As for His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾; that is, to those whom He referred to as "most of them," by way of guidance and direction.

﴿Come to what Allah has sent down﴾ of the Book that makes clear the lawful and the unlawful.

﴿And to the Messenger﴾ to whom it was sent down, so that you may come to know the reality of the matter and distinguish the unlawful from the lawful.

﴿They say: "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon"﴾: this is an explanation of their obstinacy, their refusal to be guided to the truth, and their submission to the one calling to misguidance.

﴿Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾

It has been said: the waw is for the circumstantial (hal), and the hamza entered upon it for denial and wonder; that is: do they suppose that, even though their fathers were ignorant and astray?

And it has been said: it is for coordination (ʿataf) upon another conditional clause presumed before it, and this is the more evident view. The estimate is: do they suppose that, or do they say this statement, even if their fathers did not know anything of the religion and were not guided to what is right, and even if they did not know ... etc.

Both of them are in the position of a circumstantial clause; that is: do they suppose that what their fathers were upon is what they follow in every supposed circumstance? The first has been omitted regularly in this construction, because the second indicates it clearly. How could it be otherwise, since when a thing is realized in the presence of a preventer, it is all the more realized in its absence? As in your saying: "Be good to so-and-so even if he has wronged you"; that is: be good to him if he has not wronged you and even if he has wronged you; that is: be good to him in every supposed circumstance. The first has been omitted because the second indicates it plainly, since goodness, when it is commanded in the presence of a preventer, is all the more commanded in its absence.

On this subtle point rests the emphasis and stress found in the concessive particles "in" and "law" (even if). The apodosis of "law" is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it; that is: even if their fathers knew nothing and were not guided, that suffices for them, or they say that. The sense of prevention and improbability in "law" is only with regard to their claim, not to the reality itself, and its purpose is to intensify the denial and wonder by showing that what they said calls for denial and wonder, when the fathers being ignorant and astray is a remote possibility, so how much more so when it is an undoubted reality.

It has also been said: the outcome of the two views is one, because the omitted clause is a circumstance, so what is coordinated upon it is likewise.

You know well that, on the final view, the circumstance is the combination of both clauses, not the last alone, and that the waw is for coordination, not for circumstance. The verification of this has already passed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾; so reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 105:

﴿O you who have believed, upon you is your own self﴾; i.e., keep to the matter of your own selves and their reform. It was also read with the nominative (raf'), on the basis of the inceptive (ibtida'), i.e., "your own selves are obligatory upon you."

And His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿No harm will come to you from those who are astray when you are guided﴾ is either jussive (majzum), on the basis that it is a response (jawab) to the imperative, or an emphatic prohibition (nahy mu'akkid) to it. The rā' was vowelled with ḍammah in imitation of the ḍammah of the ḍād, which was transferred to it from the rā' that was assimilated (mudghamah); the original form is lā yaḍurrukum (لا يَضُرْرُكم). This is supported by the reading with fatḥah on the rā', and by the reading of the one who read lā yaḍirkum (لا يَضِرْكم) with kasrah and ḍammah on the ḍād, from ḍāra yaḍīruhu and yaḍūruhu. Or it is nominative (marfu'), on the basis that it is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) in the position of giving the reason for what precedes it, and it is reinforced by the reading of the one who read lā yaḍīrukum (لا يَضِيرُكم); i.e., the error of those who are astray does not harm you when you are guided.

Let it not be supposed that there is in this a concession to abandon enjoining good and forbidding evil while one is able to do so; how could it be, when among the components of being guided is that one object to wrongdoing to the extent that one's capacity allows? The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand; if he is not able, then with his tongue; if he is not able, then with his heart."

It has been related that al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said one day upon the pulpit: "O people, you recite this verse and place it other than its proper place, and you do not understand what it is. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'When people see an evil and do not change it, Allah will surely overtake them all with punishment. So enjoin good and forbid evil, and do not be deceived by the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "O you who have believed..." etc., so that one of you says, "Upon me is my own self; by Allah, you must enjoin good and forbid evil, or else Allah will set over you the worst of you, who will inflict upon you the worst torment; then your best will supplicate, but it will not be answered for them.'"

And from him (ﷺ): "There is no people among whom an evil is committed or a repugnant practice is established, and they do not change it or object to it, except that it is binding upon Allah, Exalted is He, to overtake them all with punishment; then they will not be answered."

The verse was revealed when the believers were grieving over the disbelievers and wishing for their faith, while those people were in such error that they hardly ever desisted from it through commanding and forbidding.

It is also said: when a man embraced Islam, they would blame him and say to him: "You have called your fathers foolish (safahta) and have led them astray (dallaltahum)," i.e., you have attributed to them foolishness and error. So the verse was revealed as consolation to him, that the error of his fathers does not harm him nor disgrace him.

﴿To Allah﴾, not to anyone else.

﴿Your return﴾: your return on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿All together﴾: such that none of the guided or others will be left behind from Him.

﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ in the world of deeds of guidance and error. This is a promise and a warning to both groups, and an admonition that no one is held accountable for the deed of another.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 106:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to explain the rulings related to their worldly affairs, following the explanation of the circumstances related to their religious affairs. Its opening with the two particles of address and alerting (ya and ayyuha) serves to show the utmost concern for its content.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified, ﴿testimony between you﴾, with the nominative case and its annexation to the adverbial noun (zarf) in an expanded usage, is the subject (mubtada'). This is either by considering that it takes place among them, or by considering that it relates to the disputes that occur among them.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿when death approaches one of you﴾, meaning: when it draws near to him and its signs appear, is an adverbial clause (zarf) for it (the testimony). The fronting of the object (the soul, nafs, i.e., the phrase "one of you" as the object of the approach) serves to convey the complete firmness of the agent (death) with respect to the soul at the time it arrives upon it, for this is more effective in making the matter of death easy.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿at the time of bequest﴾ is a substitution (badal) for it, not an adverbial clause for death as has been supposed, nor for its approach as has been said. For in the substitution there is an alert that the bequest is among the established important matters that a Muslim should not neglect or be heedless of.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿two men﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of the subject, with an elided annexed noun, meaning: the testimony between you at that time is the testimony of two men; or it is the agent (fa'il) of "testimony between you," with its predicate elided, meaning: among what has been revealed to you, that two should testify between you.

It has been read: "testimonyun" (shahadatun) with the nominative and tanwin, and its i'rab is as previously mentioned. And it has been read: "testimonyan" (shahadatan) with the accusative and tanwin (p-89), by which its governing element is implied, which is also the governing element of "two men," meaning: let two men establish testimony between you.

﴿men of justice from among you﴾, meaning: from among your relatives, because they are more knowledgeable of the circumstances of the deceased, more sincere toward him, and closer to seeking what is best for him. It has been said: from among the Muslims. And these two are attributes of "two men."

﴿or two others﴾ is a conjunction over "two men," following it in what has been mentioned regarding the predicative and agentive function; meaning: or the testimony of two others, or that two others should testify between you, or let two others establish testimony between you.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿from other than you﴾ is an attribute of "two others," meaning: being from other than you, that is, from strangers. It has been said: from among the People of the Covenant (dhimmis). This was at the beginning of Islam, due to the scarcity of Muslims, especially during travel, and then it was abrogated. From Makhul: that it was abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and call to witness two just men from among you﴾.

﴿if you are﴾ is in the nominative case, governed by an implied verb which the following clause explains; its estimate: "if you travel" (idha darabtum). Then, when the verb was elided, the pronoun became detached. This is the view of the majority of the Basran grammarians. Al-Akhfash and the Kufans held that it is a subject (mubtada'), on the basis of the permissibility of a subject occurring after the conditional "in" (an), as its occurrence after "idha" is permissible.

So His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿you travel in the land﴾, meaning: you journey in it, has no place in terms of i'rab according to the first group, since it is an explanatory clause, and is in the nominative as a predicate according to the rest.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿then the calamity of death befalls you﴾ is a conjunction over the conditional clause, and its answer is elided because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: if you travel and then the appointed time of death approaches you at that time, and there are with you from among the relatives, or from among the people of Islam, one who undertakes the matter of testimony, as is the common usual practice in journeys, then let two others testify, or "so call two others to witness," or "so the two witnesses are two others." Thus it has been said, but the more fitting is to estimate the very same thing previously mentioned, meaning: then two others, in the sense that: the testimony between you is the testimony of two others, or then that two others should testify according to the aspects mentioned there.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿you detain them﴾ is a resumptive statement that came as an answer to what arose from the stipulation of justice, as if it were said: "How shall we act if we doubt the two witnesses?" So it is said: "you detain them," meaning: you stop them and make them wait for the oath.

﴿after the prayer﴾. It has been said that it is an attribute of "two others," and the conditional clause with its elided answer is a parenthetical insertion, its benefit being to show that what is proper is the calling to witness of relatives or people of Islam, while the calling to witness of others is only in a compelling necessity.

Yet you know well that this implies the restriction of the detention to the "two others," together with its inclusion of the first two as well, decisively; moreover, considering their being described by that is repugnant to the context of the command to call them to witness, since its outcome would be "two others whose condition is detention and oath-taking." And even if the approximation could be completed by considering the condition of doubt regarding them, as the forthcoming parenthetical clause indicates.

By "the prayer" is meant the afternoon prayer (salat al-'asr). Its not being specified is because it is already determined among them by swearing after it, since it is the time of people's gathering, the time when the angels of the night and the angels of the day meet, and because all the adherents of religions venerate it and avoid false oaths in it. It has been reported that the Prophet ﷺ at that time administered the oath to whoever swore, as will come. It has also been said: after whatever prayer it was, since it is a call to speaking the truth and a prohibition against lying and falsehood: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾.

﴿so they both swear by Allah﴾ is a conjunction over "you detain them."

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿if you doubt﴾ is a conditional clause whose answer is elided, since what preceded of detention and swearing indicates it. It is brought from His side, may He be exalted, as a parenthetical insertion between the oath and its answer, to alert to the restriction of detention and administering the oath to the state of doubt; meaning: if the heir among you doubts them of betrayal and of taking something from the estate, then detain them and administer the oath to them by Allah.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿we do not sell it for any price﴾ is the answer to the oath. This is not of the kind where an oath and a condition are combined, so that the answer of the former is mentioned instead of the answer of the latter, as is usually the case. For that occurs when the answer of the preceding one takes the place of the answer of the following one, due to the unity of their content, as in your saying: "By Allah, if you come to me, I will surely honor you." There is no doubt about the impossibility of that here, because the oath and its answer are both present, and you know that the condition is from His side.

Al-ijtira' (buying) is the exchange of the merchandise for the price, meaning: taking it in exchange for it, not giving it up in order to obtain it, as has been said, even though it entails that. For what is considered in the contract of purchase and its concept is acquisition, not the loss considered in the contract of sale. Then it was borrowed to mean taking something by removing what one has, whether tangible or abstract, with the sense of desire for what is taken and aversion from what is lost, as is considered in the source of the metaphor, as its detailed explanation has passed in the commentary on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾.

The pronoun in "by it" refers to Allah, and the meaning: we do not take for ourselves a substitute from Allah, that is, from His sanctity, a worldly commodity by profaning it and removing it through a false oath; that is, we do not swear falsely by Allah for the sake of wealth.

It has been said: the pronoun refers to the oath, so an elided annexed noun is absolutely necessary, meaning: we do not exchange the validity of the oath by Allah; that is, we do not take for ourselves a substitute from it, a worldly commodity, by removing from it the attribute of truthfulness and describing it as false; that is, we do not swear falsely as mentioned. Otherwise there is no coherence of meaning, whether by it is meant the truthful oath or the false one.

As for if it is meant as the false oath: because then what is considered in the metaphor is lost, namely that the removed thing is something desired by the swearer, such as the sanctity of the name of Allah, and the attribute of validity and truthfulness in the oath; and there is no doubt that the false oath is not like that.

As for if it is meant as the truthful one: because even though it is possible to use it as a means toward worldly gain, as with the false oath, there is no prohibition in it; but as for reaching it by abandoning its use, there is no possibility here for that to be a disavowal. Rather, one reaches it only by using the false oath, and its use is not a necessary consequence of abandoning the use of the truthful one, given the permissibility of abandoning both together; so it cannot be conceived that what is taken through using it is taken through abandoning the use of the truthful one, as in the case of estimating the annexed noun. For removing the attribute of truthfulness from the oath while the subject remains entails the definite attribution of falsehood to it. So reflect.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾, meaning: the one sworn for, implied by the context.

﴿near of kin﴾, meaning: close to us, is an emphasis on their disavowal of swearing falsely, and an exaggeration in distancing themselves from it, as if they both said: "We do not take for ourselves a substitute for the sanctity of His name in wealth, even if the consideration of the relatives were joined to it; how much more so when it is not like that. And the preservation of their own selves, although more important than the consideration of relatives, is not an addition to the wealth but returns to it."

The answer to "even if" is elided, relying on what preceded it as indication, meaning: "we do not take for it a price." The clause is conjoined to another similar clause, as detailed in the commentary on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and even if it pleases you﴾, etc.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified, ﴿and we do not conceal the testimony of Allah﴾, meaning: the testimony which Allah, may He be exalted, commanded us to establish, is conjoined to "we do not take for it," and is included together with it under the ruling of the oath.

It is reported from al-Sha'bi that he paused at "shahadah" and then began "Allah" with a prolonged vowel, by eliding the particle of oath and compensating with the interrogative particle, and also without prolongation, as in the saying "Allah, I will surely do it."

﴿Indeed we would then surely be among the sinners﴾, meaning: if we concealed it. And it has been read: "lamilathimin" with the elision of the hamza, transferring its vowel to the lam, and inserting the nun into it.

﴿Then if it is discovered﴾; i.e., it becomes known after the oath has been administered.

﴿that the two of them deserved sin﴾, as they admitted by their saying: ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the sinful﴾. That is, they committed what entails sin, namely distortion and concealment, in that some of the estate came into their hands and they claimed a right to it on some ground, as occurred in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), as will be mentioned below.

﴿Then two others﴾; i.e., two other men. This is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿shall stand in their place﴾. There is no prohibition against placing the predicate between the subject and its qualifier, which is the prepositional phrase following it. That is: they shall stand in the place of those whose treachery was discovered. The intended "place" is not the place of giving the testimony which they undertook and did not render as it was, but rather the place of detention and swearing in the manner mentioned, to bring out the truth and expose the falsehood of their claim to what was in their hands.

﴿from among those who have deserved﴾, read in the active voice according to the reading of ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās and Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with them; i.e., from among the family of the deceased, those who have deserved [it].

﴿against them, the two most entitled﴾ from among them; i.e., the two nearest to the deceased, the heirs, the most entitled to the testimony, i.e., to the oath, as you will come to know. The object of "deserved" (istahagga) is omitted; i.e., they (the two heirs) deserved, against them (the two impostors), that they be brought forward to carry out this testimony, because it is their right, and that by them they should expose the lie of the two liars. In reality, the "two others" are the ones standing in place of the first two, by placing the explicit noun in place of the pronoun.

It is also read in the passive voice, and this is the more apparent reading; i.e., from among those against whom sin was deserved, i.e., those who were wronged: the family of the deceased and his kin. Then "the two most entitled" is in the nominative, being the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it were said: "Who are the two?" It is said: "The two most entitled." Or it is an apposition (badal) to the pronoun in "shall stand," or to "two others." It has also been permitted that it be nominative governed by "deserved," with an omitted noun (mudaf); i.e., there was deserved against them the appointing of the first two from among them for testimony.

It is also read as "the first" (al-awwalīn), as an adjective of "those who," in the genitive, or in the accusative by way of praise. The meaning of priority (awwaliyya) is precedence over strangers in testimony, because they are more entitled to it. It is also read as "the first two" (al-awwaliyyayn) in the dual, its accusative being by way of praise, and it is read as "the first two" (al-awwalān).

﴿Then they shall swear by Allah﴾, conjoined to "shall stand."

﴿Indeed, our testimony﴾: the intended meaning of "testimony" is the oath, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿then the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah﴾; i.e., our oath that they are liars in what they claimed of the right to it, while our oath is itself true and sincere.

﴿is more worthy﴾ of acceptance.

﴿than their testimony﴾; i.e., than their oath, even though it is false in itself, because it has become apparent to people that they deserve sin, while our oath is free from doubt and suspicion. The comparative form (sigha al-tafdil) is used although there is no worthiness at all in their oath; it is only for the possibility of its being accepted in general, taking into account the probability of their truthfulness in claiming ownership of what appeared in their hands.

﴿And we have not transgressed﴾ is conjoined to the answer of the oath; i.e., we have not exceeded the truth in it, or we have not transgressed against them by nullifying their right.

﴿Indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾ is a resumptive sentence confirming what precedes it; i.e., indeed, if we transgress in our oath, we would be among those who wrong themselves by exposing themselves to the displeasure of Allah the Exalted and His punishment, by violating the sanctity of the name of Allah the Exalted; or we would be among those who place the truth in other than its proper place.

The meaning of the noble arrangement is this: the dying person should have two just men from among his kin or his religion witness his bequest. If he does not find them, such as when he is on a journey, then two others from outside them. Then, if doubt arises concerning them, they swear, with an emphatic oath at that time, that they did not conceal any part of the testimony or of the estate. If, after that, their lie is discovered, such as when some of the estate is found in their hands and they claim ownership of it from the deceased, then the heirs take an oath and the judgment is made according to their oaths.

Perhaps the restriction to two persons is due to the specific event, for it is reported that Tamim ibn Aws al-Dari and ʿAdī ibn Yazīd went out to Syria for trade, and they were at that time Christians, and with them was Budayl ibn Abī Maryam, the freedman of ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, who was a Muslim emigrant. When they reached Syria, Budayl fell ill, so he wrote a document containing everything he had, placed it among his goods, and did not inform them of that. He entrusted them to deliver his goods to his family, then he died. They searched his goods and found in them a silver vessel weighing three hundred mithqals, engraved with gold. So they concealed it, and delivered the goods to his family, and they found the document in them. The family asked them for the vessel, and they said: "We do not know; he only entrusted us with something and commanded us to deliver it to you, and we did so; we have no knowledge of the vessel." So they took them up to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the verse ﴿O you who have believed…﴾ was revealed. He (ﷺ) had them swear after the afternoon prayer beside the pulpit, by Allah, there is no god but He, that they had not defrauded anything of what was delivered nor concealed it. They swore to that, so the Prophet (ﷺ) released them. Then the vessel was found in Makkah, and it was said: "Whoever has it in his possession, I bought it from Tamim and ʿAdī." It was also said: when the time had lengthened, they displayed it, and this reached the Banū Sahm, who asked them for it. They said: "We had bought it from Budayl." The Banū Sahm said: "Did we not tell you: has our companion sold anything of his goods? And you said: No." They said: "We had no proof, so we disliked bringing him forward." So they took them up to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and His saying, Exalted and Majestic, was revealed: ﴿then if it is discovered…﴾. ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and al-Muṭṭalib ibn Abī Wadāʿa al-Sahmī stood up and swore by Allah after the afternoon prayer that they (Tamim and ʿAdī) had lied and betrayed, and the vessel was handed over to them. In another narration, it was handed over to the heirs of the deceased.

Know that if they were heirs of Budayl, then there is no abrogation (naskh) except in the attribute of the oath, for an heir is not made to swear absolutely; otherwise, it is abrogated.

﴿That﴾ is a new, independent statement (a resumptive clause) brought to show that what has been mentioned leads to benefits and follows the requirements of wisdom and welfare. That is, the ruling whose details were given earlier.

﴿That is more likely that they will bring the testimony in its proper form﴾: that is, it is more likely that the witnesses will give testimony in the form in which they bore it, without distortion or betrayal, out of fear of the punishment of the Hereafter. As you see, this is the wisdom behind the legislated oath with the stated intensification.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾ explains the wisdom behind the legislated return of the oath to the heirs. It is joined to an implied clause that the context points to, as if it were said: That is more likely that they will bring the testimony in its proper form, and that they will fear the punishment of the Hereafter for the sake of a false oath, or that they will fear public exposure before witnesses when their oaths are nullified and the oaths of the heirs are acted upon, so that they will refrain from the betrayal that leads to it. Whichever of the two fears occurs, the aim is achieved, which is bringing the testimony in its proper form.

It has also been said that it is conjoined to ﴿they bring﴾, with the meaning: that this is more likely to make them bring the testimony in its proper form, or more likely to make them fear public exposure through the return of the oath to the heirs, so they will not swear to the content of their testimony if they did not give it in its proper form, and thus their lying will become evident through their refusal (nukul) to swear.

As for what has been said, that the meaning is: this is more likely to lead to one of two matters, whichever of which occurs would contain the good, namely giving testimony in truth or refraining from giving it in falsehood, then it is rejected by the context, since it has no connection to the incident at all, because the witness is necessarily obliged in it to answer. Refraining from false testimony necessarily entails giving true testimony. So there are not two matters, whichever of which occurs contains good, such that the particle ﴿or﴾ would be placed between them. That would only be conceivable regarding witnesses who have not been accused of betrayal. Moreover, attributing the refraining from false testimony to the fear of the oath being returned to the heirs, while attributing giving true testimony to something else, although what requires one of them necessarily requires the other, is a purely arbitrary judgment. So reflect.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in opposing His commands, of which this ruling is one.

﴿And listen﴾ to what you are commanded, whatever it is, as listening in obedience and acceptance.

﴿And Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, those who depart from obedience. That is: if you do not fear Allah and do not listen, you would be defiant; and Allah does not guide the defiant people, that is, to the path of Paradise, or to what benefits them.(p-93)

The Day Allah gathers the messengers... ﴾ is in the accusative case as a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitute of inclusion, a noun that is related to the word it replaces through some connection) for the object of "اتَّقُوا" (be mindful of, fear). The reason is the connection between the two. The basis of substitution is not merely the relation of time and what occurs within it, or the like. It is any link that makes the mind pass from the replaced noun to the substitute in a general way, as in this case. That Allah is the Creator of all things and the Master of the Day of Judgment in particular is sufficient for this purpose. Moreover, the command to fear Allah the Exalted naturally suggests that the one to be feared is any of His affairs and any of His acts.

It has also been said that there is an omitted noun through which the inclusion is realized, meaning: "fear the punishment of Allah." In that case, the word may be in the accusative as an adverbial (*ẓarf*).

It has also been said that it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb coordinated with "اتَّقُوا" and what is coordinated with it, meaning: "and beware," or "remember the day..." etc. Reminding them of that terrible Day compels them to fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and to receive His command with a hearing that responds and obeys.

It has also been said that it is an adverb of time for His statement: ﴿does not guide﴾, meaning: He does not guide them on that day to the path of Paradise as He guides the believers.

It has also been said that it is governed by His statement ﴿and listen﴾, with an omitted noun, meaning: "listen to the news of that day."

It has also been said that it is governed by a delayed verb that has been omitted, to indicate that expression is too narrow to explain and clarify it, because of the extreme dreadfulness of what happens on it, its complete calamity and its general terrors. As if it were said: "On the Day Allah gathers the messengers, and He will say..." etc. There will be states and terrors of which the scope of speech cannot suffice to explain. Using the noble Name in place of a pronoun serves to cultivate awe and to intensify the sense of terror. The singling out of the messengers for mention does not mean that gathering is restricted to them rather than the nations, for how could that be so, when ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ (11:103)? Allah the Exalted has also said: ﴿On the Day We shall call every people with their leader﴾ (17:71). Rather, the mention is to show their nobility and preeminence, and to signal that there is no need to state explicitly the gathering of others, since it is evident that they are followers of the messengers. It also shows the lowering of the rank of the nations and their unfitness to be counted in the same row as the gathering of the messengers. How could it not be so, when the messengers, peace be upon them, are gathered in honor, while those others are dragged on their faces in chains?

﴿Then He will say﴾ to them, pointing to their discharge from the duty of conveying the message, as is fitting, as indicated by the fact that the question is directed clearly to the answer of the nations, except for the opening of the address, by saying: "Did you convey My messages?"

"ماذا" (what) in His statement, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿What response were you given?﴾ is an expression for the verbal noun of the verb, so it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdariyya*), meaning: "What kind of response were you given by your nations: an acceptance, or a rejection?"

It has also been said that it is an expression for the answer, so it is in the accusative place after the omission of the preposition, meaning: "with what answer were you answered?" Under either interpretation, directing the question at what proceeded from them, while they are witnesses to the messengers, peace be upon them, is like questioning the buried infant before the one who buried her. The shift from attributing the answer to them, by saying "ماذا أجابوا من الأنباء" (what news did they respond with), serves to show the complete belittling of their status, and the intensity of anger and wrath against them, which is not hidden.

﴿They will say﴾ is a resumptive clause, built upon a question arising from the flow of speech, as if it were said: "What will the messengers, peace be upon them, say there?" So it is said: they will say, ﴿We have no knowledge﴾. The past form is used to indicate firmness and certainty, as in His statement, ﴿And the companions of Paradise will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾ (7:44), and similar examples. They say this only by entrusting the matter to His knowledge, and His encompassing of what befell them from the side of their own people of the sufferings of the terrors and the anguish of the distresses, and as a presentation of their inability to describe it because of its vastness and dreadfulness.

﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ is the justification for that. That is, You know what they answered and what they made apparent to us, and what we did not know of what they concealed in their hearts. This contains a display of complaint, a referral of the matter to His knowledge of the afflictions they met from their people, and the calamities they endured, and a seeking of refuge with their Lord for retribution against them.

It has also been said that the meaning is: "We have no knowledge of what they innovated after us, and the judgment rests only on the outcome." This was refuted by saying that they recognize them by their marks, so how could their state be hidden from them?

You should know that what they intend at that point is that some of them were upon the truth in their time and then became disbelievers. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi, may Allah be pleased with them, that they will be seized with alarm at first, become distracted from the answer, and then answer after their minds have returned to them through bearing witness against their nations. The stated justification does not fit this view.

It has also been said that the purpose of it is: exaggeration in establishing their disgrace.

It has been read as ﴿عَلّامَ الغُيُوبِ﴾ (*ʿAllāma al-ghuyūb*, with a fatha on the mīm), in the accusative either as a vocative or as a particular praise, on the basis that the speech is complete at His statement "أنْتَ" (You), meaning: "Indeed, You are the One described with the attributes of Your perfection, known by that."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 110:

﴿When Allah said, "O Jesus, son of Mary"﴾ begins an account, in detail, of what passed between Him, exalted is He, and one of the messengers who were gathered, following the general account of what passed between Him and all of them. This is so that it serves as a model for the detailed circumstances of the rest, and the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him, is singled out for explanation from among the affairs of the other messengers, peace be upon them. Its indications also show the full terror of that Day and the utmost wretchedness of the state of those who denied the messengers. This is because his matter, peace be upon him, concerns both groups of the People of the Book, whose offences are recounted in this noble surah. Therefore, detailing it is greater against them, more productive of their regret and remorse, more weakening to their resolve, and more effective in turning them away from their error and obstinacy.

"Idh" (when) is a substitute (badal) for "the Day when Allah gathers", and the past tense form is used for the indication mentioned, namely the affirmation that the event has certainly occurred. The noble name (Allah) is made explicit in a place where a pronoun would be expected, because of the emphasis on awe mentioned earlier.

The word "ʿalā" (upon) in His saying ﴿Remember My favour upon you and upon your mother﴾ is connected to the favour itself if it is taken as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: remember My bestowing upon you both. Or it is connected to a omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it if it is taken as a noun (ism), meaning: remember My favour being upon you both. The intended meaning of his, peace be upon him, being commanded that day to recall the favour, which is included in the series of enumeration, is not that he was being charged with thanking for it and performing its obligations. It was not a time for obligation, and he, peace be upon him, had certainly fulfilled the duty of gratitude at its proper time. Rather, it is the manifestation of his matter, peace be upon him, through the enumeration of those blessings as Allah has explained them, out of regard for them and delight in mentioning them before the assembled witnesses. Thus the narration of this, as the noble composition indicates, is a rebuke and deterrent to the disbelievers who differed concerning his matter, peace be upon him, through excess and deficiency, and a refutation of both of their claims together.

﴿When I strengthened you﴾ is an adverbial clause (ẓarf) of "My favour"; that is: remember My bestowing upon you both at the time of My strengthening you. Or it is a circumstantial clause of it; that is: remember it as being at the time of My strengthening you. It is read "ʾāyadtuka" and the meaning is the same; that is: I strengthened you.

﴿with the Holy Spirit﴾: with Gabriel, peace be upon him, to establish the proof; or with the speech by which religion is revived. Its being attributed to "the Holy" (qudus) is because it is the cause of purity from the defilements of sins. Or by it the dead are revived, or souls are given eternal life.

It has been said: spirits differ in their realities. Some are pure and luminous, some are wicked and dark, some are radiant, some are turbid, some are noble, and some are base. His spirit, peace be upon him, was pure, radiant, luminous and exalted. Whichever of these is meant, it is a favour upon both of them.

﴿You speak to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) explaining his strengthening, peace be upon him; or it is a circumstantial clause of the "kāf" (you). The mention of his speaking in the state of maturity is to show that his speech in those two states was in a single, wondrous pattern, issuing from perfect reason and accompanied by the solidity of judgment and management. It has been deduced from this that he, peace be upon him, will descend from heaven, since he, peace be upon him, was raised before reaching maturity.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Allah sent him when he was thirty years old, and he remained in his mission for thirty months, then Allah raised him to Himself.

﴿And when I taught you the Book﴾ is a conjunction with His saying "when I strengthened you", governed by what governs it; that is: remember My favour upon you both at the time of My teaching you the Book.

﴿and wisdom﴾; that is, the genus of both.

﴿and the Torah and the Gospel﴾ are singled out for mention from among what the Book and wisdom comprise, to show their nobility. It has been said: "al-khaṭṭ" (writing) and wisdom mean: sound, firmly composed speech.

﴿And when you shaped from clay the form of a bird﴾; that is: you fashioned from it a form resembling the form of a bird.

﴿by My permission﴾: by My facilitation and making it easy, not on the basis that the creation issued from him, peace be upon him, in reality, but on the basis that this appeared at his hand, peace be upon him, when the causes were engaged, while the creation is in reality Allah's, exalted is He.

As His saying indicates: ﴿and you breathe into it﴾; that is: into the shaped form, ﴿and it becomes﴾; that is: that form becomes ﴿a bird by My permission﴾. For if His permission were not an expression of His bringing the bird into being, but merely of His facilitating, while the act truly proceeded from what was attributed to him, then this would be a coming-into-being from the aspect of the form. The repetition of the phrase "by My permission" in the case of the bird, although it is one thing, is to draw attention to the fact that each of the shaping and the breathing is a great and wondrous matter, which cannot be accomplished nor have any result except by His permission, exalted is He.

﴿And you heal the blind and the leper by My permission﴾ is a conjunction with "you shape".

﴿And when you bring forth the dead by My permission﴾ is a conjunction with "when you shape"; "when" is repeated in it because the bringing forth of the dead from their graves, especially after they have become dust, is a dazzling miracle and a magnificent favour, deserving of an explicit reminder of its time. It has been said: he brought forth Sam son of Noah, two men, a woman, and a girl.

The repetition of the phrase "by My permission" in the four places is for the sake of establishing the truth, by explaining that those extraordinary acts are not from Jesus, peace be upon him, but from Him, glorified is He, who manifested them at his hands as a miracle for him and a favour which He singled him out with. As for its mention in Surat Āl ʿImrān twice, that is because that is the place of report, while this is the place of enumerating favours.

﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you﴾ is a conjunction with "when you bring forth"; that is: I prevented the Jews who intended evil against you from attacking you.

﴿when you came to them with clear proofs﴾: with manifest miracles, both those mentioned and those not mentioned, such as informing them of what they eat and what they store in their houses, and the like. It is an adverbial clause of "I restrained", but not merely in consideration of his coming with them, rather in consideration of what follows it in His saying: ﴿those of them who disbelieved said: "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ For their saying this indicates that they intended to assassinate him, peace be upon him, which made restraint necessary; that is: I restrained them from you when they said that, upon your coming to them with the clear proofs. The relative pronoun was placed in the position of the pronoun "them" to censure them by what is in the clause of the relative. Thus the word "min" (of) is explicative. This (hādhā) refers to what he brought, and the masculine is used because their pointing was to what they saw, namely the thing itself in terms of what it is, or in terms of it being magic, not in terms of its being named "proofs". It is read: "inna hādhā illā sāḥirun mubīn" (this is nothing but a clear sorcerer); then "hādhā" at that point refers to Jesus, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 111:

﴿And when I inspired the disciples﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it of its sister phrases, which occur as temporal clauses (zuruf) for the favour that he was commanded to mention. Although in reality it is the very same thing that the sentences to which those temporal clauses are attached convey, namely the strengthening through the Holy Spirit, the teaching of the Book and the Wisdom, and the other enumerated extraordinary signs, nevertheless, because it differs from them by a title that indicates the utmost of beneficence, he was commanded to mention it from that aspect, and it was made to govern those temporal clauses, since the conceptual difference is sufficient to realize what is considered in the meaning of the word "idh" (when) of a plurality of relations. For "idh" is a particle placed for the time of two past relations occurring within it, one of which is known to the addressee to have occurred in it while the other is not. So it is intended to convey that the other also occurred, and it is attached to the sentence conveying the first relation, and is made a temporal complement governed by the second relation. Then the difference between the two relations may be essential, as in your saying: "Remember my kindness to you when you were kind to me," intending to alert the addressee to the occurrence of his kindness to you at the time of the occurrence of his kindness to you... and these are two relations that are essentially different. And it may be a difference by consideration, as in your saying: "Remember my kindness to you when I prevented you from disobedience," intending to alert him to the fact that his prevention from it was a kindness to him, not to another kindness occurring at that time. And of this kind is the general run of what occurs in the revelation, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my people, remember the favour of God upon you when He appointed prophets among you and made you kings﴾... the verse, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, remember the favour of God upon you when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He restrained their hands from you﴾, and other similar examples.

The meaning of His, exalted is He, inspiring them is: His, exalted is He, commanding them in the Gospel through the tongue of him, peace be upon him. It was also said: His, exalted is He, inspiring them (ilham), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We inspired the mother of Moses﴾.

The "an" (that) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That believe in Me and in My Messenger﴾ is explanatory (mufassira) for what in the inspiration contains the sense of speech. It was also said that it is verbal-masdar (masdariyya). And His, peace be upon him, being mentioned by the title of Messenger is to alert to the manner of believing in him, peace be upon him, as if it were said: Believe in My oneness in divinity and lordship, and in the messengership of My Messenger, and do not remove him from his station, neither by demeaning nor by elevating him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the flow of speech, as if it were said: "What did they say when this was inspired to them?" So it was said: They said: ﴿We believe﴾; that is, in what was mentioned of His oneness, exalted is He, and of the messengership of His Messenger, as their saying indicates.

﴿And bear witness that we are Muslims﴾; that is, sincere in our faith, ﴿Whoever submits his face to God﴾. This saying of theirs, in accordance with His inspiration and His command to them to do so, is a magnificent favour, like all the favours poured out upon him, peace be upon him, and all of that is also a favour upon his mother.

It is narrated that when he, peace be upon him, knew that he would be commanded to mention those great favours, he began to wear hair and eat leaves of trees, and would store nothing for tomorrow, saying: "For every day its sustenance." He had no house that he might see ruined, nor a child that he might see die; wherever evening found him, he spent the night there.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 112:

﴿When the disciples said﴾ is a resumed statement (isti'naf) brought to explain some of what passed between him, peace be upon him, and his people. It is disconnected from what precedes it, as the use of the noun in place of the pronoun indicates.

"Idh" is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ by way of a shift in address (iltifat). But not because the preceding address was to Jesus, peace be upon him, for that was not an address but a report of an address. Rather, it is because the address is to those addressed by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And fear Allah﴾ ... the verse; so reflect.

It is as if it were said to the Prophet ﷺ, after relating what the disciples said, which is counted among the blessings of Allah the Exalted that overflowed upon Jesus, peace be upon him: "Mention to the people the time when they said ..." and so on.

It is also said that "idh" is an adverbial complement of "qalu" (they said), intended to alert that their claim of faith and sincerity was not based on verification and certainty. The noble composition does not support this.

﴿O Jesus son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?﴾ Scholars differ over whether they were believers or not. It is said: they were unbelievers, doubting Allah's power to do what they mentioned, and doubting the truthfulness of Jesus, peace be upon him, lying in their claim of faith and sincerity. It is also said: they were believers, and their question was for reassurance and affirmation, not for removing doubt.

"Can your Lord ... ?" (hal yastatiu) is a question about the act itself, not about the capacity for it, by expressing the act through its necessary consequence. It is also said: "istita'a" here means being able in the sense demanded by wisdom and will, not in the sense demanded by power. It is also said: the meaning is "Can your Lord ... ?" in the sense of "Will your Lord respond to you?" and "istata'a" here means "ata'a" (obeyed), as "istajaba" means "ajaba" (answered).

It is recited as (hal tastati'u rabbaka), meaning: "Can you ask your Lord ...?" The sense is: "Would you ask Him for that without anything turning you away from it?" This is the recitation (qira'a) of Ali, Aisha, Ibn Abbas, Mu'adh, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and others among them, may Allah be pleased with them.

"Al-ma'ida" is the table on which the food is placed, from "madah," meaning he gave and bestowed. It is as if it bends (tamid) toward whoever approaches it. Its parallel is the saying: "a grafted tree" (shajara mut'ama). Abu Ubayd said: it is of the form fa'ila in the sense of maf'ula, like "'ishatun radiyatun" (a pleasing life).

﴿He said﴾ is a resumed statement built upon a question arising from what precedes it. It is as if it were asked: "What did Jesus, peace be upon him, say to them when they said that?" So it is said: he said, ﴿Fear Allah﴾; that is, from such questions.

﴿if you are believers﴾; that is, in the perfection of His power, the Exalted, and in the soundness of my prophethood; or, if you are truthful in your claim of faith and submission, for that necessitates taqwa and avoiding such proposals.

It is also said: he commanded them to taqwa so that it would become a means (dhari'a) for attaining what they asked for, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ ﴿and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾, and His saying: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and seek the means (wasila) to Him﴾.

[Continuing the verse, the commentary opens:] "They said" — a resumptive (istiʼnaf) clause, as before.

"We wish to eat from it" — a preface offering an excuse and clarifying what prompted them to ask. That is: we do not intend by the question to remove any doubt of ours regarding His power (subhanahu) to send it down, or regarding the validity of your prophethood, such that this would detract from faith and piety. Rather, we wish to eat from it — that is, eating for blessing (akl tabarruk). It has also been said: eating out of need and enjoyment.

"And our hearts be reassured" — through the full perfection of God's power (exalted is He), even though we had believed in Him before, for the joining of knowledge by direct witnessing (ʻilm al-mushahada) to inferential knowledge ('ilm al-istidlal) is among the things that necessitate greater tranquility and the strength of certainty.

"And we would know" — that is, with certain knowledge (ʻilman yaqiniyyan), to which no trace of doubt whatsoever approaches. It is also read as "li-yuʻlam" in the passive voice.

"That you have indeed told us the truth" — "an" here is the light form of "inna," and the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʼn) is omitted; that is: and we would know that indeed you have told us the truth regarding the claim of prophethood, and that God answers our supplication, even though we already knew this before.

"And that we may be among its witnesses" — we would bear witness concerning it to those among the Children of Israel who were not present; so that the believers among them would increase in tranquility and certainty through our testimony, and their disbelievers would come to faith because of it. Or: among those who witness it with their own eyes, as opposed to those who only hear the report.

"Upon it" (ʻalayhā) is connected to "al-shāhidīn" if the lām is taken as the definite article; and it is an explanation of what they bear witness to if the lām is taken as a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), as though it were said: "To what do they bear witness?" and the answer was: "upon it," since what is connected to the relative clause (ṣila) does not precede the relative pronoun. Or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "kānā"; or it is connected to an omitted verb that is explained by "min al-shāhidīn."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 114:

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said﴾ When he (peace be upon him) saw that they had a sound purpose in this and that they would not desist from it, he resolved to summon it down and bring it forth, and he wished to establish the proof against them in its completeness.

It is related that he (ﷺ) performed ghusl, put on a woolen garment (al-misḥ), and prayed two rak'ahs. Then he lowered his head and cast down his gaze, and then said: ﴿O Allah, our Lord﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, addressed him twice: once with the attribute of divinity (al-ulūhiyyah), which encompasses all perfections, and once with the attribute of lordship (al-rubūbiyyah), which indicates nurture and upbringing; this is to show the utmost of supplication and to emphasize the request.

﴿Send down upon us﴾: the placing of the adverbial phrase before His saying ﴿a table﴾ is for the sake of the concern with what is placed first and the arousing of anticipation for what is placed later, as has been mentioned many times.

His saying ﴿from heaven﴾ is connected either to "send down," or to an omitted element that is an attribute of "a table"; that is, existing from heaven, descending from it.

His saying ﴿that it may be for us a festival﴾ is in the position of the accusative, as an attribute of "a table." The subject of "may be" (takūnu) is the pronoun referring to the table, and its predicate is either "a festival" (ʿīdan), with "for us" (lanā) being a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from it; or "for us" and "a festival" are a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in "for us," since it occurs as a predicate and therefore carries a pronoun; or from the pronoun in "may be" according to those who permit its operation in the circumstantial phrase, meaning that the day of its descent would be a festival that we venerate.
