This attribute was attributed to the table because the honour of the day is borrowed from its honour.

It is also said: the ʿīd (festival) is "the returning joy" (al-surūr al-ʾāʾid), and for this reason the day of the festival was called ʿīd. It has been read as (takun) in the jussive mood, in answer to the imperative, as in His exalted saying: ﴿So grant me from Yourself a guardian﴾ ﴿who will inherit from me﴾, except that the jussive reading there is mutawātir (widely transmitted), whereas here it is among the irregular readings (shādhdh).

﴿For the first of us and the last of us﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "for us," with the governing element repeated; that is, a festival for our predecessors and our successors. It is related that it descended on a Sunday, and for this reason the Christians took it as a festival. It is also said: for our leaders and our followers. It is also said: the first of us and the last of us will eat from it. It has been read as (li-ūlānā wa-ukhrānā), with the meaning of the community and the group.

﴿And a sign﴾ is conjoined to "a festival."

﴿from You﴾ is connected to an omitted element which is an attribute of "a sign"; that is, existing from You, indicating the perfection of Your power and the soundness of my prophethood.

﴿And provide for us﴾; that is, the table, or thanks for it.

﴿And You are the best of providers﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl) running in the manner of a reason; that is, You are the best of those who provide, for He is the Creator of provisions and the Giver of them without recompense. And in his (peace be upon him) turning to supplication by repeating the call, which indicates the utmost of humble entreaty and earnest pleading and its increase, there is, beyond what did not occur to the minds of the petitioners of the matters that call to answer and acceptance, a clear proof that they were believers, and that their request was for attaining tranquillity, as in the saying of Abraham (peace be upon him): ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾; otherwise he would not have accepted their excuse which they mentioned, nor would he have added from himself what confirms it and brings it nearer to acceptance.

﴿Allah said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence that answers an implied question), as before.

﴿I am sending it down to you﴾: God's answer comes in the form of tanzil (the intensive form of the verb), which indicates repetition, while the supplication from him, peace be upon him, came in the form of inzal (the basic form of the verb). This is to show the completeness of kindness and grace, as in God's words: ﴿Say: God delivers you from it and from every distress...﴾ etc., after His words: ﴿If You deliver us from this...﴾ etc., together with what this contains of observing the wording used by the petitioners.

By opening the sentence with the particle of emphasis (inni, "indeed") and making its predicate a noun, there is confirmation of the promise and an indication that God will certainly fulfil it, without any obstacle that could turn Him away or any barrier that could divert it. It also implies continuity, that is: I will send down the table to you many times. It is also read with the lighter form (tukhfif, a reading with single consonant), and it has been said that inzal and tanzil have the same meaning.

﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after that﴾: that is, after its sending down.

﴿among you﴾: this is related to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the subject of "yakfur" (disbelieves).

﴿then I will punish him﴾: because of his disbelief after witnessing this astounding sign.

﴿with a punishment﴾: this is an ism al-masdar (a verbal noun) meaning "punishing". It has also been said to be a masdar (infinitive) with its augmentations removed. Its accusative case is by way of the infinitive, under the two interpretations mentioned, and it is also permissible for it to be a direct object by extension (ittisa').

God's words: ﴿I will not punish anyone﴾ are in the accusative position as an attribute of "punishment", and the pronoun refers to it; that is: I will punish him with a punishment such that I will not punish anyone else with the like of that punishment.

﴿anyone from among the worlds﴾: that is, from the peoples of their own time, or from all the worlds. It has been said: when they heard this severe threat, they feared that some of them might disbelieve, so they asked to be excused and said: "We do not want it," and so it was not sent down. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Hasan, may God have mercy on them both. The sound view, which the majority of the Ummah and the leading imams hold, is that it was indeed sent down.

It is reported that when he, peace be upon him, made the supplication he made, and was answered as he was answered, behold, a red table (sufrah) descended between two clouds, a cloud above it and a cloud below it, while they were looking at it, until it fell before them. Jesus, peace be upon him, wept and said: "O God, make me among the grateful. O God, make it a mercy for the worlds, and do not make it a mutilation and a punishment." Then he stood, performed ablution, prayed and wept. Then he uncovered the cloth and said: "In the name of God, best of providers." Behold, there was a roasted fish without scales or bones, dripping with fat, with salt at its head and vinegar at its tail, and around it were all kinds of herbs except leeks; and behold, there were five loaves, on one of which was olives, on the second honey, on the third butter, on the fourth cheese, and on the fifth dried meat. Shim'un, the head of the disciples (Hawariyyun), said: "O Spirit of God, is this from the food of this world or from the food of the Hereafter?" He said: "It is neither of them, but it is something God created by His lofty power. Eat what you ask for and give thanks, and God will supply you and increase you of His bounty." They said: "O Spirit of God, if only you would show us another sign from this sign." He said: "O fish, come to life by God's permission!" It thrashed about; then he said to it: "Return as you were," and it returned roasted. Then the table flew away. Then they disobeyed, so they were transformed into apes and swine.

It has also been said: it used to come to them every forty days, once in a while (ghibban), and rich and poor, young and old, gathered around it, eating until the shade shifted (fa'a al-fay'), and then it flew away while they watched its shadow. No poor man ate from it without becoming rich for the rest of his life, and no sick person ate from it without being healed and never falling ill again. Then God revealed to Jesus, peace be upon him, that he should make My table for the poor and the sick, not for the rich and the healthy. The people were disturbed by this, so some of them were transformed, and they became swine running in the streets and alleys and eating filth in the latrines. When the people saw this, they fled to Jesus, peace be upon him, and wept over the transformed ones. When the swine saw Jesus, peace be upon him, they wept and circled around him, and he began calling them by their names, one after another, and they wept and nodded their heads, but they could not speak. They lived three days, and then they perished.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father: that Jesus, peace be upon him, said to them: "Fast thirty days, then ask God for whatever you wish, and He will give it to you." So they fasted, and when they finished they said: "If we were to work for someone and complete his work, he would feed us." They asked God Most High for the table, and the angels came with a table they carried, on which were seven loaves and seven fishes, until they placed it before them. The last of the people ate from it just as the first of them ate.

Ka'b said: it was sent down upside down, with the angels carrying it between heaven and earth, with every kind of food on it except meat.

Qatadah said: on it was fruit from the fruits of Paradise.

'Atiyyah al-'Awfi said: a fish descended from heaven that had the taste of every food.

al-Kalbi said: a fish and five loaves descended, and they ate what God willed, while the people numbered a thousand and more. When they returned to their villages and spread the story, some who had not witnessed it laughed at them and said: "Woe to you! He has only bewitched your eyes." Whoever God wills good for, He makes firm in insight, and whoever He wills trial for, returns to his disbelief. So they were transformed into swine, remained so for three days, and then perished. They did not reproduce, did not eat, and did not drink, and this is the case with every transformed person.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 116:

﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary"﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "﴿when the Disciples said﴾", and is in the accusative (mansub) by the same governing verb that governs it, namely the implied addressed verb (mudmar al-mukhatab bihi) addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, or by an independent implied verb conjoined to that. That is: "Mention to the people the time of Allah's saying to him, peace be upon him, on the Day of Judgment, as a rebuke to the disbelievers and a silencing of them, by his affirmation, peace be upon him, before the heads of the witnesses, of servitude, and his command to them to worship Him, Mighty and Majestic." The past-tense form is used because of what has passed, indicating certainty and occurrence.

﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ The verb "to take" (al-ittikhadh) is either transitive to two objects, so that "two gods" (ilahayn) is the second object, or transitive to one object, so that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object. The main point of the statement is not that the saying is certain, while the interrogation serves to specify the speaker, as is apparent from the placing of the interrogative hamzah before the subject (mubtada') in common usage, and on this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did you do this to our gods?﴾ and its like. Rather, what is certain is the taking, and the interrogation serves to specify whether it was by his command, peace be upon him, or on their own initiative, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did you lead astray these servants of Mine, or did they themselves go astray from the way?﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿besides Allah﴾ is connected to the taking (al-ittikhadh), and its place is accusative as a circumstantial clause from its subject, meaning: transgressing Allah. Or it is connected to an implied word that is a qualifier (sifah) of "two gods", meaning: existing besides Him, exalted is He. In either case, what is meant is taking them as two by way of associating them with Him, glory be to Him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, rivals﴾, and His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And they worship besides Allah what neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾, up to His saying, glory be to Him and exalted: ﴿above what they associate﴾. For by this the rebuke is achieved, and the reproach and silencing are accomplished.

As for one who imagines that this is by way of independence, and then excuses it by saying that the Christians believe that the miracles which appeared at the hands of Jesus and Mary, upon both of them be prayer and peace, were not created by Allah, Exalted, but that they two created them, so it is valid that they took the two as independent gods in regard to some things, and did not take Him, Exalted, as a god in regard to that part, then he has strayed far from the truth. As for one who went deeper and said: the worship of Him, Exalted, together with the worship of other than Him is as if there were no worship, so whoever worships Him along with worshipping the two, it is as though he worshipped the two and did not worship Him, Exalted, then he has neglected what would benefit him and occupied himself with what does not concern him, like the one before him. For their rebuke is achieved only by what they believe and openly acknowledge, not by what is implied by some kind of interpretation. The display of the glorious Name is because it is within the scope of the statement attributed to Jesus, peace be upon him.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the opening of the speech, as if it were said: "What then does Jesus, peace be upon him, say at that time?" So it is answered: "He says." The choice of the past-tense form is for what has passed repeatedly.

﴿Glory be to You﴾: "Subhan" is a proper noun used for glorifying, and its accusative status is as a verbal noun (masdar), and its governing verb is hardly ever mentioned. (p-101) In it is intensive emphasis on transcendence (tanzih) from the standpoint of derivation from "sabh", which is going away and distancing in the land; and from the standpoint of its transfer to the pattern "taf'il"; and from the standpoint of its shift from the verbal noun to the noun specifically coined for it, which indicates the reality present in the mind; and from the standpoint of its standing in place of the verbal noun together with the verb, which is not hidden. That is: "I glorify You with a glorification befitting You, from my saying that, or from its being said of You."

As for the supposition: "from there being for You a partner in divinity", the context of the noble arrangement and its surrounding context do not support it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for me to say what is not right for me﴾ is a resumptive clause that establishes the transcendence and specifies what is transcended. "Ma" refers to the aforementioned saying; that is: it is not fitting or proper for me to say a statement that it is not right for me to say.

The choice of "laysa" (is not) over a negated verb is because its indication of the continuous negation of rightness is evident, and because of the emphasis conveyed by the preposition "bi" within its scope. Its subject is the pronoun referring back to "ma", and its predicate is "bi haqq" (with right). The prepositional phrase between them is explanatory (lil-tabyin), as in "suqyan laka" and similar expressions.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If I had said it, You would surely know it﴾ is a resumptive clause that establishes, by a demonstrative method, that the aforementioned statement did not come from him, peace be upon him. For its issuing from him necessarily entails His knowledge of it, certainly. So when His knowledge of it is negated, its issuing from him is necessarily negated, since the absence of the necessary entails the absence of what necessitates it.

﴿You know what is within myself﴾ is a resumptive clause functioning as a justification (ta'lil) for what precedes it, as if it were said: "Because You know what I conceal within myself, so how then [would You not know] what I make manifest?"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I do not know what is within Yourself﴾ is an explanation of the reality and a manifestation of its deficiency. That is: "and I do not know what You conceal of Your knowledge." His saying "within Yourself" is for the sake of verbal correspondence (al-mushakalah). It has been said: the intended meaning of "nafs" (self) is the essence (dhat), and the attribution of the known things to it is because it is the locus of the attributes, among which is the knowledge connected to them, so it was not like its attribution to the reality.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the content of the two sentences, both explicit and implicit.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 117:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Never did I say to them except what You commanded me, [to say]: Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾ is a resumptive statement (istinaf) brought to explain what proceeded from him. It includes the non-occurrence of the aforementioned statement from him in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, since it is judged that all statements other than what he was commanded to say did not proceed from him; thus the non-occurrence of the aforementioned statement is included primarily. That is: "I did not command them except with what You commanded me." The phrase "Never did I say to them" was used in deference to good manners and in observance of what occurred in the interrogative form.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾ is an explanation (tafsir) of what he was commanded. It was said that it is an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to the pronoun in "with it." It was said that it is a substitute (badal) for it, and it is not a condition of the substitute that the substituted element may be omitted absolutely, lest the relative pronoun remain without a returning pronoun. It was said that it is a predicate of an implied subject, or its object, like: "He," or "I mean."

﴿And I was a witness over them﴾: a watcher (raqib), who observes their conditions, drives them to act in accordance with Your command, and restrains them from opposition; or one who witnesses their conditions, of disbelief and belief.

﴿As long as I remained among them﴾: "ma" here is a verbal-temporal (masdariyya zarfiyya) particle, which is to be construed with a verbal noun supplied and annexed to a time-expression; and "dumtu" is its clause (silla). That is: "I was a witness over them for the duration of my remaining among them."

﴿But when You took me up﴾: by raising me to heaven, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I will take you (mutawaffika) and raise you to Me﴾. For tawaffi means taking a thing in full, and death is a kind of it. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep﴾.

﴿You were the watcher over them﴾, not other than You. So "anta" is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) or an emphasis. It was read as "al-raqib" in the nominative, on the basis that it is the predicate of "anta." The clause is the predicate of "kana," and "over them" is connected to it. That is: You were the one who preserved their deeds and observed them; so You prevented whoever You willed to protect from opposition by guiding them to the proofs and alerting them to these through sending messengers and sending down signs, and You forsook whoever among the misguided You forsook, so they said what they said.

﴿And You are a witness over all things﴾: an concluding parenthetical statement (i'tiraD tadhyili) confirming what precedes it. In it is an indication that He, Exalted is He, was the Witness over all, at the time when he, peace be upon him, was among them. "Over" is connected to "witness," and the fronting is for the sake of observing the rhyme (fasila).

﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾, and they deserve that, since they worshipped other than You.

﴿And if You forgive them, indeed You are the All-Mighty﴾; that is, the Powerful, the Capable of all things that can be decreed, and among them reward and punishment.

﴿the All-Wise﴾, who does not will or do anything except what contains wisdom and benefit. For forgiveness is commendable for every criminal: if You punish, it is justice, and if You forgive, it is grace. As for the non-forgiveness of shirk, it is only in accordance with the threat (al-wa'id, the divine threat of punishment), so there is no impossibility in it in itself that would prevent the (conditional) division.

It has also been said: the division (tarddid) is with reference to two groups, and the meaning is: if You punish them, that is, those among them who disbelieved, and if You forgive them, that is, those among them who believed.

Allah said. This is a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf, a new sentence that is not grammatically tied to what precedes it), with which the account of what will happen on the day when Allah gathers the Messengers, peace be upon them, is concluded. It also points to its outcome and result. That is, Allah, exalted is He, says on that day, following the reply of ʿIsā (Jesus), peace be upon him, indicating his truthfulness within the description of the truthful ones, among whom he is counted. The past-tense form is used here as it has been used many times in similar cases.

His, exalted is He, words: ﴿This﴾ refer to that day. It is a subject (mubtadaʾ), and its predicate (khabar) is what follows it. That is: this is the day on which some of what happens in it has been related in summary and some in detail.

﴿This is a day when the truthfulness of the truthful benefits them﴾ is read with the nominative and with the construct form (idafa). By "the truthful," as the term itself indicates, is meant those who persist in truthfulness in both abodes in religious matters, the most important of which is monotheism (tawhid), which is our present concern, and the laws and rulings connected with it, taken from the Messengers who speak the truth and sincerity and who call to it. Through this the truthfulness of ʿIsā, peace be upon him, is established, as well as that of the nations that affirm them and follow them, in belief and in action. Through this the purpose of the narration is realized, namely encouraging the hearers to believe in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), not every person who was truthful about anything whatsoever, since the offender who confesses his crime in this world will not benefit on that day from his confession and his truthfulness.

﴿Their truthfulness﴾: that is, their truthfulness in what has been mentioned of the matters of religion, since it is what brings about benefit on that day. Considering its persistence in both abodes, although there is no need for it as you know, and it has no bearing on bringing about benefit and reward, is something without basis. This reading is the one on which the majority (al-Jumhur, the majority of readers) agree, and it is the most fitting to the context and the flow of the noble text.

It has also been read as ﴿yawma﴾ (day) in the accusative. This may be either: a) that it is an adverbial complement of time (ẓarf) for "said," so that "this" then refers to His words, "Did you say…" etc.; or b) that it is the predicate of "this," in which case "this" refers to ʿIsā's reply, peace be upon him; that is, this reply from him, peace be upon him, takes place on the day when truthfulness benefits… etc.; or it refers to the question and the answer together.

It has been said: it is a predicate, but built on the fatha (vowel), and this is not correct according to the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun, the grammatical school of Basra), because it is annexed (muḍāf) to a declinable noun (mutamakkin).

It has also been read as ﴿yawmun﴾ with the nominative and tanwin (nunation), like His, exalted is He, words: ﴿And fear a day when no soul will avail another…﴾ (the verse).

﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾ is a resumptive statement brought to explain the benefit mentioned, as if it were said: "What is their benefit?" It was answered: "For them is lasting bliss and everlasting reward."

His, exalted is He, words: ﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾ are another resumptive statement, to explain that He, mighty and majestic, bestowed upon them, beyond the gardens mentioned, something of no value in comparison with it, namely His good pleasure (riḍwān), beyond which there is no end, as His words indicate: ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾, since there is nothing more honorable than it, so that the necks of aspirations might stretch toward it.

﴿That﴾ refers to attaining His good pleasure, exalted is He. It has been said it refers to attaining everything.

﴿is the great triumph﴾, because the greatness of the triumph follows the greatness of the object sought with which the triumph is connected, and you know that there is no goal beyond this at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 5, verse 120:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them﴾ is a confirmation of the truth and an alert to the falsehood of the Christians and the corruption of what they claimed concerning the Messiah and his mother. That is: to Him alone, exalted is He, belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, of rational beings and others. He disposes of them as He wills, by bringing into existence and annihilating, giving life and causing death, and commanding and forbidding, without anything among things having any part in that. The use of "ma" (what) rather than "man" (who), which is specific to rational beings, is, on the assumption that it covers all of them, an observance of the original usage, and an indication of the equality of the two groups in the impossibility of divinity, just as they are equal in the reality of being lordly creatures (marbubiyyah). And on the assumption that it is specific to non-rational beings, it is an alert to the utter deficiency of the Christians from the rank of divinity, and a humiliation of them by giving precedence to others over them.

﴿And He is over all things﴾ among things, ﴿Competent﴾, exceeding in power.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Ma'idah will be given the reward of ten good deeds, ten of his evil deeds will be erased, and ten degrees will be raised for him, according to the number of every Jew and Christian who breathes in the world."
